title: Standard MCQ pool
source: Built by scripts/build-duel-pack.mjs from public/mcq/pool.json and public/duel/mcq/: 593 ai, 144 usmle-resource, 56 amsa.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 35 weeks 4 days' gestation comes to the maternity assessment unit because her baby has moved much less than usual since the previous evening. Two years ago she had a stillbirth at 38 weeks, and that infant was small for gestational age. In this pregnancy she has diet-controlled gestational diabetes. A scan at 32 weeks showed an estimated weight on the 40th centile. She takes low-dose aspirin. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, pulse is 86/min, respirations are 16/min and temperature is 36.7 °C. Symphysis-fundal height is 35 cm. A urine dipstick shows no protein. A 40-minute cardiotocograph (CTG) shows a baseline rate of 135 bpm, baseline variability of 10 bpm, three accelerations of at least 15 bpm lasting at least 15 seconds, and no decelerations. She feels several movements during the trace. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day sonographic biometry and liquor volume assessment
Discharge with routine antenatal review at 37 weeks
Induction of labour today
Continuation of the CTG for a further 40 minutes
Maternal Kleihauer-Betke test
questions.why: Every feature of this CTG is normal by RANZCOG criteria: the baseline is 110 to 160 bpm, variability is 6 to 25 bpm, there are accelerations and there are no decelerations. Her observations and urinalysis show no sign of pre-eclampsia or infection. A normal CTG means the fetus is not hypoxic right now. It does not rule out underlying placental insufficiency or growth restriction, so it does not exclude a later poor outcome. The Stillbirth CRE guideline on decreased fetal movements says that when a woman has risk factors for growth restriction or stillbirth, she should have an ultrasound for fetal biometry and amniotic fluid volume, ideally within 24 hours, along with obstetric review. This woman has a previous small-for-gestational-age stillbirth and gestational diabetes. The scan should be arranged today. She should then be told to come back straight away, at any hour, if movements decrease again.
notes: Sending her home with routine follow-up treats the normal CTG as if it rules out compromise, which is unsafe in a woman with risk factors for stillbirth.
A single episode of reduced movements with a normal CTG and a normal assessment is not a reason for birth at 35 weeks, and preterm induction brings neonatal risks with no proven benefit.
The trace already meets every normal criterion with a good signal, so recording for longer adds no information about her placental reserve.
A Kleihauer-Betke test looks for fetomaternal haemorrhage, which would be suspected with a sinusoidal or abnormal trace, trauma or bleeding, and none of these is present here.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after vomiting about 400 mL of bright red blood at home. He has passed black stools for 2 days. He has drunk about 10 standard drinks of beer daily for 20 years, and his last drink was last night. He takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse is 116/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. He is alert and oriented. He has spider naevi on his chest and palmar erythema. The abdomen has shifting dullness, and the spleen tip is palpable. Two large-bore cannulas are inserted and a crystalloid bolus is started. Laboratory studies show: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130–180) Platelets 74 x10^9/L (150–400) INR 1.9 (0.9–1.2) Urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5–7.5) Creatinine 90 µmol/L (60–110) Albumin 26 g/L (35–50) The gastroenterology registrar plans endoscopy within the next few hours. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Terlipressin and ceftriaxone intravenously
Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR
Pantoprazole infusion as the only drug therapy
Red cell transfusion to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L
Sengstaken-Blakemore balloon tamponade tube
questions.why: This man has an upper GI bleed with features of decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis and portal hypertension: ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of chronic liver disease, low platelets, a raised INR and a low albumin. His tachycardia and borderline blood pressure point to significant blood loss. The bleed should be treated as variceal until endoscopy shows otherwise. Under Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) and Baveno VII, a vasoactive drug (terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 hours, or octreotide) should start as soon as a variceal bleed is suspected, before endoscopy. It lowers portal pressure, improves control of bleeding and reduces mortality. Patients with cirrhosis and GI bleeding should also get antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily). This reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and death. Endoscopic band ligation should follow within 12 hours. Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis, and the extra volume can raise portal pressure. A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does nothing for a variceal bleed and would delay vasoactive therapy and antibiotics.
notes: Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not predict bleeding in cirrhosis, eTG advises against routinely correcting it, and the extra volume raises portal pressure.
A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does not lower portal pressure or treat a variceal bleed, and it leaves out the vasoactive drug and antibiotics the guidelines require.
Transfusing to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L is wrong because the restrictive target is 70 to 80 g/L, and over-transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding.
Balloon tamponade is wrong because it is only a temporary rescue for bleeding that cannot be controlled after drug and endoscopic therapy, and endoscopy is already planned.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man presents to a general practice in Perth with a 7-week history of cough productive of yellow phlegm. For the past week the phlegm has been streaked with blood. He reports drenching night sweats and has lost 6 kg without trying. He was born in the Philippines, moved to Australia 4 years ago and works as a cleaner. He has no medical history, takes no regular medicines and has never smoked. His temperature is 37.9 °C, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There are crackles over the left upper zone, and there is no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. White cell count is 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), CRP is 41 mg/L (<5) and HIV serology is negative. A chest X-ray shows patchy opacification with a small cavity at the left apex. He has been given a surgical mask and moved to a separate room. Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Interferon-gamma release assay on peripheral blood
Tuberculin skin test read at 48 to 72 hours
Three sputum samples for acid-fast smear, culture and NAAT
Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest
Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage
questions.why: This man has had a productive cough for more than 3 weeks, with haemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss. He was born in a country with high TB rates, and his chest X-ray shows a cavity in the upper lobe. This is active pulmonary tuberculosis until proven otherwise. The X-ray supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm it. Confirmation needs microbiology. The Australian guidelines (CDNA SoNG, the state TB programs and eTG Antibiotic) recommend 3 sputum samples collected at least 8 hours apart, with at least 1 taken first thing in the morning. Each sample has acid-fast bacilli smear microscopy, mycobacterial culture and a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT, such as Xpert MTB/RIF). Smear microscopy and NAAT give a quick answer. NAAT also tells M. tuberculosis apart from non-tuberculous mycobacteria and detects rifampicin resistance. Culture is the gold standard and gives full drug-susceptibility results. A cavity usually means a high bacterial load, so expectorated sputum is very likely to be positive. The samples should be collected outdoors or in a well-ventilated room, away from other people. He also needs urgent referral to the state TB service and notification.
notes: An interferon-gamma release assay shows immune sensitisation to M. tuberculosis, but it cannot tell latent infection from active disease, and a negative result does not exclude active TB.
A tuberculin skin test cannot tell latent infection from active disease, can be falsely positive after BCG vaccination (common in people born in the Philippines), and needs a second visit.
CT shows the cavity and the extent of disease in more detail, but it provides no microbiological confirmation or susceptibility results and does not change the need for sputum testing.

Bronchoscopy with lavage is invasive and carries a risk of spreading infection to staff, so it is kept for patients who cannot produce sputum or whose sputum samples are negative despite strong suspicion.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of burning central chest pain that began 90 minutes after a large dinner. For 6 weeks he has had similar pain on most evenings. It is worse when he lies flat and partly eased by over-the-counter antacids, and he has acid regurgitation. For the past month, bread and steak have felt as if they stick behind his sternum. His weight has fallen from 84 kg to 79 kg over 3 months without dieting. He drinks about 4 standard drinks daily, stopped smoking 10 years ago and takes no regular medicines. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 98% on room air. He has mild epigastric tenderness and no palpable lymph nodes. A 12-lead ECG recorded during pain is normal. High-sensitivity troponin I is 2 ng/L at 0 hours and 2 ng/L at 2 hours (99th percentile 26 ng/L). Haemoglobin is 136 g/L (reference 130 to 180 g/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Eight-week trial of a proton pump inhibitor
Computed tomography coronary angiography
Barium swallow with fluoroscopy
Urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori
Urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
questions.why: The ECG taken during pain is normal, and high-sensitivity troponin is very low and unchanged at 0 and 2 hours, so acute MI is ruled out and this man is at low risk of acute coronary syndrome. His symptoms fit gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: burning retrosternal pain after meals that is worse lying flat, with acid regurgitation. He also has two alarm features. One is new dysphagia to solids. The other is unintentional loss of 5 kg, which is about 6% of his body weight. Daily alcohol and past smoking add to his risk. Under Therapeutic Guidelines (Gastrointestinal), alarm features call for an urgent gastroscopy rather than empirical treatment. The aim is to find or rule out the serious complications of reflux, such as peptic stricture, Barrett's oesophagus and oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and to take biopsies. The most important thing to prevent here is a missed or late diagnosis of cancer. A PPI can be started after the scope is booked, but it does not replace the scope.
notes: An empirical PPI trial is only for reflux without alarm features, and it can ease symptoms and heal the mucosa, which delays and hides the diagnosis of cancer.
A normal ECG during pain and unchanged troponin well below the 99th percentile mean he is low risk, and his symptoms are not cardiac, so coronary imaging does not deal with the main danger.
A barium swallow can show narrowing but cannot take a biopsy, and it is not first-line for dysphagia with weight loss, so it would only delay the gastroscopy he needs.
Test-and-treat for H. pylori is for dyspepsia without alarm features, and it does not investigate dysphagia or weight loss.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man is reviewed on the surgical ward on the morning he is due to go home. Two days ago he came to the emergency department after suddenly passing a large volume of painless maroon blood with clots. He had one more small bleed in the department and none since. He has type 2 diabetes and knee osteoarthritis. He takes metformin. For the past 3 months he has also taken an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory tablet most days for knee pain. He takes no other medicines. Today his temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. His abdomen is soft and not tender. Haemoglobin is 118 g/L (his baseline is 138 g/L; reference range 130 to 180 g/L). Colonoscopy after bowel preparation showed many diverticula in the sigmoid and descending colon, with no inflammation, active bleeding, polyp or tumour. He asks how he can lower the chance of this happening again. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to reduce his risk of recurrent bleeding?
options: Avoid nuts, seeds and popcorn
Begin regular oral mesalazine
Switch his analgesia to paracetamol
Add a proton pump inhibitor
Book an elective sigmoid colectomy
questions.why: This man had a self-limiting diverticular bleed. It was sudden, painless and large, with maroon blood and clots, and colonoscopy showed diverticulosis with no other source. Diverticular bleeding often recurs, in roughly 20 to 40% of patients over the following years. Non-aspirin NSAIDs are a well-established risk factor that can be changed. They raise the risk of a first diverticular bleed and of a repeat bleed. The British Society of Gastroenterology lower GI bleeding guideline advises stopping non-aspirin NSAIDs after a diverticular bleed, and Australian guidance (eTG) also advises avoiding NSAIDs in diverticular disease. The over-the-counter anti-inflammatory he takes every day should therefore be stopped, and regular paracetamol used for his osteoarthritis pain instead. Other sensible advice is a high-fibre diet with enough fluid, and returning urgently if he bleeds again. Avoiding nuts and seeds is an old myth, and large cohort studies show no added risk of bleeding or diverticulitis. Mesalazine does not prevent diverticular bleeding or recurrent diverticulitis.
notes: Studies show nuts, seeds and popcorn do not raise the risk of diverticular bleeding or diverticulitis, so this restriction does not help.
Mesalazine has no proven role in preventing diverticular bleeding or recurrent diverticular disease.
A proton pump inhibitor protects against upper GI bleeding from NSAIDs but does nothing for bleeding from colonic diverticula.
Elective colectomy is kept for recurrent or uncontrollable bleeding and is not offered after a first bleed that stopped by itself.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, comes to the fetal medicine clinic at 17 weeks pregnant to discuss her amniocentesis result. She conceived naturally. At 10 weeks, whole-genome cell-free DNA screening (fetal fraction 11%) showed a low chance of trisomies 21, 18 and 13 and of sex chromosome conditions, and a high chance of trisomy 16. A 7-week scan had shown one gestational sac. The 12-week scan was normal, with a nuchal translucency of 1.4 mm. Amniocentesis at 16 weeks, with QF-PCR and chromosomal microarray, showed a normal female result with no trisomy 16. Both of her previous pregnancies were uncomplicated. She has no medical history, does not smoke, and takes folic acid and iodine. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Ultrasound today shows a single live fetus with biometry consistent with dates, no anomaly seen, normal amniotic fluid and a high posterior placenta. She is blood group O RhD positive, and her antibody screen is negative. This patient is at greatest risk of which of the following complications later in this pregnancy?
options: Gestational diabetes mellitus
Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
Intrauterine growth restriction
Polyhydramnios
Red cell alloimmunisation
questions.why: The screening result was valid (adequate fetal fraction) and showed a high chance of trisomy 16, but amniocentesis found a chromosomally normal fetus. The vanishing twin explanation is unlikely because she conceived naturally and an early scan showed one sac. The most likely explanation is therefore confined placental mosaicism (CPM): the trisomic cells are in the placenta, which supplies most of the cell-free DNA. RANZCOG/HGSA (C-Obs 59) and ISPD advise amniocentesis rather than CVS for rare autosomal trisomies for exactly this reason, because the placenta itself is likely to be abnormal. CPM involving chromosome 16 is strongly linked with placental dysfunction, which raises the risk of intrauterine growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and stillbirth. A normal amniocentesis result means the fetus is reassuring, but the pregnancy is still high risk. She needs continued care with a fetal medicine or obstetric team, serial growth and Doppler scans in the second half of pregnancy, blood pressure monitoring, and counselling to report reduced fetal movements. Many units also consider low-dose aspirin.
notes: Her only risk factor is mild advanced maternal age, with a normal BMI and uncomplicated previous pregnancies, and placental mosaicism does not cause gestational diabetes.
After amniocentesis, leaking of fluid is uncommon and usually happens within days, so a procedure done a week ago with normal fluid today adds little later risk.
Placental dysfunction from trisomy 16 mosaicism tends to reduce amniotic fluid rather than increase it, and no fetal anomaly or diabetes is present to cause polyhydramnios.
She is RhD positive with a negative antibody screen, so the invasive procedure carries essentially no risk of clinically important sensitisation.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman has been on the stroke unit for 2 days. She woke on the day of admission unable to see objects on her right. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and is otherwise well. Atorvastatin 80 mg daily was started on admission. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 86/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 142/84 mm Hg and weight 68 kg. Each eye tested separately shows a congruous right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. She has no limb weakness, sensory loss or dysphasia. MRI brain shows a 30 × 20 mm acute infarct in the left medial occipital lobe with no haemorrhage on susceptibility-weighted imaging. MR angiography shows an occluded left P2 segment and no carotid stenosis. ECG shows atrial fibrillation; an ECG 3 years ago showed sinus rhythm. Echocardiography shows no valve disease. Haemoglobin is 134 g/L, platelets 241 x10^9/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L (eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73m²) and INR 1.0. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy to reduce her risk of recurrent stroke?
options: Apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily
Aspirin 100 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg orally daily
Aspirin 100 mg orally daily
Enoxaparin bridging to warfarin, target INR 2 to 3
Apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily
questions.why: This woman has had a cardioembolic posterior cerebral artery infarct caused by newly found non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is at least 5 (age 75 or over, hypertension, stroke), so her biggest risk is another embolic stroke. The Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management and eTG recommend oral anticoagulation, preferably with a DOAC rather than warfarin, for ischaemic stroke with AF. The stroke team times the start by infarct size, and with no haemorrhage on MRI an early start is reasonable. Apixaban is reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily only if two of these apply: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more. She meets none, so she needs the full dose of 5 mg twice daily. Underdosing is a common error that leaves patients unprotected. Antiplatelet therapy, alone or in combination, does much less to prevent AF-related stroke and does not replace anticoagulation. Bridging with heparin raises the risk of bleeding, including haemorrhagic change in the infarct, and gives no extra protection.
notes: Wrong: she meets none of the criteria for the reduced dose, so 2.5 mg twice daily would underdose her and leave her poorly protected from another embolic stroke.
Wrong: short-term dual antiplatelet therapy is for minor non-cardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA, and it prevents AF-related stroke much less well than anticoagulation while still causing bleeding.
Wrong: aspirin alone gives little protection from cardioembolic stroke in AF and is not a substitute for anticoagulation in a patient without contraindications.
Wrong: DOACs are preferred to warfarin in non-valvular AF, and heparin bridging after an acute infarct raises the risk of haemorrhagic transformation without lowering early recurrence.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner because of headaches for 7 weeks. They began when she started working 12-hour shifts at a desk to meet the end-of-financial-year deadline at her accounting firm. Before this she had only occasional mild headaches. The headache is a bilateral, band-like tightness that builds through the afternoon. She rates it 4/10. It now comes on every afternoon. She has no nausea or photophobia, and climbing stairs does not make it worse. She takes paracetamol 1 g about five times a week and ibuprofen 400 mg once or twice a week, which takes the edge off it. She drinks four standard drinks a week and does not smoke. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse is 74/min and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Her trapezius and temporalis muscles are tender. Passive neck flexion is full and painless. Fundoscopy shows sharp discs with venous pulsations, and the neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to prevent progression of her headache disorder?
options: Switch to paracetamol with codeine on headache days
Take ibuprofen 400 mg regularly three times a day
Start amitriptyline 10 mg each night as prevention
Use sumatriptan 50 mg at the onset of each attack
Limit acute pain relief to fewer than 10 days per month
questions.why: This woman has tension-type headache: it is bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate and not made worse by activity, she has no nausea or photophobia, her pericranial muscles are tender, and it started with a clear trigger (long hours at a desk under deadline stress). Her examination, including fundoscopy, is normal. The main risk for her is medication-overuse headache. She is already taking simple analgesics on about 25 to 35 days in every 4 weeks. ICHD-3 defines medication-overuse headache as headache on 15 or more days a month with regular overuse for more than 3 months. The threshold is 15 or more days a month for simple analgesics, and 10 or more days a month for triptans, opioids or combination analgesics. At 7 weeks she has not met the time criterion yet, but she is well over the frequency threshold. Following eTG, she should keep acute treatment to fewer than 10 days a month (roughly 2 to 3 days a week), keep a headache diary, and avoid codeine. Treatment should be mainly non-drug: posture and ergonomics, regular breaks, sleep, exercise, physiotherapy and stress management.
notes: Codeine-containing combination products cause medication-overuse headache at a lower threshold (10 or more days a month), cause dependence, and eTG advises avoiding opioids in tension-type headache.
Taking ibuprofen regularly every day guarantees analgesic overuse, which raises her risk of medication-overuse headache as well as gastrointestinal and kidney harm.
Preventive amitriptyline is kept for established chronic tension-type headache that has not responded to non-drug measures, and it does nothing about her current analgesic overuse.
Triptans do not work for tension-type headache and cause medication-overuse headache at only 10 or more days a month, so taking one with every daily attack would make things worse.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a 1-day history of worsening headache, fever, vomiting and photophobia. For 5 days before this he had right ear pain. He has no medical history, takes no medicines and has no allergies. His temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, respirations 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. He is alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. He has neck stiffness, no rash, sharp optic discs and no focal neurological deficit. The right tympanic membrane is red and bulging. Blood cultures are taken and a lumbar puncture is done. Ceftriaxone 2 g and dexamethasone 10 mg are given straight after the procedure. Results: Blood: leucocytes 19.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 185 mg/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L CSF: turbid; opening pressure 28 cmH2O; white cells 1900 x10^6/L (90% polymorphs); red cells 6 x10^6/L; protein 2.1 g/L (0.15 to 0.45); glucose 1.2 mmol/L; Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
options: Add amoxicillin
Add aciclovir
Stop dexamethasone
Switch to benzylpenicillin
Add vancomycin
questions.why: The CSF is turbid, with many polymorphs, a high protein and a CSF:serum glucose ratio of 1.2/6.0 = 0.2 (below 0.4), so this is bacterial meningitis. Gram-positive diplococci mean Streptococcus pneumoniae, and the probable source is his right acute otitis media. Some pneumococci have reduced susceptibility to penicillin and ceftriaxone. So eTG advises adding vancomycin to ceftriaxone as soon as Gram-positive diplococci are seen, and continuing both until susceptibility results are back. Treatment is then narrowed to suit the organism. Dexamethasone should continue for 4 days, because it gives the most benefit in pneumococcal meningitis. Amoxicillin covers Listeria and is added only for patients at risk: those over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised or with alcohol dependence. He has none of these risks, and Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus, not a diplococcus. Aciclovir is not needed: he has no confusion, seizures or focal signs, and the CSF picture is clearly bacterial with organisms seen. Changing to benzylpenicillin before susceptibility is known risks undertreating a resistant strain.
notes: Amoxicillin covers Listeria, which shows as Gram-positive bacilli and is a risk only in people over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised or alcohol-dependent, and he is none of these.
Aciclovir treats HSV encephalitis, but he has no encephalitic features and the CSF is clearly bacterial, with organisms seen.
Dexamethasone should continue for 4 days in pneumococcal meningitis because this is the organism where it most reduces death and hearing loss.
Narrowing to benzylpenicillin is done only after susceptibility testing confirms a sensitive strain, so changing now could undertreat a resistant pneumococcus.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department of a rural hospital 3 hours after central chest pressure began. The pain spreads to his left arm, and he has sweating and nausea. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He drinks about 4 standard drinks per week and has had no falls, injections or strenuous exercise. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 150/92 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Jugular venous pressure is not raised, the chest is clear, and there is no hepatomegaly or peripheral oedema. An ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V4. A chest X-ray shows clear lungs. Blood taken from a newly inserted cannula shows: potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2); bilirubin 10 µmol/L (<20); ALT 28 U/L (<45); AST 71 U/L (<35); ALP 80 U/L (30–110); GGT 30 U/L (<50); creatine kinase 590 U/L (<200); hs-troponin T 210 ng/L (<14). Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's aspartate aminotransferase (AST) result?
options: Alcohol-related hepatocellular injury
Release from necrotic cardiac muscle
Congestive hepatopathy from venous back-pressure
In vitro haemolysis of the blood sample
Release from injured skeletal muscle
questions.why: The AST is raised on its own. ALT, bilirubin, ALP and GGT are all normal, and this happens alongside an anterior STEMI, a raised creatine kinase and an hs-troponin T well above the 99th percentile. AST is found in cardiac muscle as well as in liver and skeletal muscle. It leaks from infarcting myocardium, which is why it was once used as a cardiac marker. ALT is much more specific to the liver, so a normal ALT with a normal cholestatic profile points away from liver disease. Here the AST is best read as part of the myocardial infarction. It does not need liver work-up, and it must not delay reperfusion. Troponin, not AST, is the marker to follow for myocardial injury.
notes: Wrong: an AST:ALT ratio above 2 can suggest alcohol, but he drinks very little, and his GGT and ALT are normal.
Wrong: congestive hepatopathy needs raised right-sided pressures, but his JVP is normal, there is no hepatomegaly or oedema, his lungs are clear, and ALT and bilirubin would usually rise too.
Wrong: in vitro haemolysis would also raise the potassium, which is normal at 4.1 mmol/L, and the sample came from a fresh cannula.
Wrong: he has had no trauma, falls, injections or exertion, and the raised troponin with ST elevation places the enzyme source in the heart, not skeletal muscle.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 50 minutes of heavy central chest pain that began while she was watching television. Over the past fortnight her known angina has come on with less exertion, and she now needs glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) most days. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, and takes metformin, perindopril, atorvastatin and aspirin. In the ED she has received aspirin 300 mg, three sublingual GTN doses and intravenous morphine, and an intravenous GTN infusion has been titrated for the past 20 minutes. She still rates the pain 7/10 and is diaphoretic. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg in both arms, respirations 18/min and SpO2 96% on room air. Two 12-lead ECGs taken 15 minutes apart show sinus rhythm with no ST-segment or T-wave changes. High-sensitivity troponin I, taken 40 minutes after onset, is 9 ng/L (99th percentile for women 16 ng/L). Chest X-ray is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Repeat high-sensitivity troponin in 1 hour
Intravenous tenecteplase bolus given now
Invasive coronary angiography within 2 hours
Computed tomography coronary angiography
Exercise stress electrocardiogram tomorrow
questions.why: This woman has a non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome. She has crescendo angina and prolonged rest pain. Her pain is still going after aspirin, repeated sublingual GTN, opioid and a titrated IV GTN infusion. The 2016 National Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS guideline, which eTG follows, classes ongoing or recurrent ischaemic pain that does not respond to medical treatment as very high risk. This applies whatever the ECG or troponin shows. Very high-risk patients need invasive coronary angiography, with revascularisation if indicated, within 2 hours. Arrange this urgently with cardiology, including the choice of P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulant. A normal ECG and a normal troponin taken 40 minutes after onset do not lower her risk, because both can be normal early in a myocardial infarction. Repeat troponin, CT coronary angiography and stress testing are for patients whose pain has settled and who are at low or intermediate risk. Fibrinolysis is only for STEMI.
notes: Serial troponin helps decide between unstable angina and NSTEMI, but the result would not change her management, because refractory pain already makes her very high risk.
Fibrinolysis gives no benefit and may cause harm in non-ST-elevation ACS, and her ECGs show no ST elevation.
CT coronary angiography is for stable, pain-free patients at low or intermediate risk, not for ongoing ischaemia that needs treatment in the catheter laboratory.
Stress testing is contraindicated while rest pain continues, and putting off assessment until tomorrow is unsafe in very high-risk ACS.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 5 months of worsening breathlessness. Over this time he has lost 20 kg, has coughed up blood-tinged sputum and his voice has become hoarse. He has COPD, and his triple-therapy inhaler has not helped. He has smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 50 years and worked for decades as a mechanic. His temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse is 110/min, respirations are 29/min, blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg and SpO2 is 92% on room air. He has finger clubbing and a hard right supraclavicular lymph node. On the right side of the chest, expansion is reduced, percussion is stony dull and breath sounds are absent. The trachea is deviated to the left. An erect PA chest X-ray, not rotated, shows a large right effusion with a meniscus reaching the 2nd anterior rib, which obscures the right heart border and hilum. The trachea and mediastinum are displaced to the left. The left lung is clear. Which of the following best explains the position of the trachea and mediastinum on this film?
options: Volume loss from lobar collapse
Compression by the accumulated fluid
Fixation by encasing pleural tumour
Hyperinflation of the left lung
Paratracheal nodal mass displacing the airway
questions.why: The film shows a large right effusion with the trachea and mediastinum pushed to the left, away from the fluid. Being pushed away from the fluid means the effusion has a mass effect: the fluid takes up enough space in the right hemithorax to move the mediastinum across. For this patient, it means the shift is not explained by a major right-sided collapse, so a central obstructing tumour has not pulled the mediastinum back towards the right. It also means the mediastinum is not held in place by pleural tumour. So ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration (no more than about 1.5 L at a time) is likely to ease his breathlessness, and it also gives fluid for diagnosis. A contrast CT chest should ideally be done before the effusion is fully drained. If a very large effusion had no shift, or the mediastinum had moved towards the effusion, that would suggest lobar or lung collapse from an endobronchial tumour, or a mediastinum fixed by mesothelioma or malignant nodes. In that case drainage would help less and could cause problems, and bronchoscopy should be considered. Tension pneumothorax is ruled out because the film shows a meniscus, not air.
notes: Collapse causes volume loss, which pulls the trachea and mediastinum towards the affected (right) side, not away from it.
A mediastinum encased by pleural tumour, as in mesothelioma, cannot move, so a large effusion would cause little or no shift.
Hyperinflation in COPD affects both lungs and does not push the mediastinum sideways, and the left lung is described as clear.
A paratracheal nodal mass widens the mediastinum and may narrow the trachea, but it would not shift the whole mediastinum away from a large right effusion.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner to discuss blood test results. She has had four months of tiredness, cold intolerance, constipation and weight gain of 5 kg. She has had type 1 diabetes since age 11 and uses insulin glargine and insulin aspart. She drinks about 4 standard drinks a week and rarely eats fresh vegetables. Her pulse is 58/min and blood pressure 114/72 mm Hg. She has a diffuse, firm, non-tender goitre and delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes. Vibration sense, joint position sense and gait are normal. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115–165) MCV 116 fL (80–100) TSH 38 mIU/L (0.4–4.0) Free T4 5.1 pmol/L (10–20) Anti-TPO antibodies strongly positive Morning cortisol 430 nmol/L (normal) Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L Serum folate 4.0 nmol/L (above 7) Serum vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor antibodies: pending Levothyroxine is started. A colleague suggests also starting oral folic acid 5 mg daily today. Starting folic acid on its own before the pending results return puts her at greatest risk of which of the following?
options: Hypokalaemia causing a cardiac arrhythmia
Adrenal crisis from unmasked cortisol deficiency
Secondary iron overload from rapid erythropoiesis
Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
Gastric adenocarcinoma from atrophic gastritis
questions.why: She has autoimmune (Hashimoto) hypothyroidism and type 1 diabetes, so she is at high risk of pernicious anaemia, another autoimmune disease. An MCV of 116 fL is too high to blame on hypothyroidism alone, and her B12 result is still pending. Folic acid alone can correct the blood count in B12 deficiency, but it does nothing for the nerve damage. So the anaemia looks better while B12-related demyelination of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts (subacute combined degeneration) gets worse, and that damage can be permanent. Australian guidance (eTG) says folate must not be given alone until B12 deficiency has been ruled out or is being treated. A low folate with a normal neurological examination does not remove this risk, because she could be low in both. Safe options are to wait for the B12 result or to give B12 alongside folate.
notes: Low potassium from rapid red cell production happens mainly when severe megaloblastic anaemia is treated with B12, and it is unlikely with her mild anaemia and normal potassium.
Adrenal crisis is the risk when levothyroxine, not folic acid, is started in untreated Addison disease, and her normal morning cortisol and electrolytes make adrenal insufficiency unlikely.
Correcting megaloblastic anaemia uses up iron and can cause iron deficiency, not iron overload.
Gastric cancer is a long-term risk of pernicious anaemia itself, and starting folic acid neither causes it nor speeds it up.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman sees her general practitioner because her breathlessness has been getting worse for 6 weeks. She now gets breathless walking to her letterbox. She sleeps on three pillows and wakes at night gasping for air. She has had no chest pain, sweating or palpitations. She had a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction 5 months ago and has had hypertension for 30 years. Her medicines are aspirin, atorvastatin, perindopril and metoprolol. Her pulse is 100/min and regular, blood pressure is 158/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 22/min and SpO2 is 94% on room air. Her jugular venous pressure is raised, her apex beat is displaced and there are crackles at both lung bases. Serum potassium is 4.3 mmol/L (reference 3.5 to 5.2). A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm at 100/min and a QRS duration of 94 ms. The S wave in V1 plus the R wave in V5 measures 41 mm. There is downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T-wave inversion in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. These changes are the same as on her ECG at hospital discharge 5 months ago. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the ST-segment and T-wave changes on this ECG?
options: Subendocardial ischaemia from a new acute coronary syndrome
Delayed ventricular depolarisation from left bundle branch block
Abnormal repolarisation caused by a low serum potassium
Left ventricular hypertrophy with secondary repolarisation changes
Characteristic ST-segment scooping caused by digoxin therapy
questions.why: The S wave in V1 plus the R wave in V5 adds up to 41 mm, which is more than the Sokolow-Lyon threshold of 35 mm. This meets the voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). With LVH, downsloping ST depression and asymmetric T-wave inversion in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) is the classic secondary repolarisation ('strain') pattern. It fits her 30 years of hypertension and her displaced apex. The changes are the same as on her discharge ECG 5 months ago, so they are long-standing and not acute. Her new decompensated heart failure still needs hospital assessment, including a troponin and an echocardiogram. The ECG itself, though, shows chronic changes from LVH, not new ischaemia. New ischaemia is unlikely because there is no chest pain and the ST-T changes are the same as 5 months ago, although a troponin is still needed. Left bundle branch block is excluded because the QRS is 94 ms, and the diagnosis needs a QRS of 120 ms or more. Hypokalaemia is excluded because her potassium is normal at 4.3 mmol/L; it also typically causes U waves and flattened T waves.
notes: There is no chest pain and the ST-T changes are the same as on the discharge ECG, so they do not point to new ischaemia, although a troponin is still needed.
A QRS duration of 94 ms rules out left bundle branch block, which needs a QRS of at least 120 ms.
Her serum potassium is normal at 4.3 mmol/L, and hypokalaemia typically causes U waves and flattened T waves, not this pattern.
She does not take digoxin, and digoxin causes a scooped ST segment, not asymmetric lateral T-wave inversion with high QRS voltages.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of thirst, polyuria and weight loss, and 1 day of vomiting. He has no past medical history. He weighs 36 kg. His first venous blood gas shows pH 6.98, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L, glucose 34.0 mmol/L and sodium 131 mmol/L. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is 6.8 mmol/L and urea is 13.2 mmol/L. Fluid replacement is started, and 1 hour later an insulin infusion is started at 0.1 units/kg/h. Five hours after arrival he says he has a severe headache, vomits, and becomes irritable and confused. His pulse is 58/min (130/min on arrival), blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg, respirations are 26/min, SpO2 is 98% on room air and temperature is 36.9 °C. GCS is 11 (E3 V3 M5). His pupils are equal and reactive. Repeat glucose is 15.2 mmol/L and sodium is 129 mmol/L. The head of the bed is raised and the fluid rate is reduced. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain now
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV over 1 hour
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Mannitol 0.5 g/kg IV over 20 minutes
Cease the insulin infusion until review
questions.why: This boy has severe DKA as his first presentation of type 1 diabetes. He has the main risk factors for cerebral oedema: young age, new diagnosis, pH below 7.1, a high urea, and a sodium that is falling instead of rising as the glucose comes down. Several hours into treatment he has a headache, vomiting, a falling GCS and a new low heart rate with high blood pressure (Cushing response). This is a clinical diagnosis of cerebral oedema. The RCH DKA guideline says to treat it straight away, without waiting for imaging. Raise the head of the bed, reduce the fluid rate, and give mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg (2.5 to 5 mL/kg of 20%) IV over 20 minutes. Hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg is an alternative. Call ICU early for airway support, and do a CT only after he is stable, to look for other causes such as a clot or bleed. CT now is wrong because imaging delays treatment that can save his life, and cerebral oedema is diagnosed clinically. Sodium bicarbonate is wrong because it does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself linked to cerebral oedema. Dexamethasone is wrong because steroids do not help this kind of brain swelling and they make hyperglycaemia worse.
notes: Wrong: CT delays urgent treatment for a diagnosis made clinically; image only once he is stable.
Wrong: bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself a risk factor for cerebral oedema.
Wrong: corticosteroids have no role in cerebral oedema from DKA and would worsen his hyperglycaemia.
Wrong: insulin is still needed to clear the ketosis, and stopping it does not treat the raised intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after a sudden, severe occipital headache that began while he was jogging. Two weeks ago he had a severe headache that settled within 30 minutes. He has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and hypertension, treated with perindopril. On arrival, his temperature is 37.3 °C, pulse 82/min, respirations 16/min, blood pressure 140/85 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13 (E3 V4 M6). He has neck stiffness and bilateral subhyaloid haemorrhages on fundoscopy, and no focal deficit. INR is 1.0 and platelets are 245 x10^9/L. Non-contrast CT shows diffuse blood in the basal cisterns, spreading into the ventricles, with dilated temporal horns. CT angiography shows a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Forty-five minutes later he vomits. His GCS is now 11 (E3 V3 M5), pulse 48/min, blood pressure 204/96 mm Hg and respirations 12/min and irregular. His pupils are still equal and reactive. Which of the following best explains the change in his vital signs?
options: Delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm
Cushing reflex from brainstem compression
Hypertensive emergency from renal disease
Vagal response to repeated vomiting
Neurogenic stunned myocardium from catecholamines
questions.why: This man has an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Blood has spread into his ventricles, and the dilated temporal horns show early hydrocephalus. Since arrival his GCS has fallen. He now has a rising systolic pressure, a slow heart rate and irregular breathing. This is Cushing's triad, a late sign that intracranial pressure is raised and the brainstem is being compressed, which means coning is imminent. Equal pupils do not rule this out, because pupil changes can come late. Do not read the rising blood pressure as something to treat on its own. It is the brain's attempt to keep up cerebral perfusion pressure, and lowering it hard could make ischaemia worse. Under eTG guidance and the Between the Flags criteria, this needs an immediate rapid response call, airway assessment, the head of the bed raised to 30 degrees, and an urgent neurosurgical review for an external ventricular drain. Delayed cerebral ischaemia usually happens on days 3 to 14, not within hours of the bleed. A hypertensive emergency does not explain the slow heart rate or the fall in GCS, and on arrival his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg.
notes: Wrong: delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm typically happens on days 3 to 14 after the bleed, not 3 hours after the headache began.
Wrong: a hypertensive emergency would not cause a falling heart rate or irregular breathing, and his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg before his GCS fell.
Wrong: a vagal response to vomiting slows the heart but lowers the blood pressure, and it would not cause a lasting fall in GCS or irregular breathing.
Wrong: neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge usually causes a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and pulmonary oedema, not a slow heart rate with severe hypertension.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father with 4 days of forceful vomiting after every feed. The vomit is milky and has never been green. He feeds eagerly straight after vomiting and has had 2 wet nappies in the past 24 hours. He was born at term and is formula fed. He weighs 4.5 kg, down from 4.9 kg 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 172/min, respirations 38/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is drowsy but rouses to voice. His hands and feet are cool and capillary refill time is 3 seconds. A peripheral cannula is placed. Venous gas: pH 7.53 (7.32 to 7.42), bicarbonate 37 mmol/L (20 to 28), lactate 1.1 mmol/L (under 2.0), Na 133 mmol/L (135 to 145), K 2.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), Cl 86 mmol/L (95 to 110), glucose 4.3 mmol/L. Ultrasound shows a pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm and a channel length of 18 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: 0.45% sodium chloride with 2.5% glucose at 18 mL/h intravenously
0.9% sodium chloride 45 mL intravenously over 15 minutes
Potassium chloride 2.25 mmol intravenously over 1 hour
Hydrocortisone 25 mg intravenously as a single dose
Laparoscopic pyloromyotomy on the next available list
questions.why: This boy has hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. The ultrasound shows a muscle wall of 5 mm or more (abnormal is 3 mm or more) and a channel of 18 mm (abnormal is 15 mm or more), and he has the typical hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. He is also in compensated shock: he is tachycardic, drowsy and cool at the hands and feet, with a capillary refill time of 3 seconds, while his blood pressure is still normal. Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency but a surgical urgency, not a surgical emergency. The first step is to treat the shock. Keep him nil by mouth and give a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride (45 mL for 4.5 kg), then reassess. After that, give 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose for maintenance plus deficit, and add potassium once he is passing urine (RCH Pyloric stenosis, Dehydration and Intravenous fluids guidelines). Surgery waits until the bicarbonate and chloride are back to normal, because operating while he is still alkalotic risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.
notes: Correct: compensated shock needs a 10 mL/kg isotonic bolus first, here 45 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride, with reassessment afterwards.
Wrong: potassium is replaced only after perfusion is restored and he is passing urine, and it does not treat the shock.
Wrong: his low potassium and alkalosis are the opposite of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which causes a high potassium and an acidosis, so steroids are not needed.
Wrong: pyloromyotomy should wait until shock and the alkalosis are corrected, because operating sooner risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.

questions.stem: A 22-month-old boy is brought to a general practice in regional Victoria with a 6-week history of cough. The cough is wet and happens by day and by night. It has not improved with 7 days of amoxicillin or with inhaled salbutamol through a spacer. His mother remembers that the cough started on the evening of a family barbecue. While eating popcorn there, he coughed and gagged for a short time and then settled. He has no eczema and no previous wheeze. He is fully immunised and has had no contact with tuberculosis. He is playful. His temperature is 37.3 °C, pulse 120/min, respirations 38/min, and SpO2 96% in room air. On examination there is reduced air entry and a fixed monophonic wheeze over the left lower zone only. A chest X-ray shows a hyperinflated left lung with the mediastinum shifted to the right. No radio-opaque object is seen. If the underlying cause is not treated, this child is most at risk of which of the following complications?
options: Tension pneumothorax
Tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Pulmonary arterial hypertension
Persistent atopic asthma
Left lower lobe bronchiectasis
questions.why: This toddler has an inhaled foreign body, most likely a popcorn kernel, in the left lower lobe bronchus. The clues are a choking episode at the start, a cough that has lasted weeks despite antibiotics and bronchodilators, one-sided monophonic wheeze with reduced air entry, and air trapping on the same side with the mediastinum pushed away. Organic objects are radiolucent, so a normal-looking X-ray does not rule out the diagnosis. Organic material left in the bronchus causes ongoing local inflammation, granulation tissue and infection beyond the blockage. This leads to recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe and then permanent damage to the airway: bronchiectasis. The risk goes up the longer the object stays in. This is why the RCH guideline recommends prompt rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia at a paediatric centre, rather than more courses of antibiotics or inhalers. Tension pneumothorax is a rare acute event, not the expected result of an object left in place. Tracheo-oesophageal fistula is a complication of an oesophageal foreign body, especially a button battery, not a bronchial one.
notes: Wrong: air trapping can rarely rupture into the pleura, but this is an uncommon acute event and not the usual consequence of a retained object.
Wrong: a fistula forms when an oesophageal foreign body such as a button battery erodes into the trachea, not from an object in the bronchus.
Wrong: pulmonary arterial hypertension needs widespread lung or vascular disease, and one blocked lobe does not cause it.
Wrong: a foreign body does not cause atopic asthma, and this child has no atopy, no earlier wheeze and no response to salbutamol.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of yellow eyes and dark urine. Two weeks ago he developed fever, anorexia and aching wrists and knees, which have since eased. He had unprotected sex with a new partner 3 months ago. He takes no medicines and drinks 6 standard drinks a week. Temperature is 37.6 °C, BP 124/78 mmHg, pulse 88/min and respiratory rate 14/min. He is alert, with scleral icterus, a tender smooth liver edge and no asterixis, and he is tolerating oral fluids. Bilirubin is 142 µmol/L (<20), ALT 2140 U/L (<40), ALP 165 U/L (30–110) and INR 1.1 (0.9–1.2). Paracetamol is undetectable. Ultrasound shows a 4 mm common bile duct without stones. HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc are positive, anti-HBs is negative, and hepatitis A IgM and HCV antibody are negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Oral tenofovir disoproxil
Supportive care and repeat hepatic testing in clinic
Subcutaneous peginterferon alfa
Intravenous acetylcysteine infusion
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
questions.why: This man has acute hepatitis B. He had a likely sexual exposure within the 1 to 6 month incubation period, then a prodrome with arthralgia, then jaundice. His tests show a hepatocellular pattern, and HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc are positive. His liver is still working well: INR is 1.1, he is alert with no asterixis, and he is drinking. So he has no features of severe hepatitis or acute liver failure. More than 95% of immunocompetent adults with acute hepatitis B clear the virus on their own. Therapeutic Guidelines and ASHM recommend supportive care for these patients. That means avoiding alcohol and liver-toxic drugs, and repeating LFTs and INR regularly until they improve, with safety-netting advice to return if he becomes confused, starts bleeding or vomits persistently. The doctor must also notify the case, arrange contact tracing (testing, vaccination, and HBIG for non-immune contacts), and repeat HBsAg at 6 months to check for chronic infection. Antivirals are only for severe acute hepatitis B: INR above 1.5, encephalopathy, or jaundice lasting more than about 4 weeks.
notes: He has acute hepatitis B with a normal INR, no encephalopathy and good oral intake, so supportive care with regular LFT and INR checks is correct, because the infection usually clears on its own in adults.
Tenofovir (or entecavir) is reserved for severe or protracted acute hepatitis B, such as INR above 1.5 or encephalopathy, and he has neither.
Interferon is contraindicated in acute hepatitis B because the immune flare it causes can tip an inflamed liver into decompensation, and it has no role in this self-limiting illness.
Acetylcysteine treats paracetamol toxicity or early acute liver failure, but his paracetamol level is undetectable and his INR and mental state are normal.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 6 hours of worsening breathlessness, chest tightness and wheeze. She had an upper respiratory tract infection 4 days ago. She has had asthma since childhood. She uses only a reliever inhaler and has never been prescribed a preventer. On arrival she speaks in short phrases and is using her accessory muscles. Pulse is 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg, temperature 37.4 °C and SpO2 91% on room air. There is widespread expiratory wheeze. The trachea is central and air entry is equal on both sides. Over the first hour she receives oxygen by nasal prongs, salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes, ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes and oral prednisolone 50 mg. She is still alert but still speaks only in phrases. Pulse is 122/min, respiratory rate 27/min and SpO2 93% on 2 L/min oxygen. Wheeze persists. A chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with no pneumothorax or consolidation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Intravenous aminophylline
Intravenous hydrocortisone
Intravenous magnesium sulfate
Intravenous salbutamol
Nebulised adrenaline
questions.why: This woman has acute severe asthma. She speaks only in phrases, uses her accessory muscles and has an SpO2 of 91% on room air. She has no features of life-threatening asthma: she is alert, with no cyanosis, no silent chest and no exhaustion. She has had an hour of optimal first-line treatment: repeated salbutamol by spacer, ipratropium, oral prednisolone and oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%. She is still in the severe category. The chest X-ray rules out a pneumothorax and consolidation. The Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG advise IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes for severe acute asthma that has not responded to first-line bronchodilators. She should keep having frequent salbutamol, and senior and ICU staff should be told. Aminophylline is not recommended as routine treatment because it adds little and causes arrhythmias and vomiting. IV hydrocortisone works no better than the oral prednisolone she has already had. IV salbutamol is kept for life-threatening asthma that does not respond, in a critical care setting. Nebulised adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction, not acute asthma.
notes: Aminophylline is not recommended as routine treatment for acute asthma: it adds little bronchodilation to inhaled therapy and has a narrow therapeutic index, with arrhythmias, seizures and vomiting.
She has already had oral prednisolone 50 mg and can swallow, so IV hydrocortisone gives no extra benefit and repeats her corticosteroid.

An IV salbutamol infusion is kept for life-threatening asthma that does not respond to other treatment, in a critical care setting; it causes more tachycardia, lactic acidosis and hypokalaemia, and she has no life-threatening features.
Nebulised adrenaline treats anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction such as croup, and she has no urticaria, angioedema, allergen exposure or stridor.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man collapses in the emergency department waiting area 20 minutes after triage. He had come in with 4 hours of central chest heaviness and nausea. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia, and takes metformin, perindopril and atorvastatin. His first rhythm is ventricular fibrillation. He receives CPR, three shocks, adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV. Spontaneous circulation returns after 12 minutes. He is being ventilated with a bag-valve-mask on 15 L/min oxygen. Pulse is 112/min, blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg, temperature is 35.6 °C and SpO2 is 97%. GCS is 3. A 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V5. A venous blood gas taken 5 minutes after return of circulation shows: pH 7.09 (7.32 to 7.42); pCO2 62 mm Hg (41 to 51); bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22 to 28); base excess -11 mmol/L (-2 to +2); lactate 9.2 mmol/L (below 2.0); potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2); glucose 15.1 mmol/L (4.0 to 7.8). Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base disturbance?
options: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis
Acute respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Metabolic acidosis with coexisting metabolic alkalosis
Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
questions.why: The pH of 7.09 shows a severe acidaemia. There are two causes, and each one lowers the pH. First, the pCO2 of 62 mm Hg is high even for a venous sample, so there is a respiratory acidosis. This comes from low cardiac output during the arrest and poor ventilation with the bag-valve-mask. Second, the bicarbonate of 18 mmol/L, base excess of -11 and lactate of 9.2 mmol/L show a lactic metabolic acidosis from 12 minutes of low tissue perfusion. If the lungs were compensating for the metabolic acidosis, Winter's formula (1.5 x 18 + 8 = 35 +/- 2 mm Hg) says the pCO2 should be low. Instead it is high, so a second, respiratory process is present. This matters for his care. ANZCOR post-resuscitation guidance asks for normocapnia, so his ventilation should be increased and adjusted to arterial gases. Do not give bicarbonate routinely. The lactate should clear once perfusion improves with reperfusion and blood pressure support (MAP at least 65 mm Hg). The mild rise in potassium and the high glucose are expected after an arrest.
notes: Wrong: if the lungs were compensating, the pCO2 would be about 35 mm Hg, but it is 62 mm Hg, so there is also a respiratory acidosis.
Wrong: renal compensation would raise the bicarbonate, and the kidneys need days to do this, but his bicarbonate is low at 18 mmol/L.
Wrong: he has nothing that causes a metabolic alkalosis, such as vomiting or diuretics, and his low bicarbonate and base excess show only a metabolic acidosis.
Wrong: in chronic respiratory acidosis the bicarbonate is raised and the pH is close to normal, but he has a low bicarbonate and severe acidaemia after an acute event.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman sees her general practitioner about a painful ulcer on the tip of her left second toe. It has not healed in 2 months. For 3 weeks, pain in her left forefoot has woken her at night, and it eases when she hangs the foot over the side of the bed. She has had type 2 diabetes for 25 years and has chronic kidney disease. She is a former smoker. Her medicines are metformin, insulin glargine and atorvastatin. Blood pressure is 146/80 mmHg, pulse 78/min and regular, and temperature 36.6°C. The left foot is cool and hairless, and the pedal pulses cannot be felt. The ulcer is 0.8 cm across, dry and punched out, with a pale base and no surrounding erythema. Probe to bone is negative. Monofilament sensation is reduced at 2 of 10 sites. eGFR is 41 mL/min/1.73 m2. Handheld Doppler studies show: right brachial systolic 146 mmHg, left brachial systolic 140 mmHg; left dorsalis pedis systolic 178 mmHg and left posterior tibial systolic 184 mmHg (ABI 1.26); left pedal waveforms monophasic; left hallux systolic 22 mmHg (toe-brachial index 0.15; normal above 0.70). Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the vascular studies?
options: Normal perfusion, so the ulcer is neuropathic in origin
Isolated digital disease with patent tibial vessels
Normal ankle readings with an artefactual toe reading
Mild disease with perfusion adequate for healing
Severe ischaemia masked by medial arterial calcification
questions.why: The answer is A. Long-standing diabetes and chronic kidney disease cause medial calcification of the tibial arteries. Calcified arteries are hard to compress with a cuff, so ankle pressures read falsely high, and an ABI that looks normal (0.9 to 1.3) does not rule out peripheral arterial disease. Diabetes Feet Australia guidelines therefore combine the ABI with Doppler waveforms and the toe-brachial index (TBI). Here, monophasic pedal waveforms and a TBI of 0.15 confirm arterial disease. The digital arteries are usually spared from calcification, so the toe pressure shows the true perfusion of the foot. A toe pressure below 30 mmHg means severe ischaemia and a low chance of healing. With rest pain and tissue loss, this is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, which needs urgent vascular imaging and referral for revascularisation. Why the other options are wrong: B wrongly takes the ABI at face value, and mild neuropathy can coexist with but does not explain the abnormal waveforms and very low TBI. C is wrong because monophasic pedal waveforms show disease at or above the ankle, not only in the toe.
notes: Wrong: an ABI in the normal range does not exclude disease in diabetes, and the monophasic waveforms and very low TBI show poor perfusion; the painful toe-tip ulcer with rest pain is ischaemic.
Wrong: monophasic pedal waveforms show disease at or above the ankle, so the tibial vessels are not patent.
Wrong: the toe pressure is the more reliable reading in calcified vessels, and it fits the rest pain, cool hairless foot and absent pulses.
Wrong: a toe pressure below 30 mmHg predicts poor healing and, with rest pain and tissue loss, means chronic limb-threatening ischaemia that needs urgent vascular referral.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, para 2, is on the birth suite 25 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 38 weeks' gestation. Her labour was induced for pre-eclampsia. She received oxytocin 10 units at the birth, and the placenta and membranes were complete. She is now bleeding heavily with clots, and the measured loss is 1,300 mL. Bimanual compression has been done, a catheter has drained 450 mL of urine, an oxytocin infusion is running, and tranexamic acid 1 g IV was given 10 minutes ago. In labour she took oral labetalol and had a magnesium sulfate infusion. She has no history of asthma. Pulse is 122/min, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg (158/102 mmHg before the birth), respirations 24/min and SpO2 98% on oxygen 15 L/min by mask. The fundus is soft and above the umbilicus. Speculum examination shows no cervical or vaginal tear. Haemoglobin is 95 g/L, platelets 146 x 10^9/L and fibrinogen 3.4 g/L. Crossmatched blood has been requested. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly
Misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually
Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly
Intrauterine balloon tamponade
Laparotomy with uterine compression suture
questions.why: This is a major primary postpartum haemorrhage (1,300 mL with tachycardia) caused by uterine atony. The fundus is soft and high, and the other Ts have been checked: no tear (trauma), a complete placenta (tissue) and normal fibrinogen and near-normal platelets (thrombin). First-line measures are already done: uterine compression, an empty bladder, oxytocin IM then by infusion, and tranexamic acid. RANZCOG C-Obs 43 and Queensland Clinical Guidelines say the next step for ongoing atony is a second-line uterotonic. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia because it can cause a hypertensive crisis, stroke or eclampsia, even though her BP has fallen from bleeding. Magnesium sulfate also adds to atony. She has no asthma, so carboprost (15-methyl PGF2-alpha) 250 micrograms IM is the right choice. It can be repeated every 15 minutes up to 8 doses (2 mg). Balloon tamponade and surgery are for bleeding that continues despite uterotonics.
notes: Wrong: ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia and hypertension because it can cause severe hypertension, stroke or eclampsia, and her current lower BP is from blood loss, not a resolved disease.
Wrong: misoprostol is slower in onset and less effective than other uterotonics, so guidelines keep it for when carboprost or ergometrine are unavailable or contraindicated.
Wrong: balloon tamponade is the next step only once uterotonics have failed, and she has not yet had a second-line uterotonic.
Wrong: laparotomy with a B-Lynch or similar suture is for haemorrhage that continues despite uterotonics and tamponade, so it is premature here.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 30 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain. It began after a fried dinner and radiates to her right shoulder. Over the past 8 months she has had brief, similar episodes after meals. Her temperature is 38.7 °C, pulse 106/min, blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. She is not jaundiced, and Murphy's sign is positive. Investigations show: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) CRP 88 mg/L (<5) Total bilirubin 24 µmol/L (<20) ALP 440 U/L (30-110) GGT 210 U/L (<40) ALT 31 U/L (<35) Lipase 30 U/L (<60) Ultrasound shows a gallbladder wall thickened to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid and a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. The common bile duct measures 5 mm, but bowel gas hides its distal end. She is given analgesia, IV fluids and IV antibiotics, and is admitted for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation before surgery?
options: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scintigraphy
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen
Repeat liver function tests in 6 weeks
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
questions.why: The ultrasound and inflammatory markers already show acute calculous cholecystitis. The question is what the liver function tests mean for her. A stone stuck in the cystic duct on its own usually causes only mild LFT changes. Her ALP and GGT are about 4 to 5 times the upper limit, with a normal ALT and a bilirubin that is only slightly raised. This cholestatic pattern suggests a common bile duct stone causing partial or intermittent blockage. A 5 mm duct and a bilirubin of 24 make complete obstruction unlikely, but they do not rule out a stone, especially since the distal duct could not be seen. That puts her at intermediate risk of choledocholithiasis. Guidelines (eTG, ASGE) recommend non-invasive duct imaging before cholecystectomy, either MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound, or else an intraoperative cholangiogram. ERCP is kept for a duct stone that has been confirmed, or for cholangitis that needs urgent drainage.
notes: ERCP carries a risk of pancreatitis, bleeding and perforation, so it is used to treat a confirmed duct stone or cholangitis needing drainage rather than to look for a stone in a woman who is not jaundiced and has a non-dilated duct.
A HIDA scan tests whether the cystic duct is patent to diagnose cholecystitis, which the ultrasound has already confirmed, and it does not show stones in the common bile duct well.
CT misses many bile duct stones because cholesterol stones are often isodense with bile, and it adds radiation without answering the question the LFTs raise.
Waiting 6 weeks to repeat the LFTs would leave a possible duct stone unchecked through cholecystectomy during this admission, risking a retained stone, cholangitis or pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man comes to a suburban general practice with 16 hours of abdominal pain. It started overnight as a vague ache around his umbilicus and has since moved to the right lower abdomen. He has vomited twice, has not eaten since yesterday, and says the walk from the car park jolted the pain. He has no diarrhoea and no urinary symptoms. He has no past medical history and takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 38.1 °C, heart rate 106/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He lies still on the couch. He is tender at McBurney's point with guarding, and pressing on the left iliac fossa causes pain on the right. Bowel sounds are present. A urine dipstick shows ketones 1+ and is negative for blood, leucocytes and nitrites. He asks if he can go home and see how he feels tomorrow. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Arrange an outpatient abdominal ultrasound and review the result tomorrow
Start oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review him in 24 hours
Withhold all analgesia until a surgeon has examined his abdomen
Give analgesia, keep nil by mouth and arrange same-day hospital referral
Request faecal calprotectin and refer him to a gastroenterologist
questions.why: This young man most likely has acute appendicitis. He has periumbilical pain that has moved to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, vomiting, fever, tachycardia, pain when jolted, guarding at McBurney's point and a positive Rovsing's sign. A normal urine dipstick does not rule it out. When appendicitis is suspected in general practice, he needs same-day transfer to an emergency department or surgical unit. The GP should phone a handover, keep him nil by mouth in case he needs theatre, give adequate analgesia, record his allergies and arrange safe transport. Giving analgesia does not hide the diagnosis or delay it. If the diagnosis is confirmed, antibiotics are given in hospital under eTG guidance, alongside appendicectomy or, for some patients, supervised non-operative care. Sending him home raises the risk of perforation, peritonitis and abscess.
notes: An outpatient scan with review the next day delays surgical assessment in a febrile, tachycardic patient with localised peritonism, and a normal scan would not exclude appendicitis.
Treating suspected appendicitis with oral antibiotics in the community, without imaging or surgical review, can mask a progressing or perforating appendix and does not follow eTG advice.
Withholding pain relief is outdated, because analgesia does not reduce diagnostic accuracy and leaving pain untreated causes avoidable suffering.
Ileocaecal Crohn's disease is unlikely after a 16-hour illness with no diarrhoea, weight loss or bleeding, and an elective gastroenterology referral would miss a surgical emergency.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after vomiting dark, coffee-ground material three times this morning. She has had black, sticky stools for 3 days. She has knee osteoarthritis and has taken naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 2 months. She also takes aspirin 100 mg daily because of a previous transient ischaemic attack. She does not drink alcohol. On arrival, her pulse is 106/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg (usually 145/85 mm Hg), respirations 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air and temperature 36.8 °C. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease. The abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no guarding. Rectal examination shows melaena. Two large-bore cannulas are inserted and 500 mL of crystalloid is given. Her pulse falls to 92/min and her blood pressure rises to 124/74 mm Hg. Haemoglobin is 97 g/L (baseline 131 g/L), platelets 302 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, urea 13.9 mmol/L, creatinine 81 µmol/L, albumin 39 g/L and bilirubin 9 µmol/L. Gastroscopy is booked for the next morning. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug to give now?
options: Intravenous pantoprazole
Intravenous terlipressin
Intravenous tranexamic acid
Intravenous ceftriaxone
Intravenous phytomenadione
questions.why: This woman has a non-variceal upper GI bleed, most likely from a peptic ulcer caused by naproxen and aspirin together. She has coffee-ground vomiting, melaena, a 34 g/L fall in haemoglobin and a urea raised out of proportion to her creatinine. She has responded to fluids. She drinks no alcohol, has no stigmata of liver disease, and her platelets, INR, albumin and bilirubin are normal, so varices are unlikely. Her Glasgow-Blatchford score is high, so she needs admission and gastroscopy within 24 hours. Her haemoglobin is above the restrictive transfusion threshold (below 70 g/L, or below 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease), so she does not need red cells. eTG and the NSW ACI guidelines recommend an IV proton pump inhibitor (for example, pantoprazole 80 mg IV) while she waits for endoscopy. Before endoscopy it reduces the number of high-risk stigmata seen and the need for endoscopic therapy. After endoscopic haemostasis of a high-risk ulcer, high-dose IV PPI lowers the risk of rebleeding. The naproxen should be stopped for good. The decision on aspirin is made with gastroenterology, and it is usually restarted within days.
notes: Terlipressin is used for suspected variceal bleeding, and she has no alcohol use, no liver stigmata and normal liver function and coagulation results.
Tranexamic acid does not reduce death from GI bleeding and increases venous thromboembolism (HALT-IT trial), so guidelines advise against using it.
Prophylactic antibiotics such as ceftriaxone lower infection and mortality rates in variceal bleeding in cirrhosis, not in non-variceal ulcer bleeding.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin or treats a deficiency-related coagulopathy, and her INR is normal and she takes no vitamin K antagonist.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors and yellow eyes. Today his wife noticed he was muddled. He has untreated gallstones and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. On arrival he is jaundiced and disoriented to time. Temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 122/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 95% on room air. The right upper quadrant is tender. Results: total bilirubin 104 µmol/L (reference <20), conjugated bilirubin 82 µmol/L, ALP 438 U/L (30–110), GGT 590 U/L (<50), ALT 112 U/L (<40), lipase 52 U/L (<60), white cell count 19.1 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), creatinine 139 µmol/L (60–110), INR 1.2 and venous lactate 3.8 mmol/L (<2.0). Ultrasound shows gallbladder calculi with a 3 mm wall and a common bile duct of 12 mm containing a distal shadowing calculus. Blood cultures are taken, and he is given IV amoxicillin, IV gentamicin and 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. His blood pressure is now 98/60 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
Percutaneous cholecystostomy
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography after 72 hours
questions.why: This man has Reynolds' pentad: jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, confusion and hypotension. Under the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 this is severe (grade III) acute cholangitis, because he has neurological and cardiovascular dysfunction. It is caused by a stone in a dilated common bile duct, with a cholestatic liver test pattern, and he also has sepsis with hypoperfusion (lactate 3.8 mmol/L and acute kidney injury). The eTG and the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard say to take blood cultures, give IV antibiotics within 60 minutes (amoxicillin plus gentamicin for biliary sepsis) and give fluids, all of which has been done. Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus from a blocked duct. Once he has been resuscitated, he needs urgent source control by decompressing the bile duct with ERCP (sphincterotomy and stone extraction, or a stent if he is too unstable), and his care should be escalated to ICU. Cholecystectomy should follow once he has recovered, ideally during the same admission. A normal lipase and a thin gallbladder wall make gallstone pancreatitis and acute cholecystitis unlikely.
notes: Wrong: cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder but does not clear the stone blocking the common bile duct, and operating on a septic, hypotensive patient is high risk. It is planned after the duct has been cleared and he has recovered.
Wrong: ultrasound has already shown a dilated duct with a stone in it, so MRCP would only delay drainage in a deteriorating septic patient.

Wrong: cholecystostomy drains the gallbladder, not the blocked common bile duct. It is used for acute cholecystitis in unfit patients, whereas percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage is the fallback if ERCP fails.
Wrong: delaying drainage by 72 hours is acceptable only in mild cholangitis that responds to antibiotics. In severe cholangitis with hypotension and confusion, this delay increases the risk of death.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman, a retired pharmacist, sees her general practitioner with 8 days of cough.
