The cough began after a coryzal illness and is now productive of rust-coloured sputum, with fevers and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. She has never smoked and has no drug allergies. Temperature is 38.4 °C, pulse 102/min, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg and SpO2 95% on room air. She is alert and oriented, with an abbreviated mental test score of 10/10. There is dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles at the right base. Urgent blood results are: white cell count 15.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 12.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), urea 6.8 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 74 µmol/L (45-90), sodium 135 mmol/L (135-145) and C-reactive protein 162 mg/L (less than 5). A chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. Which of the following is this patient's CURB-65 score?
questions.why: CURB-65 gives one point for each of five criteria: new confusion; urea above 7 mmol/L; respiratory rate of 30/min or more; systolic BP below 90 mmHg or diastolic BP of 60 mmHg or less; and age 65 years or older. This patient meets none of them. She is alert with an AMTS of 10/10. Her urea of 6.8 mmol/L is below the CURB-65 cut-off of 7, even though it sits near the top of the laboratory range. Her respiratory rate of 24/min is high, but below 30. Her BP of 112/68 mmHg is above both thresholds. At 64, she is just under the age criterion. Her score is 0, which means low-severity pneumonia. In a stable patient with SpO2 of 92% or more, this supports oral treatment at home. eTG recommends amoxicillin 1 g 8-hourly for 5 days, with review at 48 hours and a safety-net plan. Clinical judgement still applies alongside the score. Tachycardia, neutrophilia and a high CRP show a systemic inflammatory response, but they are not CURB-65 criteria.
notes: A score of 1 would need one criterion. Students reach it by scoring her respiratory rate of 24/min (the cut-off is 30 or more) or by counting her age of 64 as 65 or older.

A score of 2 would need two criteria. Students reach it by wrongly scoring the urea of 6.8 mmol/L (the cut-off is above 7) and the raised respiratory rate, or by counting the tachycardia, which is not part of CURB-65.
A score of 3 would mean high-severity pneumonia needing hospital admission. This woman is alert, normotensive, younger than 65 and has a urea below 7 mmol/L.
A score of 4 would need four criteria such as confusion and hypotension, and she has none of them. The high white cell count and CRP do not count towards the score.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 1 hour after sudden, severe, tearing chest pain that radiated between her shoulder blades while she was gardening. She fainted briefly when the pain began. She has hypertension and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Her medicines are perindopril and amlodipine. On arrival, her blood pressure is 168/94 mmHg in the left arm and 136/80 mmHg in the right arm, pulse is 104/min and SpO2 is 96% on room air. An early diastolic murmur is heard at the right sternal edge. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy and no ST elevation. CT angiography shows an intimal flap that starts just above the aortic valve and extends into the descending thoracic aorta, with a moderate high-attenuation pericardial effusion. Twenty minutes later she becomes pale and confused. Her blood pressure is 82/54 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, jugular venous pressure is raised 6 cm and her heart sounds are muffled. Two large-bore cannulas are in place and crossmatched blood is available. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Intravenous metoprolol infusion
Immediate open repair in the operating theatre
Ultrasound-guided percutaneous pericardiocentesis
Thoracic endovascular stent-graft repair
Intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion
questions.why: This woman has an acute Stanford type A aortic dissection, because the flap starts in the ascending aorta. She now has the complication most likely to kill her: cardiac tamponade from bleeding into the pericardium. The high-attenuation (blood-density) pericardial effusion, low blood pressure, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and confusion are the Beck triad with shock. Type A dissection is a surgical emergency. When it is complicated by haemopericardium and shock, the 2024 ESC guidelines and the Heart Foundation/CSANZ guidance used in Australia say she should go straight to theatre for open replacement of the ascending aorta, with blood products given while she is moved. Draining the pericardium only fixes the tamponade, and the blood pressure it restores can make the aorta bleed again. Lowering the heart rate or blood pressure is wrong while she is hypotensive. Anticoagulants make the bleeding worse.
notes: Metoprolol is the anti-impulse drug used for a dissection with high blood pressure, but in tamponade and shock it removes the compensating tachycardia and can cause cardiac arrest.

Percutaneous pericardiocentesis raises the blood pressure, which can restart bleeding from the aorta into the pericardium, so it is kept for controlled, small-volume drainage only when theatre cannot be reached in time.
Endovascular stent-graft repair is used for complicated type B (descending) dissection and cannot treat a tear in the ascending aorta just above the valve that is bleeding into the pericardium.
Heparin speeds up bleeding into the pericardium and the false lumen; giving antithrombotics because of the low-grade suspicion of a coronary syndrome is a known harmful error in dissection.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with 3 months of tiredness and breathlessness when climbing stairs at the café she manages. Her cycles are regular every 28 days. Over the past year her periods have lengthened to 7 days. On heavy days she changes a super pad every 2 hours, floods overnight and passes large clots. She has no bruising, nosebleeds or change in bowel habit. She and her partner stopped using condoms 2 months ago and hope to conceive within the next year. Her only medicine is folic acid 0.5 mg daily. Her blood pressure is 114/72 mmHg, pulse 98/min and temperature 36.7 °C. She has conjunctival pallor. Abdominal, speculum and bimanual examinations are normal. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115–165) MCV 71 fL (80–100) Platelets 438 x10^9/L (150–400) Ferritin 5 µg/L (30–300) CRP 3 mg/L (<5) TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4–4.0) Urine β-hCG negative Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral iron and a levonorgestrel intrauterine device
Oral iron and the combined oral contraceptive pill
Intravenous iron and tranexamic acid during menses
Oral iron and tranexamic acid during menses
Oral iron and referral for diagnostic hysteroscopy
questions.why: She has iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 92 g/L, MCV 71 fL, reactive thrombocytosis, ferritin 5 µg/L with a normal CRP) caused by heavy menstrual bleeding. Management must replace the deficit and treat the cause. Under eTG and the National Blood Authority guidance, oral iron is first line in a stable patient who has not yet tried it. Daily or alternate-day dosing works, and alternate-day dosing may improve absorption and tolerance. Recheck the FBC in 2 to 4 weeks (expect a rise of about 20 g/L by 3 to 4 weeks) and continue for about 3 months after the Hb normalises. The levonorgestrel IUD is usually first line for heavy menstrual bleeding (ACSQHC Clinical Care Standard), but it and the combined pill both prevent pregnancy, and she is trying to conceive. Tranexamic acid (1 g orally three to four times daily for up to 5 days during heavy bleeding) is a non-hormonal option. It reduces menstrual loss by about 40 to 50%, is taken only while bleeding and does not affect fertility. She has a normal pelvic examination and no risk factors for endometrial pathology, so invasive investigation is not needed yet. B: the LNG-IUD is contraceptive and does not suit a woman trying to conceive.
notes: Wrong: the levonorgestrel IUD is contraceptive, so it conflicts with her wish to conceive, even though it is often first line for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Wrong: the combined oral contraceptive pill suppresses ovulation and prevents the pregnancy she is trying for.
Wrong: intravenous iron is reserved for oral intolerance, failure, malabsorption or a need for rapid repletion, and she is stable and has not tried oral iron.
Wrong: hysteroscopy is not indicated in a 24-year-old with a normal pelvic examination, no endometrial risk factors and no failed medical treatment.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man is reviewed on the surgical ward at 08:00. He was admitted overnight with 26 hours of central abdominal pain that moved to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia and nausea. The emergency theatre list was full, so he is booked for laparoscopic appendicectomy this afternoon. He is fasting and receiving maintenance Hartmann's solution, and regular paracetamol is his only charted medicine. He has no past medical history and no allergies. His temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 90/min, blood pressure 128/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is tender at McBurney's point with localised guarding, and there is no generalised rigidity. White cell count is 14.1 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), neutrophils 11.6 x10^9/L (2.0–7.5), CRP 52 mg/L (<5) and creatinine 80 µmol/L (60–110). CT of the abdomen with contrast shows a 10 mm appendix with an enhancing wall and periappendiceal fat stranding, with no appendicolith, free gas or collection. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management while he awaits surgery?
options: Arrange CT-guided percutaneous drainage
Repeat CT scan with oral contrast today
Discharge on oral amoxicillin–clavulanate
Withhold opioid analgesia until surgical review
Start empirical intravenous antibiotic treatment
questions.why: This man has acute uncomplicated appendicitis. He has the classic migrating pain, McBurney's point tenderness, neutrophilia and a raised CRP, and his CT shows an inflamed appendix with no appendicolith, free gas or collection. He is stable and booked for appendicectomy, but there has already been a delay of many hours and he has had no antimicrobial cover. eTG (Antibiotic: Intra-abdominal infections, Appendicitis) advises starting empirical intravenous antibiotics when surgery for appendicitis is delayed. This treats the infection and lowers the risk of the appendix progressing to gangrene or perforation before theatre. Surgical prophylaxis is still given within 60 minutes before incision. The delay should also be flagged to the registrar. Percutaneous drainage is only for an appendiceal abscess, and he has none. Repeating the CT adds nothing, because the diagnosis is already confirmed. Treating him with antibiotics alone at home is not the standard for a patient who is booked for and agrees to surgery, and about 3 in 10 such patients need an appendicectomy within a year. Withholding pain relief is outdated: analgesia does not mask the signs of appendicitis or delay the diagnosis.
notes: Wrong: percutaneous drainage treats an appendiceal abscess or collection, and his CT shows neither.
Wrong: the contrast CT has already confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis, so another scan delays treatment and adds radiation without changing management.

Wrong: treating with antibiotics alone at home is an alternative only after a shared decision, and about 3 in 10 patients still need an appendicectomy within a year; he is booked for and agreeable to surgery, the standard treatment.
Wrong: giving opioid analgesia does not mask the signs of appendicitis or worsen diagnostic accuracy, so leaving him in pain is not appropriate.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman who works as a hairdresser sees her general practitioner with 10 weeks of right neck pain. The pain runs down the back of her arm to her middle finger and is worse when she looks up. Eight weeks ago she started regular paracetamol and ibuprofen and a supervised physiotherapy program. The pain has eased only a little, and she still drops her hair dryer. She has no hand clumsiness, change in gait or bladder symptoms. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 74/min and regular, and blood pressure 134/80 mmHg. Right elbow extension and wrist flexion are 4-/5, the same as 8 weeks ago, and the right triceps reflex is reduced. Sensation is reduced over the right middle finger. Tone, coordination and the lower limb examination are normal, and Hoffmann's sign is absent. MRI of the neck shows severe right C6-7 foraminal stenosis compressing the right C7 nerve root, with a normal cord. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Physiotherapy with review in 3 months
Same-day transfer to an emergency department
Carotid duplex ultrasonography
Outpatient referral to a spine surgeon
Rigid cervical collar for 6 weeks
questions.why: This is a right C7 radiculopathy from cervical spondylosis. The radicular pain runs to the middle finger and gets worse on neck extension. There is weakness of elbow extension and wrist flexion, a reduced triceps reflex and C7 sensory loss, and the MRI shows concordant C6-7 foraminal stenosis. Most cervical radiculopathy settles with analgesia, physiotherapy and modified activity. This patient has had 8 weeks of conservative treatment and still has an objective motor deficit, a matching MRI lesion and pain that limits her work. That combination warrants referral to a spine surgeon to assess her for decompression. Urgent assessment is not needed: there are no myelopathic symptoms, no upper motor neuron signs, her weakness is not getting worse and the cord is normal. She still needs safety netting to seek urgent review if weakness progresses, or if hand clumsiness, gait disturbance or bladder symptoms develop. Continuing physiotherapy alone delays treatment of a persisting motor deficit. Transfer to the emergency department is for myelopathy or rapidly progressive weakness. Carotid imaging investigates a TIA, which this fixed lower motor neuron deficit with radicular pain is not.
notes: Continuing physiotherapy alone and waiting 3 more months is wrong because she still has an objective motor deficit with a matching MRI lesion after 8 weeks of conservative care, so she needs a surgical opinion now.

Same-day emergency transfer is for suspected cord compression, myelopathy or rapidly progressive weakness, and she has none of these: there are no upper motor neuron signs, the cord is normal and her deficit is stable.
Carotid duplex ultrasonography is part of the workup for a TIA, but she has a fixed lower motor neuron deficit in one root pattern with radicular pain, not transient episodes of focal weakness.
Immobilising the neck in a rigid collar for weeks has no proven benefit in cervical radiculopathy and causes stiffness and muscle deconditioning.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department of a regional hospital. She has had 2 days of colicky periumbilical pain and bilious vomiting, and she has passed no flatus. She has had two caesarean sections and an open appendicectomy. Adhesive small bowel obstruction is diagnosed. She is treated with nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids with added potassium. Eight hours later her pain is constant and severe despite intravenous morphine. Temperature is 38.1°C, pulse 126/min, blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg and respirations 22/min. The abdomen is distended, with localised tenderness and guarding in the right lower quadrant, and bowel sounds are reduced. Nasogastric output so far is 1.4 L. Leukocyte count is 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0). Venous lactate is 1.5 mmol/L (less than 2.0). CT of the abdomen with intravenous contrast shows a closed loop of small bowel with reduced wall enhancement and fluid in the mesentery. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Urgent operative exploration
Water-soluble contrast challenge
Repeat venous lactate in 2 hours
Continued nasogastric drainage for 72 hours
Colonoscopic decompression
questions.why: The most serious risk in adhesive small bowel obstruction is strangulation, where the bowel loses its blood supply and dies. This patient has the warning signs. Her pain has changed from colicky to constant and is not controlled by morphine. She has a fever, a rising heart rate, localised guarding and a raised white cell count. CT shows a closed loop with reduced wall enhancement and fluid in the mesentery. The WSES Bologna guidelines say that strangulation, a closed loop, peritonitis or ischaemia on CT are reasons to stop non-operative management and operate straight away. This lets the surgeon release the bowel and remove any dead segment before it perforates and causes sepsis. Lactate often rises only once bowel has already died, so a normal value does not exclude ischaemia and should not delay the operation. In a regional hospital this means calling the surgeon now and, if no one there can operate, arranging urgent transfer. Resuscitation and antibiotics should continue while this happens.
notes: A water-soluble contrast challenge is used to predict which uncomplicated obstructions will settle without an operation, and it is not appropriate when CT shows strangulation.
Lactate rises late in bowel ischaemia, so waiting for a repeat value delays the operation while more bowel dies.
Conservative management for up to 72 hours is only for uncomplicated adhesive obstruction without signs of ischaemia, and continuing it here risks perforation.
Colonoscopic decompression treats large bowel problems such as sigmoid volvulus or pseudo-obstruction and cannot reach or relieve an obstructed small bowel loop.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 2 days after a day-surgery hysteroscopy and dilatation and curettage for heavy, irregular bleeding. Since yesterday evening she has had worsening lower abdominal pain, nausea and anorexia. The operation record describes a retroverted, bulky uterus and a view partly obscured by blood, and lists the procedure as uneventful. The histology report, released this morning, describes disordered proliferative endometrium with fragments of mature adipose tissue. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and her body mass index is 42 kg/m2. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. The lower abdomen is tender with voluntary guarding but no rigidity, and bowel sounds are reduced. There is scant brown vaginal loss. White cell count is 15.6 x 10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5) and lactate 1.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0). Fluids, analgesia and antibiotics have been started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
Erect chest X-ray
Transvaginal ultrasound of the pelvis
MRI of the pelvis with gadolinium
CT pulmonary angiography
questions.why: There should be no fat inside the uterus. Adipose tissue in the curettings means the curette went through the uterine wall into omentum, mesentery or bowel fat, so this is uterine perforation until proven otherwise. A perforation like this can injure bowel without anyone noticing, and the injury often shows itself days later. That fits this patient: fever, lower abdominal guarding, reduced bowel sounds and high inflammatory markers 2 days after surgery. She is haemodynamically stable, her lactate is normal and she has no generalised peritonitis, so there is time to image her before deciding on surgery. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the best test here. It can show free fluid, free gas, a collection or abscess, bowel wall thickening or a leak, and bleeding, and it is not limited by her body habitus. A senior gynaecologist and the general surgeons should be told now. If the CT shows a visceral injury, or if she deteriorates, she needs laparoscopy or laparotomy. Erect chest X-ray: free gas under the diaphragm is not reliable after recent uterine instrumentation, and the film shows nothing about the pelvis, collections or bowel.
notes: Free gas can enter the peritoneum through a uterine perforation during hysteroscopy, so finding it does not tell you the bowel is injured, and the film cannot show collections or pelvic disease.
With a body mass index of 42 the views are limited, and ultrasound cannot reliably find bowel injury, free gas or collections higher in the abdomen.
MRI is slow and less available as an emergency test, covers only the pelvis and is poor at showing free gas or a bowel leak in a febrile, acutely unwell patient.
She has no chest symptoms and normal oxygen saturation, and her fever, tachycardia and lower abdominal guarding point to an intra-abdominal source rather than pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to a rural emergency department with 18 hours of fevers and shaking chills and 6 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain. This morning her partner noticed that her eyes had turned yellow. She reports dark urine and pale stools. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and has no other medical history. Her temperature is 39.4 °C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She is alert and oriented. She is jaundiced and tender in the right upper quadrant. Investigations show: white cell count 16.4 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0); platelets 240 x10^9/L (150–400); total bilirubin 61 µmol/L (<20); ALP 310 U/L (30–110); GGT 402 U/L (<40); ALT 160 U/L (<35); albumin 37 g/L (35–50); creatinine 68 µmol/L (45–90); INR 1.0; venous lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2.0). Ultrasound shows a 10 mm common bile duct with a calculus in its distal end. Which of the following best describes the severity of this patient's condition according to the Tokyo Guidelines 2018?
options: Mild (Grade I), as organ dysfunction is absent
Moderate (Grade II), owing to the serum bilirubin level
Moderate (Grade II), owing to leucocytosis and pyrexia
Severe (Grade III), owing to the raised venous lactate
Severe (Grade III), owing to tachycardia and tachypnoea
questions.why: This woman meets the TG18 criteria for a definite diagnosis of acute cholangitis. She has systemic inflammation (fever with rigors and a raised white cell count), cholestasis (conjugated-pattern jaundice with ALP and GGT raised more than ALT) and imaging findings (a dilated common bile duct with a distal stone). Severity is graded from the results. Grade III (severe) needs dysfunction of at least one organ system: hypotension needing vasopressors, a reduced level of consciousness, PaO2/FiO2 below 300, oliguria or creatinine above 176 µmol/L, INR above 1.5, or platelets below 100 x10^9/L. She has none of these, because her blood pressure, mental state, oxygenation, creatinine, INR and platelets are all normal. Grade II (moderate) needs any two of: white cell count above 12 or below 4 x10^9/L, temperature of 39 °C or more, age 75 or more, bilirubin of 85 µmol/L or more, or low albumin. She meets two (white cell count 16.4 and temperature 39.4 °C), so she has Grade II cholangitis. For her, this means she is at risk of getting worse.
notes: Wrong: having no organ dysfunction only rules out Grade III, and she meets two Grade II criteria, so she is not Grade I.
Wrong: a bilirubin of 61 µmol/L is below the 85 µmol/L TG18 threshold, so it does not count towards Grade II.
Wrong: lactate is not one of the TG18 organ dysfunction criteria; a mildly raised lactate supports sepsis escalation but does not make her Grade III.
Wrong: tachycardia and tachypnoea are not TG18 organ dysfunction criteria, and her blood pressure and oxygenation are normal.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman sees her general practitioner with 2 days of constant left calf pain and swelling. She has worked at a desk from home for the past 4 months and rarely goes out. She has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill for 6 years and takes no other medicines. Before she started the pill, her periods were heavy and lasted 8 days. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. Her BMI is 31 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 99% on room air. Her left calf measures 3.5 cm more than the right and has pitting oedema. Compression ultrasound shows a non-compressible left popliteal vein, with thrombus extending into the posterior tibial and peroneal veins. Platelets are 268 x10^9/L (150 to 400), INR 1.0 and eGFR over 90 mL/min/1.73 m2. Serum beta-hCG is under 5 IU/L. Rivaroxaban is started for 3 months. She wants to avoid pregnancy for at least 2 years. Which of the following is the most appropriate contraception for this patient?
options: Her current combined oral contraceptive pill
A combined pill with 20 micrograms ethinylestradiol
An etonogestrel and ethinylestradiol vaginal ring
A fertility awareness-based method
A 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device
questions.why: She has an acute proximal DVT provoked by the combined oral contraceptive pill, with prolonged sitting and obesity adding to the risk. After an oestrogen-related VTE, the key prevention and counselling step is to stop all oestrogen-containing contraception and switch straight away to a reliable non-oestrogen method. This prevents recurrence, and it also prevents pregnancy while she takes rivaroxaban, which can harm a fetus. Under UKMEC, which Australian practice uses, any combined hormonal method with current or past VTE is category 4 (unacceptable risk). Progestogen-only methods such as the levonorgestrel intrauterine device are category 2, meaning the benefits outweigh the risks. The levonorgestrel device is the best choice here for three reasons. It is long-acting and highly effective, it needs nothing from her day to day, and it reduces menstrual bleeding. That matters because she had heavy periods before the pill, and heavy menstrual bleeding is a common, troublesome side effect of rivaroxaban in women.
notes: Her current combined pill caused this DVT, and continuing oestrogen after VTE is UKMEC category 4 because it carries a high risk of recurrence.
Lowering the oestrogen dose still leaves a combined hormonal method, which remains UKMEC category 4 after VTE because any dose of ethinylestradiol raises clotting risk.
The vaginal ring delivers ethinylestradiol, and its VTE risk is at least as high as the combined pill, so it is also category 4.
Fertility awareness-based methods fail often with typical use, which is unacceptable during DOAC treatment, and cycle tracking is unreliable just after stopping hormonal contraception.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to a general practice 5 weeks before a 7-week trip through rural Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos for travel advice. The trip includes village homestays, forest trekking and nights in open huts. She feels well. She has a new sexual partner and uses condoms inconsistently. Her last menstrual period began 3 weeks ago and was normal. She is unsure whether she could be pregnant. She takes no medicines and has no allergies. She had chickenpox at age 6, and her mother remembers it clearly. Her Australian Immunisation Register statement shows a complete childhood schedule, including one measles-mumps-rubella dose at 12 months, a 3-dose school hepatitis B course and dTpa at age 15. Temperature is 36.6 °C, blood pressure 114/72 mmHg, pulse 70/min and respiratory rate 14/min. Examination is normal. Today the doctor plans to give a second measles-mumps-rubella dose, live attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine, combined hepatitis A-typhoid vaccine and dTpa, and to prescribe doxycycline for malaria prophylaxis. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation before vaccination today?
options: Measles IgG serology
Hepatitis A IgG serology
Urine beta-hCG
G6PD activity assay
Hepatitis B surface antibody
questions.why: The plan includes two live vaccines: measles-mumps-rubella and live attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine (Imojev). The Australian Immunisation Handbook says live vaccines should not be given in pregnancy. She has had unprotected sex, is in the second half of her cycle and cannot rule out pregnancy, so a urine beta-hCG test is needed before vaccination today. If the test is negative, the live vaccines can be given on the same day. She should be told to avoid pregnancy for 28 days afterwards. If she is pregnant, the live vaccines are deferred, and an inactivated Japanese encephalitis vaccine and a different malaria plan are considered. Doxycycline is also avoided in pregnancy, so the result affects her antimalarial too. Measles serology is not needed: adults born in or after 1966 with one documented dose should simply get the second dose. Hepatitis A serology before vaccination is only for people born before 1950, people who spent their childhood in endemic areas, or people with a history of jaundice. G6PD testing is needed before primaquine or tafenoquine, not doxycycline.
notes: Adults born in or after 1966 with one documented MMR dose should get a second dose without serology, so this test would not change management.
Hepatitis A serology before vaccination is only for people born before 1950, people who spent their childhood in an endemic country, or people with a history of jaundice, and she is none of these.
G6PD testing is needed before primaquine or tafenoquine because of the risk of haemolysis, not before doxycycline prophylaxis.
Testing hepatitis B antibodies after a completed adolescent course is not routinely recommended in an immunocompetent traveller, and the result would not affect today's vaccines.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 24 hours of crampy, diffuse abdominal pain, profuse watery diarrhoea without blood, and repeated vomiting. Two days ago she looked after her grandson, who goes to childcare and had diarrhoea. Her husband started vomiting this morning. She has not travelled, taken antibiotics or been in hospital recently. She has type 2 diabetes and hypertension, and she is an ex-smoker. Her medicines are metformin, ramipril and omeprazole. Temperature is 37.8 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg lying, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Her abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding and hyperactive bowel sounds. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Creatinine is 131 µmol/L (baseline 72), potassium 3.4 mmol/L, venous lactate 1.5 mmol/L (reference below 2.0) and CRP 28 mg/L. She is given an intravenous crystalloid bolus, her metformin and ramipril are withheld, and she is to be admitted under contact precautions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: CT mesenteric angiography
Clostridioides difficile toxin assay
Faecal microscopy for ova and parasites
Two sets of blood cultures
Faecal multiplex PCR
questions.why: This woman has acute infectious diarrhoea. The likely cause is norovirus: she had sudden vomiting and watery diarrhoea two days after contact with a child who had diarrhoea, and another person in her household is now ill. She also has hypovolaemia and a prerenal acute kidney injury. Most people with acute gastroenteritis do not need a stool test. Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) recommends one in specific situations: severe illness, admission to hospital, bloody diarrhoea, immunocompromise, recent antibiotic use, symptoms lasting more than 7 days, or a suspected outbreak. She is being admitted with significant dehydration and an AKI, and her household cluster fits an outbreak. A faecal multiplex PCR is the most useful test. It detects norovirus and the common bacterial causes (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella) in one sample. The result confirms the cause, guides contact precautions and bed placement on the ward, and shows whether antibiotics are needed. CT mesenteric angiography is not indicated.
notes: Her soft abdomen, normal lactate, sinus rhythm and pain that matches the examination make mesenteric ischaemia unlikely, and contrast adds risk while she has an AKI.
She has had no recent antibiotics or hospital stay and a contact is also ill, so a test that looks only for C. difficile is too narrow.
Testing for ova and parasites is for travellers, people with diarrhoea lasting more than 7 days or immunocompromised people, and she is none of these.
With a low-grade temperature and no sepsis or immunocompromise, blood cultures are unlikely to be positive, and they would not detect the likely viral cause.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner with 4 months of loose, pale stools that are hard to flush, three to four times a day. She also has bloating, tiredness and has lost 4 kg. She has had no rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, fever or recent travel. She has Hashimoto thyroiditis treated with levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily, and her brother has type 1 diabetes. She eats a normal diet that includes bread and pasta. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse is 84/min and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Her body mass index is 19 kg/m². She has conjunctival pallor. Her abdomen is soft, mildly distended and nontender. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115–165) MCV 75 fL (80–100) Ferritin 5 µg/L (30–300) Serum folate 4.8 nmol/L (>7) Vitamin B12 310 pmol/L (150–700) CRP 3 mg/L (<5) TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.5–4.0) Tissue transglutaminase IgA 180 U/mL (<20) Endomysial antibody IgA: positive Total IgA 2.0 g/L (0.7–4.0) Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
options: HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genotyping
Colonoscopy with terminal ileal biopsies
Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies
Gluten challenge then repeat serology
Faecal elastase measurement
questions.why: This woman most likely has coeliac disease. She has steatorrhoea, weight loss, iron and folate deficiency with a normal B12 (pointing to the proximal small bowel), and a personal and family history of autoimmune disease. Her tTG-IgA is strongly positive, her EMA is positive and her total IgA is normal. Australian guidance (GESA, Coeliac Australia, eTG) says adults need small-bowel histology to confirm the diagnosis before starting a gluten-free diet. The test is gastroscopy with multiple duodenal biopsies: at least four from the second part of the duodenum and one or two from the bulb. These are taken while she is still eating gluten, and the aim is to show villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis. The no-biopsy approach used in some children is not used for Australian adults. A biopsy also gives a baseline and checks for other pathology. HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genotyping is mainly useful for ruling the disease out: about a third of the population carries these alleles, so a positive result cannot confirm coeliac disease. A gluten challenge is only needed if a patient has already cut out gluten, and she is eating a normal gluten-containing diet.
notes: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing has a high negative predictive value but is common in the general population, so a positive result cannot confirm coeliac disease.
Colonoscopy with ileal biopsies looks for Crohn's disease or microscopic colitis, and it does not sample the duodenum, where coeliac disease shows.
A gluten challenge is only needed for patients who have already stopped gluten, and she is eating a normal gluten-containing diet.
Faecal elastase tests for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and cannot confirm coeliac disease, which her serology already strongly suggests.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner with a 3-month history of tiredness, bloating, and loose, pale, offensive stools that are hard to flush. She has lost 4 kg without trying. She has Hashimoto thyroiditis treated with levothyroxine, and her sister has type 1 diabetes. She eats a normal mixed diet and rarely drinks alcohol. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 84/min and blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. She has conjunctival pallor. Her abdomen is soft, mildly distended and nontender. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 106 g/L (115–160) MCV 75 fL (80–100) Ferritin 7 microgram/L (30–300) Serum folate 5.0 nmol/L (above 7.0) TSH 2.1 mU/L (0.5–4.0) CRP 3 mg/L (below 5) Tissue transglutaminase IgA 96 U/mL (below 20) Total IgA 2.1 g/L (0.7–4.0) Faecal elastase 380 microgram/g (above 200) Stool microscopy, culture and multiplex PCR: no pathogens detected Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Strict gluten-free diet, then repeat serology in 3 months
HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genotyping
Colonoscopy with terminal ileal biopsies
Pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals
Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies while on her current diet
questions.why: She has malabsorption (steatorrhoea, weight loss, iron and folate deficiency). She also has autoimmune risk factors and a strongly positive tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA, so the serology result can be trusted. This picture is highly likely to be coeliac disease. Coeliac Australia, GESA and eTG advise that adults have the diagnosis confirmed by gastroscopy with multiple duodenal biopsies (including the duodenal bulb) while still eating gluten, to show villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytosis. A biopsy-confirmed diagnosis supports a lifelong gluten-free diet with a dietitian, replacement of iron, folate and vitamin D, bone health assessment, and screening of first-degree relatives. Starting a gluten-free diet before the biopsy can heal the mucosa and make the serology and histology falsely normal. HLA typing is useful only for ruling coeliac disease out. A normal faecal elastase and CRP make pancreatic insufficiency and Crohn disease unlikely.
notes: Removing gluten before the biopsy can heal the mucosa and normalise the serology, which leaves the diagnosis unconfirmed and would need a later gluten challenge.
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing has a high negative predictive value but is present in about a third of the population, so a positive result cannot confirm coeliac disease.
Her normal CRP, lack of blood in the stool and strongly positive tTG-IgA point to coeliac disease rather than ileal Crohn disease, so ileocolonoscopy is not the first investigation.
A normal faecal elastase of 380 microgram/g rules against exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, so enzyme replacement would not treat the cause of her steatorrhoea.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old man comes to his general practitioner for a cardiovascular risk assessment. He feels well and says his blood pressure "always jumps" at the doctor's. He takes no regular medicines, vapes nicotine daily and drinks four coffees a day. He is seated and has rested for 5 minutes, and a correctly sized cuff is used. His blood pressure is 152/94 mmHg and then 148/92 mmHg in the right arm, and 150/92 mmHg in the left arm. His pulse is 74/min. His BMI is 29 kg/m2. His fundi, heart sounds and peripheral pulses are normal. He brings a list of 9 home readings from the past 12 days. He took them on a wrist monitor he bought online, one reading each evening after dinner and coffee. They average 126/79 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG is normal. Serum potassium is 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), eGFR is above 90 mL/min/1.73 m2 and the urine albumin to creatinine ratio is 1.0 mg/mmol (below 2.5). Which of the following best describes the significance of his home readings?
options: They confirm white coat hypertension
They confirm sustained grade 1 hypertension
They indicate masked hypertension
They demonstrate a normal nocturnal dipping pattern
They are inadequate to confirm or exclude hypertension
questions.why: His repeated clinic readings of 148 to 152/92 to 94 mmHg are in the grade 1 range. He has no end-organ damage (normal fundi, ECG, eGFR and urine albumin), so the Heart Foundation guideline says to confirm the diagnosis with out-of-office measurement before labelling or treating him. A home average below 135/85 mmHg would usually point to white coat hypertension, but only if it comes from a valid protocol. That protocol is a validated upper-arm device with a correctly sized cuff, two seated readings one minute apart every morning and evening for 7 days, discarding day 1 and averaging the rest. His readings fail it. The wrist device is not validated, he took single evening readings only, he took them after caffeine, and he has too few readings. They can neither confirm nor exclude hypertension. The next step is 24-hour ambulatory monitoring or a correctly done home protocol. A diagnosis of white coat hypertension cannot rest on invalid home data. Sustained hypertension is not confirmed because the out-of-office data are unreliable and, as recorded, normal. Masked hypertension is the reverse pattern: normal in the clinic and raised outside it.
notes: White coat hypertension can only be diagnosed from a valid out-of-office measurement, and these single, post-caffeine evening readings on an unvalidated wrist device are not one.
Sustained hypertension needs a valid out-of-office average of at least 135/85 mmHg, and his recorded average is normal, though unreliable.
Masked hypertension means normal clinic but raised out-of-office readings, which is the opposite of his pattern.
Nocturnal dipping can only be judged from ambulatory readings taken during sleep, not from evening home readings taken while awake.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man sees his general practitioner because he woke 2 days ago with muffled hearing and constant ringing in his right ear. He had a cold with a blocked nose 10 days ago and says the ear feels full. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and takes no other medicines. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse 76/min and blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg. Otoscopy shows normal tympanic membranes on both sides. A 512 Hz tuning fork placed on the vertex is heard louder in the left ear. The rest of the cranial nerve examination is normal. Tympanometry shows a type A trace in both ears. Pure-tone audiometry thresholds (dB HL; normal 20 or less) are: Right air conduction: 250 Hz 35, 500 Hz 40, 1 kHz 45, 2 kHz 55, 4 kHz 60 Right bone conduction (masked): 250 Hz 30, 500 Hz 40, 1 kHz 45, 2 kHz 50, 4 kHz 60 Left air and bone conduction: 10 to 15 at every frequency Which of the following best describes this audiogram?
options: Right conductive loss
Right mixed loss
Right sensorineural loss
Left sensorineural loss
Bilateral sensorineural loss
questions.why: The right ear's air conduction thresholds are 35 to 60 dB HL and fall away in the high frequencies. The masked bone conduction thresholds are raised by the same amount, never more than 5 dB from air conduction. That means there is no meaningful air-bone gap (a gap of 10 dB or less is within test variability), so the loss is sensorineural. The type A tympanograms (normal canal volume, pressure and compliance) rule out a middle ear effusion or Eustachian tube dysfunction after his cold, and the normal otoscopy rules out wax or a perforation. The Weber test lateralising to the left, the better ear, fits a right sensorineural loss. The right ear is more than 30 dB worse than the left over at least three contiguous frequencies, and the loss came on within 72 hours, so this meets the definition of sudden sensorineural hearing loss. He needs same-day ENT contact, prompt corticosteroids and MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma. The feeling of fullness is a common symptom of the sensorineural loss itself, not a sign of a middle ear cause.
notes: A conductive loss would show normal bone conduction with a gap of more than 10 dB to air conduction, usually an abnormal tympanogram, and a Weber lateralising to the affected right ear, and none of these are present.
A mixed loss needs raised bone conduction thresholds plus an air-bone gap of more than 10 dB, but the largest gap here is 5 dB, which is within test variability.
Left air and bone conduction thresholds are normal (10 to 15 dB HL); the Weber is louder on the left because that is the better-hearing cochlea, not the affected one.
Bilateral loss would need raised thresholds in both ears, but every left threshold is within the normal range of 20 dB HL or less, so the loss is one-sided.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is reviewed on the cardiology ward of a metropolitan hospital before discharge. He was admitted 5 days ago with 3 months of worsening exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea and ankle swelling, 18 months after an anterior STEMI treated with PCI. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and knee osteoarthritis. With IV furosemide he has diuresed 6 kg and now walks the ward corridor without breathlessness. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. His discharge medicines are oral furosemide 40 mg mane, bisoprolol 2.5 mg, sacubitril/valsartan 24/26 mg twice a day, spironolactone 12.5 mg, dapagliflozin 10 mg, aspirin, atorvastatin and metformin. Temperature is 36.6 °C, pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, respirations 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. The JVP is not raised and there is no pitting oedema. Serum sodium is 137 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.2) and creatinine 104 µmol/L (60–110). Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to give him before discharge?
options: Weigh himself each morning and book a GP review if he gains more than 2 kg in 2 days
Limit his fluid intake to 1 litre per day whatever his thirst or sodium level
Rest at home and avoid walking until his cardiology review in 6 weeks
Use a potassium-based salt substitute to cut the sodium in his cooking
Stop his bisoprolol if he feels more tired during the next few weeks
questions.why: This man has HFrEF from an ischaemic cardiomyopathy and has just been discharged after his first decompensation. His biggest near-term risk is fluid building up again and bringing him back to hospital. Weight gain from fluid usually shows up before breathlessness or visible oedema. The Heart Foundation/CSANZ guidelines and eTG recommend that he weighs himself every morning, on the same scales, after voiding and before breakfast. He should see his GP promptly if he gains more than 2 kg over 2 days or if his swelling or breathlessness gets worse. He should call 000 for chest pain or severe breathlessness. Self-monitoring like this, as part of a heart failure disease-management program, lowers readmission and death. A strict 1 L fluid limit is not routine; restriction to about 1.5 L/day is kept for severe congestion or hyponatraemia, and his sodium is normal. Supervised exercise and cardiac rehabilitation are recommended in stable HFrEF, so bed rest is wrong. Potassium-based salt substitutes risk hyperkalaemia in a patient on an ARNI plus an MRA whose potassium is already 4.8 mmol/L.
notes: Routine strict fluid restriction is not recommended; about 1.5 L/day is kept for severe congestion or hyponatraemia, and his sodium is normal.
Regular exercise and cardiac rehabilitation improve symptoms and lower hospitalisation in stable HFrEF, so avoiding walking is harmful.
Potassium chloride salt substitutes can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia in a patient on sacubitril/valsartan and spironolactone whose potassium is already high-normal.
Fatigue early in beta-blocker treatment is common and usually short-lived, and stopping it removes a proven mortality benefit and can bring on ischaemia or arrhythmia.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the emergency department 90 minutes after sudden onset of sharp right-sided pain and breathlessness. Both started while he was sitting at his desk at work. The pain is worse with deep breaths and has not eased with rest. He has no cough, fever, haemoptysis, leg swelling, recent travel or trauma. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and takes no medicines. He is 191 cm tall and weighs 68 kg. His temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 22/min, blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He speaks in full sentences. The trachea is central and the jugular venous pressure is not raised. Over the right hemithorax, expansion is reduced, the percussion note is hyper-resonant and breath sounds are reduced. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 104/min with no ST-segment or T-wave changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Arterial blood gas analysis
Inspiratory posteroanterior chest radiograph
CT pulmonary angiography
Expiratory posteroanterior chest radiograph
Serum D-dimer concentration
questions.why: This tall, thin young man who smokes has sudden one-sided pleuritic pain and breathlessness. He has reduced expansion, a hyper-resonant percussion note and reduced breath sounds on the right, so the most likely diagnosis is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and needs decompression straight away, before any imaging. Here there are no features of tension: his blood pressure is normal, the trachea is central and the JVP is not raised. That means there is time to confirm the diagnosis. The first-line test is a standard erect posteroanterior chest radiograph taken in inspiration (BTS 2023, used in Australian EDs). It shows the visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it, lets you measure the size of the pneumothorax (2 cm or more at the hilum is large) and shows any mediastinal shift. Together with his symptoms, this guides the choice between observation, needle aspiration, an ambulatory device or a drain. CT is kept for unclear or complex cases.
notes: An arterial blood gas does not confirm or size a pneumothorax, and with an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air it is not needed to assess his oxygenation.
CT pulmonary angiography involves radiation and contrast and looks for pulmonary embolism, which is unlikely here with no risk factors and clear one-sided signs of air in the pleural space.
Expiratory films are no longer recommended because they add little to detection over a standard inspiratory film and can make the size of the pneumothorax harder to judge.
A D-dimer is non-specific, does not confirm a pneumothorax, and should not come before imaging when the examination already points strongly to another diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of 10 weeks of crampy right lower abdominal pain and four to six loose stools a day. Some stools are streaked by blood, and they wake him from sleep. He has lost 4 kg without trying and has had occasional night sweats. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and has taken ibuprofen most days for the pain. He has not travelled and has had no antibiotics in the past 3 months. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 92/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. He is tender in the right iliac fossa, where there is vague fullness but no guarding. A soft perianal skin tag is present. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (130–180), CRP 42 mg/L (<5) and albumin 31 g/L (35–50). Faecal calprotectin is 640 µg/g (<50). Stool bacterial and parasite PCR, culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin are negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsies
Magnetic resonance enterography
Wireless capsule endoscopy
Serum ASCA and ANCA antibodies
Ileocolonoscopy with biopsies
questions.why: This young man most likely has ileocolonic Crohn's disease. The clues are a chronic history (over 6 weeks) of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea with blood, weight loss, low-grade fever, a perianal skin tag, smoking, raised inflammatory markers, low albumin and a very high faecal calprotectin, with negative stool tests for infection. Under GESA and eTG guidance, diagnosis needs ileocolonoscopy, meaning colonoscopy that passes into the terminal ileum, with biopsies from the ileum and from each colonic segment, including normal-looking areas. This shows how far the disease extends and whether there are skip lesions or rectal sparing. Histology can show patchy transmural-type inflammation and non-caseating granulomas, and it can exclude intestinal tuberculosis, infection and malignancy. Small-bowel imaging is added after the diagnosis to stage the disease, not to make it. He should also stop ibuprofen and get urgent referral to gastroenterology.
notes: Flexible sigmoidoscopy only reaches the distal colon, so it would miss ileocaecal disease, and the rectum and sigmoid are often spared in Crohn's disease.
MR enterography is useful for staging small-bowel extent, strictures and fistulae once the diagnosis is made, but it gives no tissue and cannot confirm the diagnosis.
Capsule endoscopy takes no biopsies and is not a first-line test, and an ileocaecal mass or stricture puts him at risk of the capsule getting stuck.
ASCA and ANCA serology has low sensitivity and specificity, so it cannot confirm or exclude Crohn's disease, and guidelines do not recommend it for diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with breathlessness and wheeze that began 6 hours ago, two days into a head cold. She has had asthma since childhood and uses only a salbutamol reliever. When she arrived 70 minutes ago, she could speak only in phrases and was using her accessory muscles. Since then she has had salbutamol 12 puffs and ipratropium 8 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes for three doses, prednisolone 50 mg orally, and oxygen by nasal prongs. She is alert but still speaks in phrases and uses her accessory muscles. Temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 118/min, respirations 28/min, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg and SpO2 94% on 2 L/min oxygen. There is widespread expiratory wheeze with equal air entry on both sides, and no rash or lip swelling. Venous blood gas: pH 7.44, pCO2 36 mmHg (reference 41–51), lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation, with no pneumothorax or consolidation. Salbutamol is being continued. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Intravenous aminophylline
Intravenous magnesium sulfate
Intramuscular adrenaline
Intravenous hydrocortisone
Intravenous ceftriaxone
questions.why: This is severe acute asthma (she speaks only in phrases and uses her accessory muscles) that has not responded well to an hour of standard treatment. She has had repeated salbutamol and ipratropium by spacer, oral prednisolone within the first hour, and oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 92–96%. The Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG advise adding IV magnesium sulfate (10 mmol over 20 minutes in adults) for severe or life-threatening asthma that responds poorly to the first bronchodilators. Salbutamol continues alongside it. She has no life-threatening features: she is alert, her SpO2 is 90% or above, her pCO2 is low rather than normal or rising, and her chest is not silent. So she does not yet need intubation, but she needs senior review and close monitoring. Aminophylline is not recommended in Australian guidelines because it adds little to standard treatment and causes arrhythmias, vomiting and seizures. IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or impending arrest, and she has no urticaria, angioedema or hypotension. IV hydrocortisone adds nothing when oral prednisolone has been given and can be swallowed.
notes: Aminophylline is not recommended in Australian guidelines: it gives little extra bronchodilation and has a narrow therapeutic index, with a risk of arrhythmias and seizures.
IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or near-arrest, and she has no urticaria, angioedema, stridor or hypotension.
She has already had oral prednisolone and can swallow; IV corticosteroid is no more effective and is only needed when oral intake is not possible.
A viral cold triggered this attack, and with no fever, purulent sputum or consolidation there is no indication for antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 40 minutes after her horse fell on her during a trail ride, crushing the right side of her chest. She had right-sided pleuritic pain straight away and has become steadily more breathless during transport. She has no past medical history and takes only a combined oral contraceptive pill. On arrival she is agitated and can speak only in single words. Temperature is 36.4 °C, pulse 138/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, and oxygen saturation 85% on 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask. Her trachea is deviated to the left and her neck veins are distended. There is bruising and tenderness over the right lateral ribs. The right hemithorax is hyper-resonant to percussion, and breath sounds are absent on the right. Heart sounds are clearly audible. Two large-bore cannulae are in place and blood has been sent for group and hold. A mobile chest X-ray has been requested, and the radiographer will arrive in 10 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Portable chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis before any chest procedure
Subxiphoid pericardiocentesis guided by bedside ultrasound
Rapid sequence intubation followed by positive-pressure ventilation
Needle decompression at the fifth intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line
Intravenous bolus of 1 L warmed crystalloid over 15 minutes
questions.why: This woman has a right tension pneumothorax after blunt chest trauma, with obstructive shock. She has hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the injured side, and a hyper-resonant hemithorax with absent breath sounds. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. ATLS (11th edition) and eTG advise treating it as soon as it is recognised, without waiting for imaging. In adults, the preferred site for needle decompression is the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, because the chest wall is thinner there and the catheter is more likely to reach the pleura than at the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line. Finger thoracostomy at the same site is an acceptable alternative. After decompression, an intercostal catheter is placed in the safe triangle and connected to an underwater seal. A chest X-ray should be done only after that.
notes: Wrong: tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically, and waiting 10 minutes for a film in a hypotensive, hypoxic patient risks cardiac arrest.

Wrong: tamponade is unlikely because her trachea is deviated, one side of her chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds, and her heart sounds are clear, so the chest needs decompressing rather than the pericardium.
Wrong: positive-pressure ventilation forces more air into the pleural space and can quickly worsen a tension pneumothorax and cause arrest if the chest has not been decompressed first.
Wrong: her shock is obstructive, not caused by blood loss, so fluid will not restore venous return while the tension pneumothorax is untreated, and giving it delays the treatment that saves her life.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is reviewed on the medical ward on day 3 of treatment for herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis, confirmed by CSF PCR. She has rheumatoid arthritis, and her weekly methotrexate has been withheld since admission. She weighs 70 kg and is receiving aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. She is still drowsy and has been drinking little. Her maintenance drip was taken down yesterday when the cannula tissued, and it was not restarted. Her urine output over the past 12 hours is 250 mL. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 98/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Her mucous membranes are dry, and there is no new focal neurological deficit. Serum creatinine is 164 µmol/L (72 µmol/L on admission; reference 45–90), urea 11.8 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L and potassium 4.6 mmol/L. Urine microscopy shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Stop the antiviral and start oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily
Stop the antiviral and start intravenous foscarnet
Continue the current regimen and add intravenous furosemide 40 mg
Arrange urgent haemodialysis through a temporary vascular catheter
Start isotonic crystalloid and reduce antiviral dosing to match renal function
questions.why: This patient has acute kidney injury from aciclovir crystal nephropathy. Aciclovir is cleared by the kidneys and is poorly soluble in urine, so high-dose IV therapy in a dehydrated patient lets crystals form in the renal tubules. This is the main complication to prevent during treatment of HSV encephalitis, and it is why eTG advises keeping the patient well hydrated and monitoring renal function throughout. Her intake is poor, her drip has been stopped, she is oliguric with dry mucous membranes, her creatinine has more than doubled and her urine shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals. The right step is to restart isotonic IV fluids and adjust the aciclovir dose to her estimated creatinine clearance. Her Cockcroft-Gault clearance is about 30 mL/min, which calls for 10 mg/kg every 12 hours. IV therapy should continue for the full course, at least 14 to 21 days in an immunosuppressed patient, because stopping or under-treating HSV encephalitis carries high mortality and neurological morbidity. The injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment. Methotrexate should stay withheld, because it is also cleared by the kidneys and would add toxicity.
notes: Wrong: oral valaciclovir is not recommended for acute HSV encephalitis while the patient is drowsy and still in the IV phase, and it is converted to aciclovir, so it would not prevent crystal formation.
Wrong: foscarnet is reserved for aciclovir-resistant HSV and is more nephrotoxic, so it would make her kidney injury worse.
Wrong: furosemide would deepen her volume depletion and does nothing to clear crystals, and keeping full-dose aciclovir at this clearance would cause further accumulation and toxicity.
Wrong: she has no indication for urgent dialysis (no hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemic complications), and this injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 11 pm by his mother with noisy breathing. He has had a runny nose and fever for 2 days, and this evening developed a barking cough and a hoarse cry. He is fully immunised and has no medical history. He weighs 12 kg. On arrival he was agitated, with stridor at rest, marked sternal and subcostal recession, and SpO2 91% in room air. He was given nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 (5 mL undiluted) and oral dexamethasone 7.2 mg (0.6 mg/kg), with oxygen held near his face. Sixty minutes later he is sitting on his mother's lap and playing. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 132/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and SpO2 97% in room air. He has an occasional barking cough, no stridor at rest and no chest wall recession. His mother would like to take him home now because his older sister is home alone with a neighbour. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge home now with written advice on when to return
Obtain a lateral neck X-ray before deciding on discharge
Give a second nebulised adrenaline treatment before discharge
Observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline treatment
Arrange admission to intensive care for elective intubation
questions.why: This child had severe croup: stridor at rest, a marked increase in work of breathing, agitation and hypoxaemia. Nebulised adrenaline works within minutes but wears off within about 2 hours. Dexamethasone takes several hours to reach full effect, so the obstruction can come back once the adrenaline wears off. The RCH Croup CPG says to observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose. Discharge is appropriate only if there is still no stridor at rest at that point, with clear safety-netting advice. The improvement at 60 minutes is likely the adrenaline effect and is not proof that the illness is settling. A mild tachycardia is expected after adrenaline. Discharging now risks the obstruction returning at home in the middle of the night. A lateral neck X-ray is not needed in typical croup, would not change management and could upset the child. Giving more adrenaline to a child with no stridor at rest has no benefit, and it would only restart the observation period. Intubation is for impending airway failure, such as exhaustion, ongoing hypoxaemia or repeated adrenaline needs, and this child has responded well.
notes: Correct: the adrenaline effect lasts only about 2 hours, before the steroid has fully taken effect, so the RCH advises observing for at least 3 hours after the last dose and discharging only if there is still no stridor at rest.
Wrong: croup is a clinical diagnosis and this course is typical, so imaging would not change management and upsetting the child can worsen obstruction.
Wrong: adrenaline is given for severe obstruction such as stridor at rest with marked work of breathing, and has no preventive role in a child who has none.
Wrong: intubation is kept for a tiring child, ongoing hypoxaemia or repeated adrenaline needs, none of which this improving child has.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner 6 weeks after she was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis. Before the diagnosis she had 10 weeks of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea and left-sided abdominal cramps. Stool pathogen tests were negative. Ileocolonoscopy found continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 30 cm and a normal proximal colon and terminal ileum. Biopsies showed crypt distortion with no granulomas and no dysplasia. She now takes oral mesalazine and mesalazine enemas. She has 1 to 2 formed stools a day with no blood. She has never smoked. Her mother was diagnosed with bowel cancer at age 62. No other relatives have had bowel cancer. Temperature is 36.7°C, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg and pulse 72/min. Her abdomen is soft and not tender. Haemoglobin is 129 g/L (115–165), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), ALP 74 U/L (30–110) and GGT 18 U/L (<40). She asks how her bowel cancer risk will be checked. Which of the following is the most appropriate surveillance plan for this patient?
options: Colonoscopy every 5 years from age 45
Colonoscopy from 8 years after disease onset
Faecal immunochemical test every 2 years from age 45
Colonoscopy every year starting now
CT colonography every 5 years starting now
questions.why: Ulcerative colitis that reaches beyond the rectum raises the risk of colorectal cancer. Her colitis runs from the rectum to 30 cm, so it is left-sided (Montreal E2) and not proctitis alone. The risk depends on how long she has had colitis, how much colon is involved and how much inflammation there is. Cancer Council Australia and GESA recommend a first colonoscopy about 8 years after symptoms began. This colonoscopy restages the disease and uses chromoendoscopy or multiple biopsies to look for dysplasia. After that, the interval (1, 3 or 5 years) is set by risk factors such as ongoing inflammation, strictures, past dysplasia, PSC and family history. Her mother's cancer at 62 may shorten later intervals, but it does not change the start point. Population or family-history screening does not apply to her, because her colitis is the bigger risk and needs colonoscopy with targeted biopsies. Annual colonoscopy straight away is only for coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.
notes: Colonoscopy every 5 years from 45 is family-history screening for a first-degree relative diagnosed under 55, which does not fit her history and starts too late for her colitis risk.
Two-yearly faecal immunochemical tests are average-risk population screening, and they cannot detect flat colitis-associated dysplasia or tell it apart from inflammatory bleeding.
Annual colonoscopy from diagnosis is for patients who also have primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.
CT colonography cannot take biopsies or show flat dysplasia, so it is not used for surveillance in inflammatory bowel disease.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 8 hours of constant, severe epigastric pain that radiates to her back, with repeated vomiting. The pain began 2 hours after a large evening meal. She drinks 2 standard drinks on weekends and does not smoke. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Her BMI is 34 kg/m2. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rigidity and no jaundice. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST changes. Results: lipase 2400 U/L (reference <60), white cell count 13.2 x10^9/L, CRP 40 mg/L, total bilirubin 22 µmol/L (<20), ALT 186 U/L (<35), ALP 140 U/L (30–110), corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.8 mmol/L and creatinine 78 µmol/L. IV fluids and titrated opioid analgesia have been started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the pancreas
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
Transabdominal hepatobiliary ultrasonography
Serum amylase concentration
questions.why: She already meets 2 of the 3 criteria for acute pancreatitis: typical epigastric pain going through to the back, and a lipase more than 3 times the upper limit. The diagnosis is made, so the next step is to find the cause. Gallstones cause about half of all cases. An early ALT above about 150 U/L strongly suggests a biliary cause, and her obesity and diabetes add to the risk. Her calcium and triglycerides are normal and she drinks little alcohol. Australian guidance (eTG) and international guidance say every patient with acute pancreatitis should have a transabdominal ultrasound on admission to look for gallstones and a dilated bile duct. This is because a gallstone cause changes management: ERCP if there is cholangitis or a persisting duct stone, and cholecystectomy in the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis. The test is quick, cheap, uses no radiation and can be done at the bedside. Early contrast CT does not help when the diagnosis is already clear. ERCP is for cholangitis or a proven obstruction that persists. MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound are second-line tests for when the ultrasound is unclear or no cause is found. Amylase adds nothing once the lipase is raised.
notes: Contrast CT is for when the diagnosis is uncertain, or for looking for necrosis if she deteriorates after 72 hours; the diagnosis is already made, and CT in the first days underestimates necrosis and is poor at showing gallstones.
ERCP is invasive, carries a risk of making pancreatitis worse, and in the early phase is only for cholangitis or a proven persisting bile duct obstruction, neither of which has been shown here.
MRCP is a second-line test for suspected duct stones when the ultrasound is unclear or the liver tests stay abnormal; it should not come before the first-line ultrasound.
Amylase is less specific than lipase and clears sooner, so it adds nothing to a lipase already more than 30 times the upper limit and does not show the cause.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man who works as a mechanic sees his general practitioner because of tiredness for 4 months. He drinks about 4 L of water a day. He gets up three times a night to pass urine, even when he avoids drinks in the evening. He has gained 15 kg over 2 years and has not lost weight recently. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and takes no other medicines. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. His father has type 2 diabetes. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 138/86 mm Hg and respiratory rate 14/min. His BMI is 36 kg/m². He has velvety, darkened skin in both axillae and looks well hydrated. Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+, ketones negative, protein negative and specific gravity 1.025. A random fingerprick reading on the practice meter is 15.2 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Oral glucose tolerance test
Water deprivation test
Glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies
Serum C-peptide level
Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c)
questions.why: This man has the typical symptoms of hyperglycaemia: thirst, polyuria and nocturia that continues when he drinks less in the evening. He also has metabolic risk factors: obesity, acanthosis nigricans, hypertension, smoking and a family history of type 2 diabetes. His urine is concentrated and full of glucose, and he has no ketones, which points to type 2 diabetes. A fingerprick meter reading is not enough to diagnose diabetes, so the RACGP handbook and eTG require a laboratory test. HbA1c is the most appropriate test. A level of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more diagnoses diabetes, he does not need to fast for it, and Medicare funds it for diagnosis. Because he has symptoms, one abnormal laboratory result is enough and no repeat test on another day is needed. A fasting or random venous plasma glucose would also be acceptable, but neither is among the options. An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for equivocal results or pregnancy. The water deprivation test, GAD antibodies and C-peptide do not confirm that he has diabetes.
notes: An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for equivocal fasting (5.5 to 6.9 mmol/L) or random (5.5 to 11.0 mmol/L) glucose results or for pregnancy, and it is unnecessary and burdensome in a patient with symptoms and marked hyperglycaemia.

A water deprivation test looks for diabetes insipidus, but his urine is concentrated (specific gravity 1.025) and full of glucose, which shows an osmotic diuresis, and fluid restriction could make his dehydration worse.

GAD antibodies help classify suspected type 1 diabetes or latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (for example in a lean patient with weight loss or ketosis), but they do not confirm that diabetes is present.
C-peptide measures how much insulin the pancreas can still make and helps classify the type of diabetes, but it does not diagnose diabetes and can be misleadingly low during hyperglycaemia.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner for her annual diabetes review. She has had type 2 diabetes for 14 years. Over the past 4 months, small print has become harder to read with her right eye, even with new reading glasses. She also has hypertension and dyslipidaemia. Her medicines are metformin 1 g twice daily, modified-release gliclazide 60 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Her last eye examination was 2 years ago. Blood pressure is 144/86 mmHg and pulse is 76/min. Visual acuity is 6/18 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left, and the right eye does not improve with a pinhole. Both lenses are clear. Good-quality non-mydriatic retinal photographs show microaneurysms and dot and blot haemorrhages in both eyes, and a ring of hard exudates within one disc diameter of the right fovea. There are no new vessels and no venous beading. HbA1c is 8.8% (73 mmol/mol). Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause of the reduced vision in her right eye?
options: Fundus fluorescein angiography
Optical coherence tomography
B-scan ocular ultrasonography
Automated visual field perimetry
Dilated repeat retinal photography
questions.why: She has non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes. In the right eye she has hard exudates near the fovea and slowly worsening central vision that a pinhole does not correct, so a refractive error is not the cause. This pattern points to diabetic macular oedema, which causes most vision loss in diabetes and can occur at any stage of retinopathy. Retinal photographs are two-dimensional and cannot show retinal thickening, so they cannot confirm or exclude macular oedema. The NHMRC diabetic retinopathy guideline and the RACGP handbook advise referral to an ophthalmologist. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the non-invasive test that confirms the diagnosis. It measures central retinal thickness, shows intraretinal and subretinal fluid, and is used to decide on and monitor anti-VEGF treatment. Fluorescein angiography is an invasive second-line test. Ultrasound is only needed when the fundus cannot be seen. Visual field testing and repeat photographs cannot assess retinal thickness.
notes: Fluorescein angiography is invasive, carries a risk of dye reactions, and is kept for assessing ischaemia or new vessels or for planning laser, so it is not the first test to confirm macular oedema.
B-scan ultrasound is used when the view of the retina is blocked, for example by vitreous haemorrhage or dense cataract, but her lenses are clear and the fundus can be seen.
Automated perimetry tests peripheral visual fields for glaucoma or neurological disease, and it cannot show the structural macular changes behind her central blur.
Repeat photographs after dilation give a better view but are still two-dimensional, so they cannot measure retinal thickness or reliably exclude macular oedema.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman, para 3, is in the birth suite 40 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth of twins at 37 weeks' gestation. The placenta is complete and there are no genital tract tears. She keeps bleeding despite intramuscular oxytocin, an oxytocin infusion, intramuscular ergometrine, intramuscular carboprost, an indwelling urinary catheter and bimanual compression. She has been given intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g. The weighed blood loss is 2,000 mL and the blood contains clots. She has no history of a bleeding disorder and takes no regular medicines. Her temperature is 36.3 °C, pulse is 130/min, blood pressure is 86/48 mm Hg, respirations are 26/min and SpO2 is 96% on 6 L/min of oxygen. The fundus is intermittently soft. Two 16-gauge cannulas are in place, the massive transfusion protocol has been activated, O-negative red cells are running and theatre is being prepared. Point-of-care haemoglobin is 82 g/L (reference 115–160 g/L). Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to guide further blood component replacement?
options: Serum D-dimer concentration
Activated partial thromboplastin time
Plasma fibrinogen (Clauss) concentration
Platelet count
Repeat haemoglobin concentration
questions.why: This woman has a major primary postpartum haemorrhage (2,000 mL and still bleeding) from uterine atony. Her risk factors are twins, which overdistend the uterus, and multiparity. Large blood loss leads to dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy, which makes the bleeding worse. In obstetric haemorrhage, fibrinogen is the first clotting factor to fall to a critical level. It falls well before the platelet count or the clotting times change. A fibrinogen level below 2 g/L is the best early lab predictor of progression to severe PPH. RANZCOG, the Queensland Clinical Guidelines and the National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Module 5 all advise measuring it (Clauss fibrinogen, or FIBTEM on viscoelastic testing where available) and repeating it often. Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is given to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L. The fact that she is forming clots does not rule out a falling fibrinogen.
