Adding immunoglobulin is for people with fewer than 3 doses or an unknown history, or who are immunocompromised. None of these applies to him.
Protection fades after a primary course. With his last dose over 15 years ago, he needs a booster whether or not the wound is tetanus-prone.
questions.why: Under the Australian Immunisation Handbook, a person with 3 or more documented doses needs a booster if the last dose was over 5 years ago for a tetanus-prone wound (over 10 years for a clean wound). Tetanus immunoglobulin is only for fewer than 3 or unknown doses, or immunocompromise.

questions.stem: Daniel, 32, was punched in the nose. Both sides of his septum have smooth, fluctuant, red-purple swellings that do not shrink with decongestant. You explain that without drainage today the septal cartilage may die, leaving a perforation or a saddle nose. What is the main mechanism of the cartilage necrosis?
options: It compresses the anterior ethmoidal artery, infarcting the cartilage's own vessels
Bacterial enzymes from nasal flora digest the cartilage within the first few hours
Raised pressure in Kiesselbach's plexus causes venous thrombosis within the cartilage
It lifts the mucoperichondrium off avascular cartilage that relies on it for nutrients
notes: The cartilage has no intrinsic vessels to infarct. The anterior ethmoidal artery supplies the mucosa, not vessels inside the cartilage.
Infection (septal abscess) is a later complication of an undrained haematoma. It is not the main early mechanism, and it does not happen within hours.
Kiesselbach's plexus is a mucosal plexus in Little's area. Thrombosis there does not explain necrosis of cartilage that has no blood vessels.
questions.why: Septal cartilage has no blood vessels of its own. It gets its nutrients by diffusion from the overlying mucoperichondrium. A haematoma separates the two, so the cartilage becomes ischaemic and can die within days. A bilateral haematoma is the highest risk.

questions.stem: Daniel's CT angiogram shows that the right external jugular vein is cut beneath a glass wound over the sternocleidomastoid. Before the wound was occluded, a sucking noise was heard with each inspiration while he sat upright. Which anatomical feature best explains why the cut vein stayed open and drew in air?
options: It lies within the carotid sheath, splinted open by the common carotid artery
It has no valves along its course, so air passes freely towards the heart
It pierces the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, which binds its wall open
It lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, which tents the vein open with each breath
notes: The internal jugular vein lies in the carotid sheath. The external jugular vein is superficial, outside the sheath.
The external jugular vein does have valves, near its end and above the clavicle, though they are often incompetent; whether it has valves does not explain why the cut wall stays open.
The external jugular vein crosses superficial to sternocleidomastoid, which is why it is visible and why this wound reached it.
questions.why: The external jugular vein runs superficial to sternocleidomastoid, deep to platysma. Above the clavicle it pierces the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, and its wall is fixed to that fascia there. A cut vein therefore stays open instead of collapsing, and negative venous pressure during inspiration draws air in.

questions.stem: In a GP clinic, you have told Minh Nguyen, 29, who has Crohn's disease, in plain words that his blood test shows long-term hepatitis B. He is anxious and asks: "Does this mean I can't have the new injection?" He wants treatment for his flare soon. Which response is best?
options: No; biologics aren't safe with hepatitis B, so we'll keep you on azathioprine alone.
Yes, after a short delay: an antiviral tablet starts first to keep the virus quiet.
Yes, straight away; your virus level is low, so it can't flare on the injection.
Not until the virus has fully cleared, which we'll recheck in about six months.
notes: Hepatitis B does not rule out biologics once he has antiviral cover, and azathioprine can reactivate the virus too, so staying on it alone gives no protection.
A low HBV DNA does not protect him: anyone who is HBsAg positive can reactivate on immunosuppression, so the biologic must wait for antiviral cover.
Chronic hepatitis B rarely clears, so waiting for clearance would mean leaving his flare untreated with no end date. Antiviral cover is what lets treatment go ahead.
questions.why: Chronic hepatitis B is not a reason to refuse a biologic. Antiviral prophylaxis is started first, so the biologic comes after a short delay. Saying this answers his real worry honestly and without jargon.

questions.stem: Minh Nguyen, 29, has Crohn's disease, takes azathioprine and is tapering prednisolone. He is about to start an anti-TNF agent. Results: HBsAg positive, total anti-HBc positive, IgM anti-HBc negative, HBeAg negative, HBV DNA 850 IU/mL, ALT 52 U/L, INR normal. Which hepatitis B plan is most appropriate?
options: Monitor HBV DNA and ALT 3-monthly; start an antiviral only if the DNA rises
Give a hepatitis B vaccine course and recheck anti-HBs before the biologic
Start lamivudine with the biologic and stop it once Crohn's is in remission
Start entecavir or tenofovir now; continue during and for 12+ months after
notes: Monitoring and acting only if the DNA rises is a plan for HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc-positive patients. In HBsAg-positive patients reactivation risk is high, so prophylaxis is needed.
He already has the infection (HBsAg positive), so vaccination cannot protect him. It is for his partner and household contacts if they are not immune.
Lamivudine quickly breeds resistance during long courses, and stopping it at remission is too early: reactivation can happen during and after immunosuppression.
questions.why: Anyone who is HBsAg positive needs antiviral prophylaxis before immunosuppression, whatever the viral load. The choice is entecavir 0.5 mg or tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg daily, given throughout immunosuppression and for at least 12 months after it stops, as the specialist advises.

questions.stem: Minh Nguyen, 29, has chronic hepatitis B, probably acquired from his mother at birth, with an HBV DNA of only 850 IU/mL. He asks why a virus at such a low level could cause a severe hepatitis once he starts biologic therapy. Which feature of hepatitis B biology best explains why it persists and can reactivate?
options: Covalently closed circular DNA stays in hepatocyte nuclei as a template for replication
Latent viral genomes persist in sensory ganglia and travel back along the axons
The virus persists mainly in B lymphocytes, which expand when T-cell control is lost
Replication requires integration into host DNA, which steroids switch on directly
notes: Latency in sensory ganglia is how herpesviruses such as varicella-zoster behave. HBV is hepatotropic and persists in hepatocytes.
Persistence in B cells describes Epstein-Barr virus. The HBV reservoir is the hepatocyte nucleus.
Integration of HBV DNA happens and contributes to HCC, but it is not needed for replication. The template for replication is cccDNA.
questions.why: HBV cccDNA sits as a stable minichromosome in the nuclei of infected hepatocytes, and antivirals do not remove it. When immunosuppression removes immune control, replication rises. The hepatitis that follows is caused by T cells destroying infected hepatocytes, often as immune function recovers.

questions.stem: Minh Nguyen, 29, has ileocolonic Crohn's disease with cramping right-sided abdominal pain. On examination he has tenderness and fullness in the right iliac fossa, which fits terminal ileal disease. If he later needs an ileocaecal resection, which artery supplies the terminal ileum, caecum and appendix?
options: Right colic artery, a branch of the superior mesenteric artery
Middle colic artery, a branch of the superior mesenteric artery
Ileocolic artery, the terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery
Left colic artery, a branch of the inferior mesenteric artery
notes: The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon, not the terminal ileum or caecum.
The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon.
The IMA and its left colic branch supply the distal transverse colon and the descending colon, not the right iliac fossa bowel.
questions.why: The ileocolic artery, the final branch of the SMA, supplies the terminal ileum, caecum and appendix (via the appendicular artery). It is the vessel divided in an ileocaecal resection for Crohn's disease.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old boy in the ED has 5 days of worsening forceful vomiting after feeds and is hungry straight afterwards. His mother thinks it is reflux. You are taking a focused history. Which question most urgently screens for a surgical emergency that must be excluded before anything else?
options: Does he arch his back or cry during and after feeds?
How many wet nappies has he had in the last 12 hours?
Has anyone else in the family had an operation as a baby?
Has any of the vomit ever been green or yellow?
notes: Back arching points towards reflux. It does not screen for a time-critical surgical cause.
Wet nappies help you judge how dehydrated he is, but they do not tell you whether there is an obstruction below the pylorus.
A parent who had pyloric stenosis supports that diagnosis, but pyloric stenosis is a surgical urgency, not the emergency you need to rule out first.
questions.why: Bilious (green) vomiting in an infant means malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. It needs an urgent contrast study and surgical review, so always ask directly about the colour of the vomit.

questions.stem: The 4.0 kg boy with pyloric stenosis has had a 40 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride. His HR is now 152 and CRT 2 s. His gas showed Cl 88, K 3.0 and HCO3 36. He is nil by mouth and has not passed urine yet. Which IV fluid plan is best for the next 24 hours?
options: 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at 24 mL/h
0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at 16 mL/h
0.45% sodium chloride with 2.5% glucose at 24 mL/h
0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at 33 mL/h
notes: 16 mL/h is maintenance only. It does not replace his deficit, so rehydration and correction of the alkalosis, and therefore surgery, are delayed.
Hypotonic fluid carries a risk of hyponatraemia and gives less of the chloride he needs to correct the alkalosis. Isotonic fluid is recommended.
33 mL/h replaces a 10% deficit in 24 hours. The RCH guideline replaces no more than 5% over 24 hours on top of maintenance.
questions.why: Maintenance for 4 kg is 16 mL/h. A 5% deficit is 200 mL over 24 h, about 8 mL/h, so the total is about 24 mL/h of isotonic 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose. The chloride corrects the hypochloraemic alkalosis. Add potassium once he is passing urine.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old boy has vomited gastric contents for 5 days and is about 9% dehydrated. His arrival venous gas shows pH 7.52, HCO3 36, Cl 88, K 3.0 and Na 134. What is the main cause of his low potassium?
options: Potassium lost directly in the gastric juice he has vomited
Potassium moving into cells because of the alkalaemia alone
Low potassium intake because he cannot keep his feeds down
Renal loss, as aldosterone drives distal Na+ reabsorption in exchange for K+ and H+
notes: Gastric juice contains only about 10 mmol/L of potassium, so what is lost in the vomit makes up only a small part of the deficit.
The alkalaemia does move some potassium into cells, but this shift is small and does not explain a fall to 3.0.
Low intake over a few days adds little; the kidneys conserve potassium well unless aldosterone is driving them to excrete it.
questions.why: Losing volume activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Aldosterone makes the distal nephron reabsorb sodium and secrete K+ and H+ in exchange. With so little chloride available, bicarbonate is also kept. So the potassium is lost mainly through the kidneys, and this also keeps the alkalosis going (paradoxical aciduria).

questions.stem: The ultrasound of this 5-week-old boy shows a pyloric muscle wall 5 mm thick and a channel 19 mm long. After he is rehydrated, the paediatric surgeon plans a pyloromyotomy. Which description best matches what the operation does?
options: The longitudinal muscle is divided across and then closed over the mucosa
The hypertrophied circular muscle is split lengthwise, leaving the mucosa intact
The full thickness of the wall is cut lengthwise and then sewn closed crosswise
The thickened mucosa and submucosa are cut out to widen the pyloric channel
notes: The thickened layer is the circular muscle, not the longitudinal muscle, and the muscle is split and left open, not divided across and closed.
Cutting through the full wall and closing it crosswise is a Heineke-Mikulicz pyloroplasty, an adult procedure that opens the bowel lumen.
The mucosa is not the thickened layer, and cutting it out would open the lumen and cause a leak.
questions.why: In pyloric stenosis it is mainly the circular muscle layer of the pylorus that hypertrophies. Ramstedt pyloromyotomy splits the serosa and this muscle lengthwise until the submucosa bulges into the gap. The mucosa is left intact, and an unrecognised mucosal perforation is the main complication to avoid.

questions.stem: In a GP consultation, Linh says: "Jasper has had this cough every day for five weeks and nothing is working." Jasper is 2 years 4 months old. Amoxicillin, prednisolone liquid and a salbutamol puffer with a spacer have all failed. Which history question is most likely to uncover a cause that earlier clinics missed?
options: "Is the cough worse at night, with cold air or when Jasper runs around?"
"Does anyone in the family have asthma, eczema or hay fever?"
"How did the cough start? Any choking or gagging while eating or playing?"
"Has Jasper been near anyone with tuberculosis, or travelled overseas?"
notes: Triggers like night, cold air and exercise point to asthma, which was already treated and did not respond; asking about them will not find a missed cause.
Asking about atopy and family history helps judge asthma risk, but asthma has already been treated without effect, and this question would not reveal the choking event.
TB is worth asking about when there is lobar collapse, but it is far less likely in a well toddler with no contact or travel, and it is not the cause most often missed here.
questions.why: Inhaled foreign body peaks at 1 to 3 years. The choking episode is often brief, and parents may forget it or not mention it, so you must ask directly about a sudden start and any choking or gagging (here, on mixed nuts) in any toddler whose cough has not responded to treatment.

questions.stem: Jasper, 2 years 4 months, choked on mixed nuts at a party 5 weeks ago and has coughed ever since. On the right he has reduced air entry, a dull base and a monophonic wheeze. The CXR shows right lower lobe collapse with volume loss. RR 44, SpO2 96% in room air, afebrile. What is the most appropriate next step from general practice?
options: Phone the paediatric team today for rigid bronchoscopy; keep Jasper nil by mouth
Book an outpatient CT chest and review Jasper with the result next week
Start amoxicillin–clavulanate for pneumonia and review in 48 hours
Arrange inspiratory and expiratory films, and refer only if air trapping is seen
notes: Waiting a week is unsafe, because the nut can move and block a larger airway. Even if CT were done, he would still need bronchoscopy to remove it.
This is a mechanical obstruction, so antibiotics will not fix it. He has already failed amoxicillin, and more antibiotics only delay diagnosis and raise the risk of bronchiectasis.
Normal extra films do not exclude a foreign body, and this history with focal signs already justifies bronchoscopy, so making referral depend on more imaging delays care.
questions.why: A suspected inhaled foreign body needs same-day referral to a paediatric centre for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia, which both confirms and removes it. Keep the child fasted for the anaesthetic, and call 000 if there is stridor, distress or falling SpO2.

questions.stem: Jasper's CXR shows a triangular opacity at the right lung base. The trachea and mediastinum are shifted to the right, the right hilum is lowered, and there are no air bronchograms and no effusion. He choked on nuts 5 weeks ago. What mechanism best explains this X-ray pattern?
options: Fluid in the right pleural space compressing the lower lobe
Ball-valve obstruction trapping air in the lobe beyond the nut
Inflammatory exudate filling the alveoli while lobe volume is kept
Complete bronchial block, with the trapped gas absorbed into capillary blood
notes: An effusion takes up space and pushes the mediastinum away from it, and the report says there is no effusion.
A ball-valve obstruction lets air in but not out, causing hyperinflation and a shift away from the affected side, which is the opposite of this film.
Consolidation keeps the lobe's volume, so there is no shift, and it usually shows air bronchograms. Neither fits this film.
questions.why: When a bronchus is completely blocked, the gas beyond it keeps diffusing into pulmonary capillary blood, whose total gas pressure is below atmospheric, so the lobe deflates (absorption atelectasis). The resulting volume loss pulls the trachea, mediastinum and hilum towards the collapsed side.

questions.stem: Jasper's frontal CXR shows a triangular opacity at the right base, medially and behind the heart. The outline of the medial right hemidiaphragm is lost but the right heart border is preserved. Which lobe has collapsed, and on what anatomical basis?
options: Right middle lobe, as it lies against the right heart border
Right lower lobe, as it lies posteriorly on the diaphragm behind the heart
Right upper lobe, as it collapses down towards the right hilum
Right middle and lower lobes together, below the oblique fissure
notes: Middle lobe collapse would blur the right heart border, which is preserved here, and it would not usually hide the medial hemidiaphragm.
Upper lobe collapse causes an opacity at the top of the lung and lifts the hilum, but this hilum is lowered and the opacity is at the base.
If the middle lobe were also collapsed, the right heart border would be lost as well, but here it is preserved.
questions.why: Silhouette sign: when the hemidiaphragm outline is lost but the right heart border stays sharp, the disease is in the lower lobe, which sits posteriorly on the diaphragm. The middle lobe lies against the right atrium, so middle lobe disease blurs the right heart border.

questions.stem: Liam, 10, has moderate intellectual disability and uses only a few single words. He has settled with his tablet after you greeted him with simple words and gestures. His parent says he hits his own tummy. You are about to examine his abdomen at the GP clinic. Which approach is most likely to pick up tenderness reliably?
options: Ask him to rate his pain 0 to 10 on a number scale as you press each quadrant
Let him keep his tablet, palpate gently starting away from the area and watch his face
Start with deep palpation of the left iliac fossa to find the sore spot quickly
Ask his parent to hold his arms still so you can complete a full abdominal exam
notes: A numeric rating scale needs language and number concepts that Liam does not have, so his answers would not be reliable.
Starting deep at the likely painful spot will upset him, and then you cannot tell tenderness anywhere else from general distress.
Holding him down is distressing and makes guarding hard to interpret. Calm engagement got his cooperation in this station.
questions.why: In a non-verbal child, pain is judged from behaviour: grimacing, guarding and a rise in heart rate. Keeping him calm with a familiar object and palpating gently, starting away from the suspected area, lets you see these signs before distress hides them.

questions.stem: Liam, 10, 31 kg, passes hard pellet stools every 4 to 5 days and has soiled twice this week. He has a firm, tender left iliac fossa mass. He is afebrile, not vomiting and his abdomen is not distended. You are his GP. Which is the most appropriate first treatment for his faecal loading?
options: Oral macrogol, increasing the daily sachets until stools are soft and runny
Sodium phosphate enema in the clinic today, then advice on dietary fibre
Increase dietary fibre and fluids alone, and review him in 4 weeks
Lactulose 10 mL twice daily on its own until the stools soften
notes: Australian paediatric guidelines advise against enemas as first-line treatment in children. They are invasive and distressing, and phosphate enemas risk electrolyte problems, especially in a child who cannot cooperate.
Fibre and fluids support maintenance but cannot clear an established faecal mass. Waiting 4 weeks leaves him in pain.
Lactulose on its own is less effective than macrogol for disimpaction and often causes bloating and cramps.
questions.why: For a child with faecal impaction, first-line treatment is oral macrogol disimpaction, with the dose increased step by step (RCH guideline) until the stools are soft and runny. Maintenance then continues for months, along with fluids, fibre and a toileting routine.

questions.stem: Liam, 10, had his risperidone increased to 0.5 mg twice a day 6 weeks ago. Since then his parent says he is stiffer, drools more and cannot sit still. On examination at the GP clinic he has mild cogwheel rigidity and a tremor. Which mechanism best explains these findings?
options: Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the mesolimbic pathway
Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway
Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway
Serotonin 5-HT2A receptor blockade in the cerebral cortex
notes: Mesolimbic D2 blockade produces the intended antipsychotic and anti-aggression effect, not rigidity or tremor.
Tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade raises prolactin, which risperidone often does, but it does not cause movement disorders.
5-HT2A antagonism actually lowers the risk of extrapyramidal effects with atypical antipsychotics. It does not cause them.
questions.why: Blocking D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway upsets the dopamine and acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia. This causes extrapyramidal effects: parkinsonism (rigidity, tremor, drooling) and akathisia. Akathisia can look like agitation and lead to the dose being wrongly increased.

questions.stem: Liam, 10, is non-verbal. He has been pulling at the left side of his face and refusing crunchy food. At the GP clinic you find a carious, tender lower left molar with swelling of the gum next to it. Which nerve carries pain from the pulp of this tooth?
options: Posterior superior alveolar nerve, from the maxillary division
Buccal branch of the facial nerve
Lingual nerve, from the mandibular division
Inferior alveolar nerve, from the mandibular division
notes: The posterior superior alveolar nerve (V2) supplies the upper molars, not the lower teeth.
The facial nerve's buccal branch is motor to the muscles of facial expression. It carries no sensation from the teeth.
The lingual nerve carries general sensation from the front two-thirds of the tongue and the lingual gum, not from the tooth pulp.
questions.why: The mandibular teeth get their sensory supply from the inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve. It runs through the mandibular canal. Because V3 also supplies the ear and temple, dental pain can be referred there, which fits Liam pulling at his face.

questions.stem: Margaret Hollis, 74, is in ED with right upper quadrant pain and known gallstones. You tell the examiner you will now test for Murphy's sign. Which technique correctly tests for Murphy's sign?
options: Press deep in the right iliac fossa, then let go quickly and watch for pain
Fingers under the right costal margin, midclavicular line, as she breathes in deeply
Press in the left iliac fossa and ask whether she feels pain in the right iliac fossa
Hand over the right lower ribs, strike it gently with the other fist and watch for pain
notes: This tests for rebound tenderness, a sign of peritonism. It does not test the gallbladder.
This is Rovsing's sign, used in suspected appendicitis. It does not test the gallbladder.
This is a liver or renal punch test. It is non-specific and is not Murphy's sign.
questions.why: Murphy's sign: press under the right costal margin at the midclavicular line and ask her to breathe in deeply. If she stops breathing in suddenly from pain, the sign is positive, because the inflamed gallbladder moves down onto your fingers. It suggests acute cholecystitis and should not happen on the left. Margaret's is negative.

questions.stem: Margaret, 74, has potassium 2.8 mmol/L, flattened T waves and new U waves, and creatinine 128 µmol/L (baseline 78). She is nil by mouth and vomiting, with a peripheral cannula and cardiac monitoring in the ED. How should her potassium be replaced?
options: IV KCl diluted in fluid via the peripheral line at no more than 10 mmol/h, repeating UEC
KCl 20 mmol undiluted as a slow IV push over 5 minutes to reverse the ECG changes
Oral slow-release KCl 1.2 g tablets, two tablets three times daily with water
Hold all potassium until the kidney injury resolves, to avoid causing hyperkalaemia
notes: Undiluted potassium given by bolus can cause fatal arrhythmias and cardiac arrest; IV KCl must always be diluted and infused at a controlled rate.
She is nil by mouth with a bowel obstruction and vomiting, so oral tablets will not be absorbed reliably and need IV replacement instead.
A prerenal AKI with urine still being made does not stop cautious replacement; leaving potassium at 2.8 with ECG changes risks arrhythmia.
questions.why: She has moderate hypokalaemia with ECG changes and cannot take anything orally, so give diluted IV KCl. Through a peripheral line the rate should be no more than 10 mmol/h, with cardiac monitoring and repeat potassium (and magnesium) checks.

questions.stem: Margaret, 74, has vomited about 6 times a day for 2 days and can barely drink. Venous gas: pH 7.43, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, chloride 93 mmol/L, potassium 2.8 mmol/L. Creatinine has risen from 78 to 128 micromol/L. Which mechanism causes most of her potassium loss?
options: Renal loss, as aldosterone and distal bicarbonate delivery drive collecting duct secretion
Direct loss in the vomit, because gastric juice is very rich in potassium
Potassium moving into cells because of the rise in blood pH alone
Low intake over 2 days while the kidneys keep holding on to potassium normally
notes: Gastric juice holds little potassium (about 5 to 10 mmol/L). Its loss mainly removes hydrogen and chloride ions, which causes the alkalosis.
Alkalosis moves a little potassium into cells, but her mild alkalosis cannot explain a potassium of 2.8 on its own.
Low intake adds a little, but the kidneys are not conserving potassium here: aldosterone and bicarbonaturia make them lose it.
questions.why: Most of the potassium is lost through the kidneys, not in the vomit. Losing fluid switches on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and the extra bicarbonate reaching the distal nephron increases potassium secretion by principal cells. Gastric juice holds only about 5 to 10 mmol/L of potassium.

questions.stem: Margaret, 74, has known gallstones and has never had biliary surgery or ERCP. Her X-ray shows small bowel obstruction, gas in the biliary tree and a 3 cm calcified stone in the right lower quadrant. By which route has the stone most likely reached the small bowel?
options: Through the ampulla of Vater after passing down the common bile duct
Through a fistula between the gallbladder and the hepatic flexure of the colon
Through a fistula between the gallbladder and the gastric antrum
Through a fistula between the gallbladder and the duodenum
notes: A 3 cm stone cannot pass through the ampulla. Gas in the biliary tree without a previous sphincterotomy points to a fistula.
A stone that enters the colon does not reach the terminal ileum. It usually passes, or if it lodges, it lodges in the sigmoid colon.
Fistulas into the stomach are rare, and a stone that impacts there blocks the gastric outlet (Bouveret syndrome), not the terminal ileum.
questions.why: Repeated inflammation sticks the gallbladder to the duodenum, which lies right next to it, and a fistula forms. The stone passes through it and lodges at the terminal ileum, the narrowest part of the small bowel. Air passes back through the fistula, which gives the pneumobilia.

questions.stem: Daniel, 27, has newly confirmed HIV-1 with a viral load of 86,000 copies/mL. He lives with his partner Sam and they do not use condoms. He asks: "When will I stop being a risk to Sam through sex?" Which plain-language answer is most accurate?
options: "Once you have taken your tablets every day for about four weeks."
"Once your viral load has stayed undetectable for at least six months."
"Once your CD4 count has climbed back up into the normal range."
"Only if Sam also takes PrEP, because treatment alone never removes the risk."
notes: Four weeks of ART lowers the viral load but rarely makes it undetectable, and U=U needs 6 months of sustained suppression, not just a set number of weeks of tablets.
Whether HIV is passed on depends on the viral load, not the CD4 count. The CD4 count can stay below normal even when the viral load is fully suppressed.
A viral load that stays suppressed prevents sexual transmission on its own. PrEP protects Sam only during the time before Daniel is durably undetectable.
questions.why: U=U: people on ART whose viral load has stayed below 200 copies/mL for at least 6 months do not pass HIV on through sex. Until then, condoms (or PrEP for Sam) are still needed.

questions.stem: Daniel, 27, has newly confirmed HIV-1. CD4 410 cells/microlitre (22%), viral load 86,000 copies/mL, no transmitted resistance, HLA-B*5701 negative, eGFR above 90, not immune to hepatitis B. He feels well and asks whether he really needs tablets yet. On current Australian guidance, what is the best plan for ART?
options: Defer ART until CD4 falls below 350 cells/microlitre, with CD4 checks every 3 months
Offer ART soon, whatever the CD4 count, once he is ready to commit to daily dosing
Start trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis now and begin ART in 6 months
Defer ART until hepatitis B vaccination is complete and immunity is confirmed
notes: Waiting for the CD4 count to fall is outdated practice; trials such as START showed clear benefit from treating straight away at higher CD4 counts.
Pneumocystis prophylaxis is for a CD4 below 200 or below 14%, which he does not have, and there is no reason to delay ART.
Vaccination can be given alongside ART; waiting for it leaves him with a high viral load and very infectious for months.
questions.why: Australian (and international) guidelines recommend offering ART to everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count, starting soon after diagnosis. Early ART protects his immune system and, once he is undetectable, prevents transmission.

questions.stem: Daniel, 27, with newly diagnosed HIV-1, has been told ART will make his viral load undetectable within 3 to 6 months. He asks why he can't stop the tablets once the virus is undetectable. What is the main reason HIV rebounds within weeks when ART is stopped?
options: Integrated provirus in long-lived resting memory CD4 T cells is not touched by ART
Ongoing reverse transcriptase errors make the virus resistant to every regimen in time
Free virions persist in plasma at a level just below the viral load assay's limit
HIV persists in B cells and plasma cells, which antiretroviral drugs cannot enter
notes: With good adherence, suppressive combination ART prevents resistance from emerging; resistance is a consequence of poor adherence, not why rebound happens.
Any very low-level viraemia comes from the reservoir and is not the source of rebound; the long-lived pool of integrated provirus is.
B cells don't carry CD4, so they aren't a major HIV reservoir. The latent reservoir is mainly in resting memory CD4 T cells.
questions.why: HIV integrates its DNA into the host genome. In latently infected resting memory CD4 T cells this provirus is silent, so ART, which only blocks new rounds of replication, cannot clear it. When those cells reactivate off treatment, the virus rebounds.

questions.stem: Daniel, 27, had a seroconversion-type illness 2 months ago and now has confirmed HIV-1 with a blood CD4 count of 410 cells/microlitre. He asks whether his blood test shows all of the damage. In acute HIV infection, where does the earliest and greatest loss of CD4 T cells occur?
options: Thymic cortex, where T cell precursors undergo maturation and selection
Bone marrow, where the common lymphoid progenitor cells arise and divide
Red pulp of the spleen, where old and damaged blood cells are filtered out
Lamina propria of the gut mucosa, part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue
notes: The thymus can be affected in HIV, but it holds immature T cells with little CCR5 and is not where most CD4 cells are lost in acute infection.
Bone marrow progenitors aren't the main target of HIV, and haematopoiesis is largely preserved in early infection.
The red pulp filters blood cells and holds few CCR5-expressing memory CD4 T cells, so it is not where massive early depletion occurs.
questions.why: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue contains most of the body's CCR5-expressing activated memory CD4 T cells, so it is severely depleted within weeks of infection, well before the blood CD4 count shows it. The blood CD4 count underestimates the early damage.

questions.stem: Mrs Halloran, 52, comes to your suburban GP clinic. She woke two days ago with hearing loss in her left ear. Otoscopy is normal in both ears. You do Weber and Rinne tests with a 512 Hz tuning fork. Which pair of findings points to a left sensorineural loss?
options: Weber lateralises to the left; Rinne negative on the left
Weber lateralises to the right; Rinne positive on both sides
Weber lateralises to the left; Rinne positive on both sides
Weber is central; Rinne negative on the left
notes: This is the pattern for a left conductive loss, such as wax or an effusion: the sound goes to the affected ear and bone conduction beats air conduction.
A Weber that goes to the left with a positive Rinne on both sides does not fit either pattern; a left sensorineural loss sends the Weber away from the left ear.
A central Weber means the two ears are symmetrical, and a negative left Rinne would mean a conductive loss, so this fits neither picture.
questions.why: In sensorineural loss the Weber is heard in the better (right) ear, and the Rinne stays positive on both sides because the middle ear still conducts air better than bone. Tuning forks only screen, so confirm with an audiogram.

questions.stem: Mrs Halloran, 52 and 72 kg, has a new left sensorineural loss of 40 to 70 dB on today's audiogram, which started two days ago. She has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.4%) and an eGFR of 87. You have contacted ENT and requested an MRI of the internal auditory canals. What is the most appropriate treatment to start in general practice today?
options: Hold steroids until MRI excludes a vestibular schwannoma, then start prednisolone
Oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for 5 days, a lower dose because of her diabetes
Oral valaciclovir with prednisolone to cover a viral cochleitis after her cold
Oral prednisolone about 1 mg/kg (capped near 60 to 70 mg) each morning, then taper
notes: The MRI must not delay steroids. Treatment is time-critical, and the MRI is still needed later whatever the response.
Lowering the dose because of diabetes undertreats a time-critical condition. The answer is to monitor and manage her glucose, not to reduce the steroid.
Antivirals have not been shown to help in sudden sensorineural hearing loss and are not recommended, even after a viral illness.
questions.why: Start high-dose oral prednisolone (about 1 mg/kg, capped at the local maximum) the same day, without waiting for the MRI, because earlier treatment gives a better chance of recovery. Diabetes is a reason to plan glucose monitoring, not to lower the dose.

questions.stem: Mrs Halloran, 52, has type 2 diabetes on metformin. She will start prednisolone 60 mg at 8 am with breakfast for sudden sensorineural hearing loss. Her BGL this morning is 8.2 mmol/L. Which mechanism best explains the glucose pattern you warn her to expect?
options: Hepatic gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, peaking in the afternoon and evening
Glucagon surge overnight, causing the highest readings fasting on waking
Direct beta-cell toxicity, causing sustained absolute insulin deficiency
Reduced metformin absorption, raising glucose evenly across the whole day
notes: A single morning dose of prednisolone mostly wears off overnight, so fasting readings are usually the least affected. A peak on waking is the opposite of the usual pattern.
Steroids impair insulin action and secretion reversibly. They do not destroy beta cells or cause absolute insulin deficiency like type 1 diabetes.
Prednisolone does not meaningfully reduce metformin absorption, and the rise in glucose is not even across the day; it follows the timing of the dose.
questions.why: Glucocorticoids increase hepatic gluconeogenesis and cause peripheral insulin resistance. A morning dose of prednisolone raises glucose mainly in the afternoon and evening, so that is when she should check her BGL, and fasting readings may stay near baseline.

questions.stem: Mrs Halloran, 52, has diabetes and hypertension, her mother had a stroke, and she was briefly unsteady yesterday. She now has sudden left sensorineural hearing loss. You consider an anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) stroke. Why can an AICA infarct cause sudden one-sided hearing loss?
options: The cochlea is supplied by the stylomastoid artery, a branch of AICA
AICA supplies the primary auditory cortex in the superior temporal gyrus
The labyrinthine artery, the inner ear's end-artery supply, usually arises from AICA
AICA supplies the medial geniculate body, the thalamic relay for hearing
notes: The stylomastoid artery comes from the posterior auricular or occipital artery and supplies the middle ear and facial canal, not the cochlea.
The auditory cortex is supplied by the middle cerebral artery, and because hearing is represented on both sides, a one-sided cortical lesion does not cause one-sided deafness.
The medial geniculate body is supplied by branches of the posterior cerebral artery, and a one-sided lesion above the cochlear nuclei does not cause one-sided deafness.
questions.why: The labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery usually arises from AICA. It runs with cranial nerves VII and VIII in the internal acoustic meatus and is an end artery to the cochlea and vestibule, so an AICA occlusion can cause sudden one-sided deafness and vertigo.

questions.stem: You are resuscitating Jenny, 51, in day-surgery recovery 3 hours after a hysteroscopy and D&C for heavy irregular bleeding. She is pale and in pain, and you suspect bleeding inside her abdomen. She asks quietly, "Did they find cancer? Is something wrong with me?" Histology has not been reported. What is the best response?
options: "No, the operation was recorded as uneventful, so cancer is very unlikely."
"The tissue results aren't back yet; right now I'm treating bleeding inside your tummy."
"Your scan showed a thick womb lining, so cancer is likely, but we will know soon."
"That's for your surgeon to discuss with you at your follow-up clinic appointment."
notes: This is false reassurance: an uneventful operation record says nothing about histology, and her 14 mm endometrium at 51 means cancer has not been excluded.
This guesses at a diagnosis before histology, causes needless distress, and doesn't address the emergency happening right now.
This brushes off a frightened patient and says nothing about the urgent problem that is being treated.
questions.why: Be honest that the histology isn't back, don't guess either way, and tell her plainly what you're dealing with now and what you're doing about it. She is reassured by honesty and a clear plan.

questions.stem: Jenny, 51, has been given 1 L of crystalloid and oxygen after her D&C. BP is now 96/60 (125/75 pre-op), HR 114, CRT 3 s, no urine. Hb 98 g/L (126 pre-op), lactate 3.8, lower abdominal guarding, shoulder-tip pain. Fat-like tissue was noted in the curettings. The MET team is present. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Transfuse red cells now and arrange urgent laparoscopy or laparotomy
Give a further 1 L crystalloid bolus and reassess in 30 minutes
Arrange urgent contrast CT abdomen and pelvis before deciding on surgery
Repeat haemoglobin in one hour and transfuse if it falls below 70 g/L
notes: Shock that has not responded to crystalloid means ongoing haemorrhage. More crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and red cells and worsens coagulopathy, so it should be limited.
CT is for a perforation in a stable patient. An unstable, peritonitic patient should not leave for the scanner, and surgery is needed whatever the scan shows.
An early haemoglobin underestimates acute blood loss. Transfusion in active haemorrhage is guided by haemodynamics and ongoing loss, not by waiting for a threshold.
questions.why: Her shock barely responded to 1 L of crystalloid, so she is still bleeding. She needs blood now (O negative or group-specific if crossmatched blood is not ready, with the MTP if bleeding is major) and surgical control. Fat in the curettings means uterine perforation, and she must be explored for visceral injury.

questions.stem: Part 2 asks about Jenny's risk of uterine cancer. She is 51, nulliparous, weighs 108 kg, has type 2 diabetes and has had irregular, heavy cycles for 2 years. Her pre-operative ultrasound showed a 14 mm endometrium. What is the main mechanism by which her obesity raises her risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer?
options: Adipose aromatase converts androgens to oestrone, unopposed by progesterone in anovulation
Hyperinsulinaemia raises SHBG, increasing the free oestradiol reaching the endometrium
Persistent corpus luteum secretes excess progesterone, driving endometrial proliferation
Raised FSH in the perimenopause directly stimulates endometrial gland proliferation
notes: Hyperinsulinaemia lowers SHBG, not raises it; that is how it increases free oestrogen.
Progesterone protects the endometrium; she is likely anovulatory, so she has too little progesterone, not too much.
FSH acts on ovarian follicles, not directly on the endometrium.
questions.why: Aromatase in fat converts androstenedione to oestrone. With anovulatory cycles there is no luteal progesterone to oppose it, and unopposed oestrogen (helped by hyperinsulinaemia and IGF-1) drives hyperplasia and endometrioid cancer.

questions.stem: Jenny, 51, is 3 hours after a D&C in which the curette probably perforated the uterus. She has lower abdominal guarding, intra-abdominal bleeding and new pain at the tip of her right shoulder, which hurts more when she breathes deeply. Which nerve pathway best explains her shoulder-tip pain?
options: Uterine visceral afferents entering the cord at T10–L1, referred to the shoulder
Lower intercostal nerves supplying the peripheral diaphragmatic peritoneum
Vagal afferents from the liver capsule, referred via the cervical plexus
Phrenic nerve (C3–C5) from diaphragmatic peritoneum, referred to the C4 dermatome
notes: Uterine afferents at T10–L1 refer pain to the lower abdomen, lower back and thighs, not the shoulder.
The lower intercostal nerves supply the peripheral diaphragm and refer pain to the lower chest and abdominal wall, not the shoulder.
Liver capsule stretch causes right upper quadrant pain; vagal afferents don't produce somatic referred pain to the shoulder.
questions.why: Blood tracks up and irritates the peritoneum under the central diaphragm, which is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5). The pain is referred to the shoulder tip, the C4 dermatome supplied by the supraclavicular nerves, which share those segments.

questions.stem: You are the team leader in birth suite room 1. A 24-year-old woman gave birth vaginally 40 minutes ago and is still bleeding heavily with clots. Help has been called. On palpation the fundus is soft, boggy and above the umbilicus. The placenta was checked and is complete. What is your immediate manual action?
options: Perform a speculum examination to look for a cervical or vaginal tear
Rub up a contraction with fundal massage and expel clots from the uterus
Begin bimanual uterine compression with a fist in the anterior fornix
Explore the uterine cavity manually at the bedside for retained tissue
notes: You do inspect for trauma, but with a soft fundus the uterus has to be contracted first. Here inspection showed only a graze.
Bimanual compression is the next manual step if bleeding continues despite fundal massage and uterotonics. It is not the first thing you do.
The placenta and membranes were checked complete. Manual exploration needs anaesthesia and is done in theatre, not as a first bedside step.
questions.why: A soft, boggy fundus means atony (Tone). The first manual step is to rub up a contraction with fundal massage and expel clots, done alongside emptying the bladder and giving uterotonics.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old, 40 minutes after vaginal birth, has lost 1,500 mL and is still bleeding with HR 140 and BP 90/50. Fundal massage and uterotonics are under way. Bloods show fibrinogen 2.3 g/L, INR 1.1 and platelets 168. How should tranexamic acid be given?
options: 1 g IV, but only if a repeat fibrinogen falls below 2 g/L
2 g orally now, repeated after 6 hours if bleeding persists
1 g IV over 10 minutes now; a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 min
1 g IV over 10 minutes, starting once crossmatched blood arrives
notes: Tranexamic acid is not held back for a low fibrinogen. It is given early in all PPH, and fibrinogen is replaced separately with cryoprecipitate.
An oral dose is too slowly absorbed for a woman who is actively bleeding and in shock. The IV route is standard.
Tranexamic acid should not wait for blood products. The benefit falls with every delay, so give it now alongside resuscitation.
questions.why: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes should be given as soon as possible, and within 3 hours of birth, in every PPH. Give a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes. The benefit falls the longer it is delayed.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with a major primary PPH has lost about 1,500 mL in 40 minutes and has HR 140 and BP 90/50. Her booking Hb was 124 g/L. The first Hb, taken when the cannula went in, is 96 g/L. Why does this early Hb underestimate how much blood she has lost?
options: Splenic contraction releases stored red cells and raises the Hb for the first few hours
An erythropoietin surge releases reticulocytes quickly, which hides the fall in Hb
Whole blood is lost, so Hb falls only as plasma refill and IV fluids dilute what remains
The lower Hb of pregnancy has a dilutional floor, so the Hb cannot fall any further
notes: Splenic red cell reserve is small in humans and does not explain the gap; the main reason is that whole blood is lost.
Erythropoietin-driven reticulocytosis takes days to appear, not minutes, so it cannot mask an acute fall.
There is no floor stopping the Hb from falling. Pregnancy haemodilution lowers the baseline, but Hb can still fall steeply as the blood is diluted.
questions.why: Acute haemorrhage loses cells and plasma together, so the Hb concentration barely changes at first. It falls only over hours as interstitial fluid moves into the vessels and crystalloid is given. Transfuse on the clinical picture and ongoing loss, not on the early Hb.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old has a major PPH from uterine atony that is not responding to uterotonics and a balloon tamponade. The consultant asks interventional radiology to embolise the uterine arteries, reaching them through the femoral artery. Which vessel do the uterine arteries arise from?
options: The external iliac artery
The posterior division of the internal iliac artery
The ovarian artery, a branch of the abdominal aorta
The anterior division of the internal iliac artery
notes: The external iliac artery supplies the lower limb and gives the inferior epigastric artery, not the uterine artery.
The posterior division gives parietal branches (iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal), not visceral pelvic branches.
The ovarian artery joins the uterine artery near the cornua, but the main supply to the uterus is the uterine artery from the internal iliac.
questions.why: The uterine artery branches from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. It runs in the base of the broad ligament and crosses above the ureter beside the cervix. This is the target for embolisation and for surgical ligation in PPH that does not respond to treatment.

questions.stem: Hannah, 36, is 12 weeks 4 days pregnant and in a fetal medicine clinic. Her NIPT result is valid (fetal fraction 9%) and shows a high chance of trisomy 16. Her 12-week scan was normal. She believed NIPT tests the baby's own DNA and gives a definite answer. Which explanation is most appropriate to give her?
options: Because your scan was normal, this result is most likely a laboratory error
It's a screening test of mostly placental DNA, so only a diagnostic test can tell us
The test is about 99% accurate, so your baby very likely has trisomy 16
We'll repeat the blood test, and that will tell us whether the baby is affected
notes: This is false reassurance. A normal 12-week scan cannot exclude mosaic trisomy 16, and a valid high-chance result needs diagnostic testing.

The published high accuracy figures apply mainly to trisomy 21. For rare autosomal trisomies the positive predictive value is low, mostly because of confined placental mosaicism, so this overstates the risk.
A repeat NIPT measures the same placental DNA, so it cannot diagnose the fetus and would only delay diagnostic testing.
questions.why: Most of the cell-free DNA that NIPT measures comes from the placenta, so the test gives a chance, not a diagnosis. A high-chance result must be confirmed by a diagnostic test (here, amniocentesis) before any decision is made.

questions.stem: Hannah, 36, is 12 weeks 4 days pregnant. She has a valid high-chance NIPT result for trisomy 16 (fetal fraction 9%), and her 12-week scan was structurally normal. After non-directive counselling she wants to find out whether the baby is affected. Which diagnostic approach should be offered?
options: Amniocentesis from about 15 weeks
Chorionic villus sampling at 12 to 13 weeks
Repeat NIPT in 4 weeks, then test if still high chance
Morphology scan at 18 to 20 weeks, then test if abnormal
notes: CVS samples chorionic villi, which probably carry trisomy 16. The result may be falsely positive or mosaic and then need an amniocentesis anyway.
A repeat NIPT analyses the same placental cell-free DNA, so it would probably stay high chance, cannot diagnose and delays decisions.
A normal morphology scan cannot exclude mosaic trisomy 16, and waiting until 20 weeks narrows her options for no gain.
questions.why: For a rare autosomal trisomy, amniocentesis is preferred. It samples amniocytes of fetal origin, whereas the placenta probably carries the trisomy. It is done from about 15 weeks and the procedure-related miscarriage risk is under 1%.

questions.stem: Hannah, 36, is 12 weeks 4 days pregnant. She is reading her NIPT report, which says 'fetal fraction 9% (minimum for a result 4%)', and asks what this number means. What does the fetal fraction measure?
options: The proportion of fetal cells among the nucleated cells in her blood
The proportion of sequencing reads that map to chromosome 16
The probability that the high-chance result is a true positive
The proportion of cell-free DNA in her plasma that comes from the placenta
notes: NIPT analyses fragments of cell-free DNA, not intact fetal cells, which are very scarce in maternal blood.
An excess of chromosome 16 reads is the signal used to call the trisomy. Fetal fraction is a quality measure of the whole sample.
That is the positive predictive value, which depends on prevalence and placental mosaicism and is low for rare autosomal trisomies. Fetal fraction does not tell you this.
questions.why: Fetal fraction is the share of total cell-free DNA in maternal plasma that comes from the placenta (mainly apoptotic trophoblast). It must reach a threshold for a reliable result. It is lower earlier in pregnancy and at higher maternal weight.

questions.stem: During your focused examination of Hannah, 36, G2P1, who is 12 weeks 4 days pregnant with a singleton and dates confirmed on scan, you palpate her abdomen to assess uterine size. Where would you expect to find the uterine fundus at this gestation?
options: Not palpable, as the uterus stays a pelvic organ until about 16 weeks
Midway between the pubic symphysis and the umbilicus
At the level of the umbilicus
Just palpable above the pubic symphysis
notes: The uterus becomes an abdominal organ at about 12 weeks, not 16, so the fundus is usually just palpable at this gestation.
A fundus midway between the symphysis and the umbilicus fits about 16 weeks. That would be large for dates here.
A fundus at the umbilicus fits about 20 weeks. That would be much larger than expected at 12 weeks 4 days.
questions.why: The uterus rises out of the pelvis at about 12 weeks, so the fundus can just be felt above the pubic symphysis. It reaches midway to the umbilicus at about 16 weeks and the umbilicus at about 20 weeks.

questions.stem: Mrs Rao, 33, is on the birth suite with a primary PPH of 1,500 mL. Her fundus stays soft despite fundal massage and oxytocin. She has had analgesia and has agreed to bimanual compression. The examiner asks you to show it on the model. Where do you place your hands?
options: Fist in the posterior fornix; abdominal hand pressing the fundus down towards the pelvis
Fist inside the uterine cavity; abdominal hand pressing firmly over the suprapubic region
Fist in the anterior fornix; abdominal hand behind the uterus, pressing it forwards
Two fingers on the cervix; abdominal hand rubbing the fundus in firm circular movements
notes: A fist in the posterior fornix does not give a firm surface to squeeze the uterine body against, and pushing the fundus down only moves the uterus without compressing it.
Putting a hand inside the uterine cavity is manual exploration or removal under anaesthesia, not bimanual compression, and suprapubic pressure does not compress the uterine body.
Fingers on the cervix with fundal rubbing is just fundal massage, which has already failed; it does not compress the uterus between two hands.
questions.why: In bimanual compression a closed fist goes in the anterior vaginal fornix and the abdominal hand cups the back of the uterus. The uterine body is squeezed between the two hands. Keep it up until the bleeding is controlled or she is in theatre.

questions.stem: Mrs Rao, 33, gave birth vaginally 30 minutes ago and has a primary PPH of 1,500 mL from an atonic uterus. She is having oxytocin and second-line uterotonics. HR 124, BP 92/56. She has no bleeding disorder and takes no anticoagulants. How should tranexamic acid be used for her?
options: 1 g IV over 10 minutes now, with a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes
1 g orally now, then repeated every 8 hours for 24 hours
1 g IV, but only once results show a fibrinogen below 2 g/L
1 g IV, but only if bleeding continues more than 3 hours after the birth
notes: Oral tranexamic acid is too slow and unreliable for a woman bleeding heavily in shock; it is given IV in PPH.
Tranexamic acid is given early whatever the cause, without waiting for coagulation results; low fibrinogen needs replacement with fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate.
Benefit is greatest when given early, and there is no benefit (and possible harm) when it is started more than 3 hours after birth.
questions.why: Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes as soon as possible in PPH, within 3 hours of birth, whatever the cause. Give a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours. The benefit falls the longer it is delayed.

questions.stem: Mrs Rao, 33, has a soft, boggy fundus above the umbilicus 25 minutes after the birth of a 4.3 kg baby, and blood and clots keep coming through the cervix. Her clotting is normal. What is the main way the uterus normally stops bleeding from the placental bed after birth?
options: Platelet plugs and fibrin at the placental bed seal the spiral arteries without help
Sympathetic vasoconstriction of the uterine arteries reduces blood flow to the uterus
Prostaglandins from the decidua directly constrict the spiral arteries without help
Contracting, interlacing myometrial fibres kink and compress the spiral arteries
notes: Clotting helps but cannot seal open spiral arteries carrying about 500 to 700 mL/min at term on its own, so atony bleeds even with normal coagulation.
The uterine circulation is near maximally dilated at term and responds little to sympathetic tone; vasoconstriction is not the main way bleeding stops.
Prostaglandins act mainly by making the myometrium contract (as carboprost does), not by directly constricting the spiral arteries on their own.
questions.why: Interlacing myometrial fibres contract and retract around the spiral arteries that run through them, squeezing the vessels shut (the 'living ligatures'). In atony this mechanical squeeze is lost, so the placental bed bleeds heavily even when clotting is normal.

questions.stem: Mrs Rao, 33, is still bleeding from an atonic uterus after 1,500 mL of loss. The registrar says that if the bleeding goes on after the retained tissue is removed, uterine artery embolisation or ligation may be needed. The uterine artery is a branch of which vessel?
options: Posterior division of the internal iliac artery
Anterior division of the internal iliac artery
External iliac artery, just above the inguinal ligament
Abdominal aorta, just below the renal arteries
notes: The posterior division gives the iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries, which supply the body wall and buttock, not the pelvic organs.
The external iliac artery supplies the lower limb and gives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries, not the uterine artery.
The vessel that arises from the aorta below the renal arteries is the ovarian artery, which joins up with the uterine artery but is a separate vessel.
questions.why: The uterine artery comes off the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. It runs medially in the base of the broad ligament and crosses above the ureter ('water under the bridge') near the cervix, which is why the ureter is at risk during ligation.

questions.stem: Mr Pereira, 54, has clinic BP readings of 150 to 154/92 to 94 mmHg. His diary has single evening readings, mostly taken after coffee, on a device not known to be validated. You ask him to repeat home monitoring on a validated upper-arm device with a correctly sized cuff, seated and rested. Which instruction best describes the protocol he should follow?
options: One reading each evening after work for 14 days, then average all of them
Three readings each morning for 3 days, then record only the lowest one
Two readings a minute apart, morning and evening for 7 days, discarding day 1
Two readings whenever he feels stressed or unwell, over the next month
notes: Single readings in the evening only are what made his diary unreliable. They leave out morning readings and there are too few to average reliably.
Three days is too short, and keeping only the lowest reading biases the average downwards. Every valid reading after day 1 should be averaged.
Readings taken only when stressed or unwell are biased upwards and don't show his usual resting blood pressure. The protocol needs scheduled, rested readings.
questions.why: A valid home protocol is duplicate readings 1 minute apart, morning and evening, for 7 days. Discard day 1 and average the rest. Hypertension is confirmed if the home average is 135/85 mmHg or higher.

questions.stem: Mr Pereira, 54, has repeated clinic BP readings of 150 to 154/92 to 94 mmHg. His home diary averages 124/78 mmHg but was taken unreliably. His fundi, ECG, eGFR and urine albumin to creatinine ratio are normal. He has no symptoms and leaves on a 3-month caravan trip in 2 weeks. What is the most appropriate next step for his blood pressure?
options: Arrange 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring and review the result before he leaves
Start amlodipine 5 mg daily now and review him by telehealth during his trip
Reassure him this is white coat hypertension and recheck his BP in 12 months
Request a transthoracic echocardiogram to look for LVH before deciding further
notes: Treatment isn't justified yet. The diagnosis isn't confirmed, he has no end-organ damage, and he may have white coat hypertension, so he could end up on tablets he doesn't need.
White coat hypertension can't be diagnosed from an invalid diary. Even when it is confirmed, it carries some risk and needs closer follow-up than every 12 months.
An echocardiogram isn't routine in uncomplicated grade 1 hypertension, and it doesn't answer the main question, which is whether his out-of-office blood pressure is raised.
questions.why: In grade 1 clinic hypertension without organ damage, confirm the diagnosis out of the office before treating. 24-hour ABPM is preferred: a daytime average of 135/85 mmHg or higher, or a 24-hour average of 130/80 mmHg or higher, confirms hypertension. Doing it now lets him be reviewed before the trip.

questions.stem: Mr Pereira, 54, snores loudly, has witnessed pauses in his breathing, wakes unrefreshed and has a neck circumference of 42 cm. His clinic BP is 150 to 154/92 to 94 mmHg. You suspect obstructive sleep apnoea is contributing to his raised blood pressure. Which mechanism best explains how obstructive sleep apnoea raises blood pressure?
options: Hypercapnia causes systemic vasodilation, and cardiac output rises to compensate
Atrial stretch suppresses natriuretic peptide release, so sodium is retained overnight
Increased vagal tone during each apnoea raises peripheral vascular resistance
Repeated hypoxaemia and arousals drive chemoreflex sympathetic overactivity
notes: Overall, hypercapnia and hypoxaemia in OSA cause sympathetic vasoconstriction, not a vasodilation-driven rise in cardiac output.
Straining against a closed airway stretches the atria and increases natriuretic peptide release, which is why OSA causes nocturia. It doesn't suppress it.
Vagal activity slows the heart during apnoeas but doesn't raise vascular resistance. The pressor effect comes from the sympathetic system.
questions.why: Recurrent apnoeas cause intermittent hypoxaemia and arousals. These activate carotid body chemoreflexes and the sympathetic nervous system, causing vasoconstriction and renin release, and the effect persists into the day. This is why OSA is a recognised secondary cause of hypertension.

questions.stem: You measure Mr Pereira's BP in both arms. In this case the arms differed by only 2 mmHg. Suppose instead his left arm had read 22 mmHg lower than his right, consistently, with a weaker left radial pulse. Narrowing of which vessel would best explain this?
options: Brachiocephalic trunk, before it gives off the right subclavian artery
Left subclavian artery, near where it arises from the aortic arch
Left common carotid artery, as it arises from the aortic arch
Left vertebral artery, after it arises from the left subclavian artery
notes: The brachiocephalic trunk supplies the right arm through the right subclavian artery, so narrowing there would lower the right arm reading, not the left.
The left common carotid artery supplies the head and neck, not the arm, so narrowing it wouldn't change the brachial pressure.
The vertebral artery branches off the subclavian and supplies the brain. Narrowing it doesn't affect arm blood flow, which comes from the subclavian further along.
questions.why: The left subclavian artery arises directly from the aortic arch and supplies the left arm. Narrowing near its origin, usually from atherosclerosis, lowers the left arm pressure. A difference between the arms of more than 10 mmHg should prompt you to look for subclavian stenosis.

questions.stem: Mrs Costa, 29, is at 39+4 weeks on an oxytocin induction. Her membranes were ruptured artificially 20 minutes ago, with the head high at station -2. The fetal heart has dropped to 70 bpm for 3 minutes, and Sam confirms it is separate from the maternal pulse. You have explained what you are doing and she agrees. Which examination is the priority now?
options: Abdominal palpation to estimate how many fifths of the head are palpable
Digital vaginal examination to feel for the umbilical cord
Sterile speculum examination to look at the liquor and for bleeding
Palpation of the uterus between contractions for tenderness
notes: The head level is already known (station -2). Counting fifths does not exclude cord prolapse or change what you do next.
A speculum is slower and does not let you elevate the presenting part. A digital examination both finds a prolapsed cord and treats it.
Checking for tenderness is reasonable for abruption, but she has no pain or bleeding. With a recent ARM and a high head, cord prolapse must be excluded first.
questions.why: A sudden prolonged deceleration soon after ARM with a high head needs a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse. It is the only one of these steps that finds the cause and lets you treat it straight away by lifting the presenting part.

questions.stem: At 11:48 the cord is still pulsating below the presenting part and the fetal heart is about 90 bpm with reduced variability. The cervix is 5 cm, station -2. You are holding the presenting part up, the oxytocin is off and she is knee-chest. What plan for birth should the obstetric team make?
options: Fetal scalp blood sampling for lactate to decide how urgently to deliver
Category 2 caesarean, aiming for birth within about 75 minutes
Category 1 caesarean, aiming for birth as fast as is safely possible
Fill the bladder and continue labour towards an assisted vaginal birth
notes: Fetal blood sampling only delays birth. A prolonged deceleration or bradycardia that does not recover needs birth expedited, not sampling.
Category 2 is for compromise that is not an immediate threat to life. A pulsating, compressed cord with bradycardia is an immediate threat, so this is category 1.
Filling the bladder is only for when birth will be delayed, such as during transfer. Vaginal birth is an option only at full dilatation, and she is 5 cm.
questions.why: Cord prolapse with a persistent bradycardia before full dilatation is an immediate threat to the fetus's life. It needs a category 1 caesarean, aiming for birth as fast as is safely possible (generally within 30 minutes), while the presenting part stays elevated until birth.

questions.stem: Mrs Costa's BP was 110/65 before an epidural top-up. Fifteen minutes later, lying semi-recumbent, it is 84/50 with a maternal pulse of 105 to 108. She is alert and afebrile, with no bleeding. What is the main mechanism of her fall in blood pressure?
options: Sympathetic block causing vasodilation, venous pooling and reduced preload
Systemic local anaesthetic absorption directly depressing the myocardium
Block of the cardiac accelerator fibres (T1 to T4) causing primary bradycardia
Histamine release from the local anaesthetic causing anaphylactoid vasodilation
notes: Myocardial depression is a sign of local anaesthetic toxicity, which comes with neurological symptoms. She is alert, and a standard top-up does not cause this.
A high block reaching T1 to T4 would cause bradycardia. She is tachycardic, which shows her cardiac sympathetic drive and baroreflex are intact.
Amide local anaesthetics rarely release histamine. She has no rash, wheeze or other features of anaphylaxis.
questions.why: Neuraxial local anaesthetic blocks sympathetic vasomotor outflow, causing arterial and venous dilation. Venous return falls, made worse by aortocaval compression. Uteroplacental flow has no autoregulation, so it falls with her BP. The tachycardia is the baroreflex response.

questions.stem: After ARM, Sam's vaginal examination found Mrs Costa 5 cm dilated, vertex LOA, 3/5 of the head palpable abdominally and station -2. Twenty minutes later a cord prolapse is found. What does station -2 describe?
options: The leading part of the vertex is 2 cm below the level of the ischial spines
Two-fifths of the fetal head remain palpable above the pelvic brim
The leading part of the vertex is 2 cm above the plane of the pelvic inlet
The leading bony part of the fetal skull is 2 cm above the ischial spines
notes: Below the spines is a positive station (+2). A head that low would be well engaged and unlikely to allow a cord prolapse.
Fifths palpable is an abdominal measure of descent, and she is 3/5 palpable. It is not the same as station on vaginal examination.
Station is measured from the ischial spines, not the pelvic inlet. The inlet is a higher plane at the brim of the pelvis.
questions.why: Station is the level of the leading bony part of the fetal skull relative to the ischial spines: negative above, positive below. At -2 the head is high and not engaged, which leaves room for the cord to slip past after ARM.

questions.stem: Mr Kostas, 66, is tearful in your GP rooms. His biopsy shows Gleason 4+3=7 (Grade Group 3), and he believes this means "7 out of 10, so I am 70% dead". Which plain-language explanation best corrects his misunderstanding?
options: The score shows how much of your prostate is cancer; 7 means a moderate amount is involved
The score is your risk of spread out of 10, so 7 means it has probably already spread
The score describes how abnormal the cells look; scores start at 6, so 7 is in the middle
4+3 and 3+4 both add up to 7, so your outlook is the same as anyone with a score of 7
notes: Gleason grades how the glands look, not how much cancer there is; volume shows up in other features, such as the number of positive cores.
Gleason is not a score out of 10 for spread; spread is assessed by staging (MRI, PSMA PET/CT), and telling him it has probably spread is false and alarming.
4+3 is worse than 3+4 (Grade Group 3 vs 2) because pattern 4 is the main pattern, so the totals being equal does not mean the outlook is the same.
questions.why: Gleason grades only how the glands look under the microscope. Patterns 1 and 2 are no longer used, so the lowest score is 3+3=6, and 4+3=7 (Grade Group 3 of 5) is intermediate risk. It is not a percentage or a fraction of 10.

questions.stem: Mr Kostas, 66, ECOG 0, with controlled hypertension, has Gleason 4+3=7 (Grade Group 3) prostate cancer in 4 of 14 left-sided cores, PSA 9.4 ng/mL and clinical stage cT1c. If his PSMA PET/CT shows no spread, which management should the urology MDT offer him?
options: Radical prostatectomy, or external beam radiotherapy with 4–6 months of hormone therapy
Active surveillance with 6-monthly PSA, repeat MRI and repeat biopsy at 12 months
Androgen deprivation therapy alone with a GnRH agonist, continued long term
Watchful waiting, with hormone therapy started only if symptoms of progression develop
notes: Active surveillance suits low-risk disease (Grade Group 1) and selected favourable intermediate-risk cases; it is not usually advised for Grade Group 3.
Androgen deprivation therapy alone does not cure localised disease; it is used for metastatic disease or men unfit for curative treatment.
Watchful waiting is for men with limited life expectancy; a fit 66-year-old with curable disease would lose his chance of cure.
questions.why: Unfavourable intermediate-risk localised disease (Grade Group 3) in a fit man with a long life expectancy needs curative treatment. The options are radical prostatectomy, or radiotherapy with short-course (about 4–6 months) androgen deprivation therapy.

questions.stem: Mr Kostas, 66, asks why his PSA was 9.4 ng/mL when he was told PSA also rises with an enlarged or inflamed prostate. PSA is a protease that the prostate secretes into its ducts to liquefy semen. Which mechanism best explains a raised serum PSA in these conditions?
options: Malignant cells make a cancer-specific form of PSA that normal prostate cells do not
Disrupted gland architecture lets PSA leak from the ducts into the circulation
Reduced renal clearance with age allows normally secreted PSA to build up in serum
Inflammation makes the liver synthesise PSA as part of the acute phase response
notes: There is no cancer-only PSA; benign and malignant prostate epithelium both make it, and cancer cells actually make less PSA per cell.
PSA rises with age because the gland gets bigger, not because the kidneys clear less of it; reduced renal clearance is not the reason a PSA is raised.
PSA (kallikrein-3) comes from prostatic epithelium, not the liver, and it is not an acute phase reactant.
questions.why: PSA normally goes into the ducts, and only small amounts reach the blood. Cancer, BPH, prostatitis and instrumentation all disrupt the basal cell layer and basement membrane, so more PSA leaks into the blood. This is why PSA is organ-specific but not cancer-specific.

questions.stem: Mr Kostas, 66, is worried about losing his erections after treatment. His MRI shows an 11 mm lesion in the left posterolateral peripheral zone, and the neurovascular bundles look normal. Where do the cavernous nerves that supply erection run in relation to the prostate?
options: Anteriorly, within the dorsal venous complex over the prostatic apex
Medially, alongside the ejaculatory ducts within the central zone
Within the transition zone, wrapped around the prostatic urethra
Posterolaterally, in the neurovascular bundles outside the prostatic capsule
notes: The dorsal venous complex lies anteriorly and is controlled during prostatectomy; the cavernous nerves run posterolaterally, not inside it.
The ejaculatory ducts pass through the central zone, but the cavernous nerves run outside the gland, not alongside these ducts.
The transition zone surrounds the urethra and is where BPH arises; the erectile nerves run outside the capsule, not within the gland.
questions.why: The cavernous nerves (parasympathetic, S2–4, from the pelvic plexus) run in the neurovascular bundles posterolateral to the prostate, at about 5 and 7 o'clock. Nerve-sparing prostatectomy aims to preserve them, but a posterolateral tumour may limit nerve sparing on that side.

questions.stem: In ED at night you are examining a 12 kg 2-year-old with 2 days of coryza, then a barking cough, hoarse cry and stridor at rest. The child is sitting upright on the mother's lap and is consolable. How should you carry out your examination?
options: Observe from a distance on mother's lap, counting RR and looking for recession and tug
Lie the child supine on the couch to auscultate and inspect the chest for recession
Inspect the oropharynx with a tongue depressor and torch to exclude epiglottitis
Ask the nurse to take a capillary blood gas first to judge the severity objectively
notes: Lying the child flat and handling them upsets them and makes the airway obstruction worse. The station shows this: the stridor gets much louder.
Never examine the throat in a child with stridor. Distress worsens the obstruction, and in epiglottitis a tongue depressor can cause complete obstruction.
Croup is diagnosed and graded clinically. A blood gas does not change management and the needle upsets the child, which worsens the obstruction.
questions.why: In croup, being upset makes the dynamic obstruction worse. Assess behaviour, stridor and work of breathing by watching, with the child upright and calm on the parent's lap. Do as little hands-on examination as you can.

questions.stem: At 23:00 the same 12 kg 2-year-old with croup is agitated with loud stridor at rest, marked recession, tracheal tug, RR 52 and SpO2 91% in room air. No medicines have been given yet. Dexamethasone has been charted and a senior is coming. Which adrenaline order is right for this child?
options: Adrenaline 1:1000, 0.5 mL diluted to 5 mL with saline, nebulised
Adrenaline 1:1000, 0.12 mL (0.01 mg/kg) intramuscularly into the lateral thigh
Adrenaline 1:1000, 5 mL undiluted, nebulised via an oxygen-driven mask
Adrenaline 1:10 000, 1.2 mL (0.01 mg/kg) intravenously over 1 minute
notes: 0.5 mL is only a tenth of the croup dose. That is a racemic-adrenaline regimen, not the Australian 1:1000 regimen of 5 mL undiluted.
IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg treats anaphylaxis. This child has no allergic features, and croup is treated with nebulised adrenaline acting directly on the laryngeal mucosa.
IV adrenaline is a cardiac arrest or peri-arrest drug. It has no role in croup and puts the child at risk of arrhythmias and severe hypertension.
questions.why: For severe croup, give nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 (1 mg/mL), 5 mL undiluted (0.5 mL/kg, capped at 5 mL, so 5 mL for 12 kg). Run it on oxygen because SpO2 is under 92%. It works within minutes but lasts about 2 hours, so observe for at least 3 hours after the last dose.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with croup has loud stridor that is mainly inspiratory and gets worse when the child cries and breathes in hard. What is the main reason the stridor in croup is heard mostly on inspiration?
options: In inspiration, positive pleural pressure compresses the narrowed intrathoracic trachea
In inspiration, pressure inside the extrathoracic airway falls below atmospheric pressure
In inspiration, the vocal cords adduct, narrowing the glottis that is already swollen
In inspiration, small-airway bronchospasm traps air and creates turbulent flow
notes: Pleural pressure is negative during inspiration. Intrathoracic airways are compressed in forced expiration, which is why intrathoracic obstruction gives expiratory noise.
The vocal cords abduct during inspiration, opening the glottis. They do not adduct.
Bronchospasm of the small airways causes expiratory wheeze, as in asthma. It does not cause inspiratory stridor from upper airway oedema.
questions.why: The subglottic narrowing in croup is outside the chest. On inspiration, pressure inside the lumen falls below atmospheric pressure, so the swollen extrathoracic airway is pulled narrower and flow becomes turbulent. Hard breathing when the child is upset makes this worse.

questions.stem: The mother of a 2-year-old with croup asks why a simple cold has made breathing so hard. You explain that croup causes inflammatory swelling just below the vocal cords, inside a rigid ring that cannot stretch outward. Which structure forms this ring?
options: Thyroid cartilage, at the level of the vocal cords
Epiglottis, overlying the laryngeal inlet
First tracheal ring, just below the larynx
Cricoid cartilage, just below the vocal cords
notes: The thyroid cartilage is open at the back and sits at glottic level. It does not form a complete ring around the subglottis, where croup swelling is greatest.
The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap above the glottis. It is the swollen structure in epiglottitis, not in croup.
Tracheal rings are C-shaped and open at the back, closed only by the trachealis muscle, so they are not complete rigid rings.
