questions.why: The cricoid is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway, and it surrounds the subglottis. Mucosal oedema there can only narrow the lumen inward. Airway resistance rises steeply as the radius falls, so in a toddler a little swelling causes marked obstruction.

questions.stem: On the postnatal ward, a 14-hour-old term baby with suspected early-onset GBS sepsis is being stabilised. The mother was GBS positive and had one dose of benzylpenicillin 2 hours before a quick birth. She is tearful and asks you, "Did I cause this?" Which response is best?
options: It may be because you stayed home after your waters broke; that delayed the antibiotics
We can't say anything about the cause until the final culture result at 5 days
GBS is carried by many healthy women; you didn't cause this or do anything wrong
Please don't worry; babies treated this quickly nearly always recover completely
notes: This blames the mother. It is unkind, it doesn't help, and the timing of labour was not something she could control.
This avoids her question. You can reassure her about blame now without waiting for any result.
This is false reassurance. The baby is in septic shock and you cannot promise a full recovery.
questions.why: Answer her question honestly: GBS carriage is common and normal, it is nobody's fault, and you won't promise how things will turn out. After that, check what she has understood and offer to help her stay with the baby and express breast milk.

questions.stem: A 14-hour-old baby born at 38+5 weeks, weighing 3.2 kg, has suspected early-onset sepsis with shock. The mother is GBS positive. A blood culture has just been taken, and a lumbar puncture is deferred because the baby is unstable. Which empirical antibiotic regimen should you give now?
options: Benzylpenicillin 192 mg IV 12-hourly plus gentamicin 16 mg IV 24-hourly
Benzylpenicillin 192 mg IV 12-hourly plus gentamicin 24 mg IV 24-hourly
Ceftriaxone 160 mg IV 24-hourly plus benzylpenicillin 192 mg IV 12-hourly
Flucloxacillin 160 mg IV 12-hourly plus gentamicin 16 mg IV 24-hourly
notes: 24 mg is 7.5 mg/kg, the dose for older children. A term neonate in the first week gets 5 mg/kg, because a higher dose risks toxicity.
Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because it displaces bilirubin and can precipitate with calcium. If meningitis is suspected, the regimen uses a cephalosporin such as cefotaxime.
Flucloxacillin is aimed at staphylococci, which matter in late-onset sepsis. It is not the empirical choice for early-onset sepsis from maternal flora such as GBS.
questions.why: For early-onset sepsis the RCH guideline uses benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg 12-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg 24-hourly, with doses from the Australasian Neonatal Medicines Formulary for a term baby in the first week. This covers GBS, Listeria and E. coli. Give it straight after the blood culture.

questions.stem: A 14-hour-old term baby has septic shock, with a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L, neutropenia with toxic changes and bilateral hazy opacification on chest X-ray. Bloods were taken about 4 hours after symptoms began, and the CRP is only 6 mg/L. What best explains the low CRP?
options: Neonatal hepatocytes cannot synthesise CRP until the second week of life
The intrapartum benzylpenicillin has suppressed the baby's acute-phase response
CRP is made by neutrophils, so the neutropenia limits its production
Hepatic CRP synthesis is driven by IL-6 and takes 12 to 24 hours to rise
notes: Newborns can make CRP from birth. The value is low here because of timing, not because the liver is immature.
Antibiotics do not block the hepatic acute-phase response, and one dose to the mother would not suppress it in the baby.
CRP comes from hepatocytes, not neutrophils, so the neutrophil count does not limit how much is made.
questions.why: CRP is an acute-phase protein made by the liver in response to IL-6 and other cytokines. It rises over 12 to 24 hours and peaks at about 36 to 48 hours, so a low early CRP does not exclude sepsis. Repeat it within 12 to 24 hours.

questions.stem: A 14-hour-old baby with shock and SpO2 of 91% has improved with fluid, but the registrar still wants duct-dependent congenital heart disease excluded and asks you to measure pre- and post-ductal SpO2. Where should the pre-ductal probe go, and why?
options: Left hand: the left subclavian artery always arises proximal to the ductus
Right hand: right subclavian comes off the brachiocephalic trunk, proximal to the duct
Either foot: the femoral arteries arise from the aorta proximal to the duct
Either hand: both subclavian arteries leave the arch proximal to the duct
notes: The left subclavian arises close to where the ductus joins the aorta, and it may receive ductal blood, so the left hand is not a reliable pre-ductal site.
The legs are supplied by the descending aorta beyond the duct, so a foot is the post-ductal site.
The left subclavian is too close to the ductal insertion to be reliably pre-ductal, so only the right hand is used.
questions.why: The right subclavian artery comes off the brachiocephalic trunk, the first branch of the arch, well before the ductus arteriosus joins the aorta. That makes the right hand reliably pre-ductal, and a foot is post-ductal.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old with bronchiolitis is now well enough to go home after admission. You are giving the anxious mother safety-netting advice before discharge. Which sign should prompt her to call 000 rather than bring the baby back to the ED?
options: Feeding less than half the usual amount over a day
Fewer than half the usual number of wet nappies
A pause in breathing, or a blue or grey colour
Breathing faster, with more sucking in under the ribs
notes: Poor feeding (less than half the usual amount) is a reason to come back to the ED, but it is not an emergency that needs an ambulance.
Fewer wet nappies points to dehydration and needs prompt review in the ED, not a 000 call.
Harder or faster breathing is a sign of getting worse and needs an urgent return to the ED. Apnoea or colour change is what calls for 000.
questions.why: Apnoea or cyanosis means the infant may be about to stop breathing, so the mother should call 000. Worse breathing, poor feeding, drowsiness or fewer wet nappies mean an urgent return to the ED.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old (6 kg) with bronchiolitis has SpO2 96% on 1 L/min by nasal prongs. In a feeding trial the baby took 40 of 150 mL, stopping to breathe, with HR 175, and has passed no urine in the 2 hours since arrival. The baby is alert with a CRT of 2 s. Which hydration plan should you start first?
options: Nasogastric formula at 16 mL/h (2/3 maintenance)
Nasogastric formula at 24 mL/h (full maintenance)
IV 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at 24 mL/h
IV 0.18% sodium chloride with 4% glucose at 16 mL/h
notes: Full maintenance risks fluid overload and hyponatraemia, because ADH secretion is raised in bronchiolitis. Start at 2/3 maintenance.
IV fluid is second line after NG feeds, and full maintenance is too much given the raised ADH. If IV is needed, give it at 16 mL/h.
This fluid is hypotonic and carries a risk of hyponatraemia. If IV fluid is needed, it should be isotonic with glucose.
questions.why: When oral intake is not enough in bronchiolitis, nasogastric feeds come first, at 2/3 maintenance: 4 mL/kg/h × 6 kg = 24 mL/h, and 2/3 of that is 16 mL/h. The lower rate allows for increased ADH secretion. IV isotonic fluid with glucose is kept for when NG feeds fail or are unsafe.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old with 3 days of coryza and cough has widespread fine crackles and wheeze on both sides. SpO2 is 87% in room air, with RR 64, and rises to 96% on just 1 L/min of oxygen by nasal prongs. Which mechanism best explains the hypoxaemia?
options: Diffusion impairment from thickened alveolar–capillary membranes
Right-to-left shunt of blood through a patent foramen ovale
Alveolar hypoventilation from central respiratory depression
V/Q mismatch from small airways blocked by oedema, mucus and debris
notes: Diffusion impairment comes from interstitial disease. Bronchiolitis is a disease of the small airways, not of the alveolar–capillary membrane.
A true shunt barely responds to extra oxygen, but this infant's SpO2 rose from 87% to 96% on 1 L/min.
This infant is breathing fast at 64 and is alert. That is not the central depression of breathing that hypoventilation would need.
questions.why: In bronchiolitis, oedema, mucus and sloughed epithelium block the bronchioles. Poorly ventilated alveoli are still perfused, which creates low V/Q units. Hypoxaemia from V/Q mismatch improves well with low-flow oxygen, as it did here.

questions.stem: Examining the abdomen of a 4-month-old with bronchiolitis, you feel a soft liver edge 2 cm below the right costal margin. On percussion, the upper border of liver dullness is lower than expected and the liver span is normal for age. What best explains this finding?
options: Hepatomegaly from venous congestion in right heart failure
A normal liver pushed down by a diaphragm flattened by hyperinflation
Hepatomegaly from viral hepatitis as part of a systemic infection
Riedel's lobe, a tongue-like downward extension of the right lobe
notes: Congestion from heart failure enlarges the liver, so the span would be increased. Here the span is normal and the upper border is low.
Hepatitis would enlarge the liver and increase its span. It would not move the upper border of dullness downward.
Riedel's lobe is an anatomical variant of the lower edge. It does not explain a low upper border of liver dullness in a hyperinflated infant.
questions.why: Air trapping in bronchiolitis hyperinflates the lungs and flattens the diaphragm, which pushes a normal-sized liver down. When the upper border is low and the span is normal, the liver has been displaced, not enlarged. Percussing the upper border is how you tell displacement from hepatomegaly.

questions.stem: Ms Mitchell, 31, agrees to rabies pre-exposure vaccination before 4 weeks of trekking in rural Cambodia and Laos, where she will see stray dogs and temple monkeys. You are safety netting before she leaves. What should you tell her to do if a monkey scratches her?
options: Apply a pressure bandage, immobilise the limb, and seek care if she becomes unwell
Watch how the animal behaves, and seek care only if it gets sick within 10 days
Wash the wound with soap and water for 15 minutes, then get medical care the same day
Clean it with antiseptic; after pre-exposure vaccination she needs no further doses
notes: Pressure immobilisation is first aid for snake and funnel-web spider bites. It does nothing for rabies or Australian bat lyssavirus, and waiting for symptoms is fatal because clinical rabies is almost always lethal.
Watching the animal for 10 days only applies to a dog or cat that can be reliably observed. It does not apply to monkeys or strays on a trek, and it must never delay post-exposure treatment.
Pre-exposure vaccination does not replace post-exposure treatment. It removes the need for immunoglobulin, but she still needs 2 booster doses (days 0 and 3) after any bite or scratch.
questions.why: Wash the wound well with soap and water for about 15 minutes, then get post-exposure care urgently, even after pre-exposure vaccination. Vaccinated travellers still need 2 more doses. Unvaccinated travellers need immunoglobulin plus a vaccine course, and immunoglobulin is often unavailable in rural areas.

questions.stem: Ms Mitchell, 31, will spend days 15 to 40 of her trip trekking in forested north-eastern Cambodia and southern Laos, sleeping in open huts. She has no contraindications and chooses doxycycline for malaria chemoprophylaxis. Which regimen should you prescribe?
options: 100 mg orally daily, 1–2 days before entering until 4 weeks after leaving the risk area
100 mg orally daily, 1–2 days before entering until 7 days after leaving the risk area
200 mg orally weekly, 1 week before entering until 4 weeks after leaving the risk area
100 mg orally daily, only on the days she is in the risk area, stopping when she leaves
notes: Stopping 7 days after leaving is the atovaquone-proguanil schedule. That drug also acts on liver-stage parasites, but doxycycline does not, so stopping it after 7 days risks malaria.
Weekly dosing belongs to drugs like mefloquine. Doxycycline has a short half-life and must be taken daily to protect her.
Stopping doxycycline on leaving the risk area leaves parasites still developing in the liver uncovered. These can cause falciparum malaria in the weeks after she leaves.
questions.why: Doxycycline 100 mg daily starts 1 to 2 days before entering the malarious area and continues for 4 weeks after leaving. It kills only blood-stage parasites, so it has to cover parasites that come out of the liver after she leaves. She should take it with food and water, stay upright afterwards, and protect herself from the sun.

questions.stem: Ms Mitchell, 31, needs a second MMR dose today. She also chooses the live attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine (Imojev). You explain that live vaccines are given on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart. What is the main reason for this rule?
options: Antibodies made to the first vaccine cross-neutralise the second live virus
Interferon induced by the first live vaccine limits replication of the second
Live vaccines given a few weeks apart cause much more fever and rash
The first vaccine causes lymphopenia that blocks the response to any later vaccine
notes: Measles-mumps-rubella antibodies do not neutralise the Japanese encephalitis vaccine virus, which is built on a yellow fever backbone. The interference is non-specific and innate, not antibody-mediated.
The rule is about protecting efficacy, not safety. Reactogenicity does not rise much when live vaccines are given a few weeks apart.
Any transient immune effect does not stop inactivated vaccines working. That is why inactivated vaccines can be given at any interval, and only live vaccines follow the 4-week rule.
questions.why: A live vaccine replicates and sets off an innate, interferon-mediated antiviral state. A second live vaccine given within about 4 weeks may not replicate enough to produce a full immune response. Given on the same day, both replicate before that response develops.

questions.stem: Today you will give Ms Mitchell, 31, several intramuscular vaccines, using both deltoids. You aim for the middle of the deltoid, midway between the acromion and the deltoid tuberosity. If an injection goes too high, just below the acromion, which structure is it most likely to injure?
options: Axillary nerve, where it winds around the surgical neck of the humerus
Radial nerve, where it runs in the spiral groove of the humerus
Cephalic vein, where it runs in the deltopectoral groove
Subacromial (subdeltoid) bursa, causing shoulder injury after vaccination
notes: The axillary nerve runs about 5 to 7 cm below the acromion. It is at risk from an injection placed too low or too far back, not too high.
The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove on the back of the mid-humerus, below the deltoid insertion. It is at risk only from an injection given much too low.
The cephalic vein lies in the deltopectoral groove at the front edge of the deltoid. It is not under the high point just below the acromion.
questions.why: An injection just under the acromion can go into the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa or the rotator cuff. This causes shoulder injury related to vaccine administration (SIRVA), with pain and reduced movement. Landmarking the mid-deltoid avoids the bursa above and the axillary nerve below.

questions.stem: At 18:55 the 27-month-old is alert, playing and drinking after a 3-minute febrile seizure. While you plan discharge, the frightened parent asks, "What do I do if it happens again?" What is the best first aid advice to give?
options: Lie them on their side, time it, nothing in the mouth; call 000 if it lasts 5 min or more
Hold the limbs firmly, put a spoon between the teeth; call 000 if it lasts 10 minutes
Give paracetamol straight away, sponge with cool water; drive to ED if over 15 minutes
Sit them upright and give sips of water to stop choking; call 000 if the lips go dusky
notes: Holding the limbs down can injure the child, putting objects in the mouth risks dental injury and aspiration, and 10 minutes is too long to wait before calling 000.
A seizing child can't swallow safely, cool sponging and antipyretics don't stop seizures, and waiting 15 minutes delays treatment of possible status epilepticus.
Giving fluids by mouth during or right after a seizure risks aspiration; the child should lie on their side, and the trigger to call 000 is a seizure lasting 5 minutes.
questions.why: Seizure first aid is: note the time, recovery position, nothing in the mouth, don't restrain, stay with the child. Call an ambulance (000) if the seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, breathing is difficult or the child doesn't wake properly.

questions.stem: A 27-month-old (13 kg) had a single 3-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure with fever. Red throat, runny nose, normal ears, clear chest, no meningism or rash, BGL 5.6 mmol/L. Fifty minutes after the seizure the child has GCS 15 and is playing and drinking. What is the most appropriate approach to investigation?
options: No further tests; discharge once at baseline, with first aid teaching and GP follow-up
Catheter urine sample for microscopy and culture before discharge
FBC, electrolytes, calcium and blood culture, then discharge if all are normal
Outpatient EEG and MRI brain to look for an underlying epileptic cause
notes: Urine is collected for a fever with no source. This child has a clear viral URTI source.
Routine bloods do not change management after a simple febrile seizure in a well child who has fully recovered.
EEG and neuroimaging are not indicated after a simple febrile seizure and do not predict recurrence or later epilepsy.
questions.why: After a simple febrile seizure with a clear source and full recovery, no routine bloods, EEG or imaging are needed (RCH guideline). Look for the source of the fever, and send urine only if no source is found.

questions.stem: The parent of a 27-month-old who has just had a simple febrile seizure during a viral URTI asks why fever causes fits in small children but not in adults. An older sibling had a febrile seizure at age 2. Which mechanism best explains febrile seizures in this age group?
options: Fever-induced cerebral oedema that raises intracranial pressure
An immature brain with a low, often inherited, seizure threshold that fever lowers
Direct viral invasion of the cortex causing a brief, self-limiting encephalitis
Hypoglycaemia from poor intake, as young children have small glycogen stores
notes: Fever doesn't cause meaningful cerebral oedema or raised ICP. A child with raised ICP would not be back to GCS 15 and playing within an hour.
Viral invasion of brain tissue is encephalitis, which causes ongoing drowsiness or focal signs, not full recovery within an hour.
Hypoglycaemia can cause seizures, but this child's BGL was 5.6 mmol/L and recovery happened without glucose.
questions.why: The developing brain is more excitable and has a lower seizure threshold. Fever lowers that threshold further, and there is a strong genetic predisposition, which is why the risk falls away after about 6 years and runs in families.

questions.stem: Suppose this febrile 27-month-old had stayed drowsy with neck stiffness after the seizure. A lumbar puncture would then be needed to look for meningitis. With the child held in the lateral position, which interspace and landmark should you use?
options: T12/L1 interspace, at the level of the twelfth ribs
L1/L2 interspace, at the level of the lower costal margins
S1/S2 level, between the posterior superior iliac spines
L3/L4 or L4/L5 interspace, at or just below the line joining the iliac crests
notes: T12/L1 is at or above the conus medullaris, so a needle here risks injuring the spinal cord.
L1/L2 is about where the conus ends at this age, so it's too high to be safe. The costal margin isn't a reliable lumbar landmark.
The sacral vertebrae are fused, so there's no interspace to enter at S1/S2, and this is below the usual safe LP site.
questions.why: By around age 2 the conus medullaris ends at about L1 to L2. A needle at L3/L4 or L4/L5, found at the line joining the iliac crests (Tuffier's line), enters the thecal sac below the cord.

questions.stem: A term baby (39+2 weeks) is floppy and apnoeic at birth. After drying and warming, the heart rate is 70/min. You start mask ventilation in air at 40 seconds, but the chest is not rising. What is your next step?
options: Start chest compressions at a ratio of 3:1 with ventilation
Increase the oxygen to 100% and continue the same ventilation
Reposition the head to neutral, reseal the mask and give jaw support
Go straight to tracheal intubation before trying other steps
notes: Compressions start only if the heart rate stays below 60/min after 30 seconds of effective ventilation, and this heart rate is 70 with no chest rise yet.
More oxygen does nothing if no gas reaches the lungs, and a term baby starts in air.
>Intubation is an advanced airway step for when simple corrections fail; repositioning, the mask seal and jaw support come first.
questions.why: If the chest does not rise, the ventilation is not working. Fix the airway and the mask first: head in neutral, a better mask seal, jaw support (the start of the MR SOPA steps). Chest rise followed by a rising heart rate shows the ventilation is effective.

questions.stem: The term baby (3.4 kg) needed mask ventilation at birth and is now breathing on its own, pink and responding. At 30 minutes of age, before any feed, the meter blood glucose is 2.2 mmol/L. A laboratory glucose has been sent. What is the most appropriate management now?
options: IV 10% glucose 6.8 mL bolus, then start a glucose infusion
40% glucose gel 1.7 mL into the cheek, breastfeed, recheck BGL in 30 to 60 min
Formula top-up feed now, then recheck the BGL before the next feed in 3 hours
Wait for the laboratory glucose result before giving any treatment
notes: IV 10% glucose 2 mL/kg is the next step if the BGL stays below 2.6 despite gel and feeds, or if the baby is unwell; this baby is stable.
A feed alone with a recheck 3 hours later is too slow for a BGL of 2.2 mmol/L; give gel first, then feed, and recheck in 30 to 60 minutes.
A meter is less accurate at low values, so confirm with a lab glucose, but do not hold treatment while you wait.
questions.why: A BGL below 2.6 mmol/L in a well baby is treated with 40% glucose gel 0.5 mL/kg (1.7 mL for 3.4 kg) into the buccal mucosa, then a breastfeed or colostrum, with a recheck 30 to 60 minutes later. IV glucose is for a BGL that stays low or a baby who is unwell.

questions.stem: A term baby had 8 minutes of fetal bradycardia (about 70) before birth and is apnoeic, with a heart rate of 70. Once the mask technique is corrected and the chest rises, the heart rate climbs to 120 by 2 minutes and 140 by 3 minutes, with no compressions or drugs. Which mechanism best explains the rise in heart rate?
options: Aerating the lungs drops pulmonary resistance, oxygenating the hypoxic myocardium
Lung inflation triggers a vagal reflex that directly speeds the sinoatrial node
Positive pressure raises intrathoracic pressure and so increases venous return
Ventilation lowers pCO2, and the fall in pCO2 directly speeds the sinoatrial node
notes: Vagal stimulation slows the sinoatrial node rather than speeding it up, so a vagal reflex cannot explain the rise in heart rate.
Positive pressure ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return to the heart rather than increasing it.
The bradycardia comes from hypoxia, not carbon dioxide; the cord pCO2 was within range, and it is oxygen reaching the heart that brings the rate back.
questions.why: Newborn bradycardia at birth is caused by hypoxia. Inflating the lungs lowers pulmonary vascular resistance, so more blood flows through the lungs and oxygenated blood reaches the heart, and the heart rate recovers. That is why the heart rate is the best sign that ventilation is working.

questions.stem: During resuscitation of a newborn, the midwife puts the pulse oximeter probe on the right wrist so the SpO2 can be compared with the ANZCOR preductal targets (for example 70 to 90% at 3 minutes). What is the anatomical reason the right wrist gives a preductal reading?
options: The right radial artery fills from the pulmonary trunk until the ductus closes
The left subclavian arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, so either wrist is preductal
The lower limbs receive umbilical venous blood via the ductus venosus, reading high
The right subclavian arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, proximal to the ductus
notes: The pulmonary trunk sends blood through the ductus to the descending aorta, not to the right arm, so this is wrong.
The left subclavian comes straight off the aortic arch, right next to where the ductus joins, so the left arm may get some ductal blood.
The ductus venosus carries umbilical venous blood to the IVC; the legs are supplied from below the ductus and give postductal, often lower, readings.
questions.why: The right arm is supplied by the right subclavian artery, which comes off the brachiocephalic trunk before the point where the ductus arteriosus joins the aorta (the isthmus). Its saturation therefore matches the blood going to the brain and heart, without deoxygenated blood shunted right-to-left through the ductus.

questions.stem: You are taking a history from James, 50, in the ED. He has had an hour of heavy central chest pain going to his left jaw, with sweating. No ECG has been done yet. Three minutes in he says, "It's just indigestion, isn't it? I need to get back to work." What is the best response?
options: "It's most likely reflux, so I'll get you some antacid and you can head back soon."
"We can't tell until the troponin comes back, so let's wait for that result first."
"It might be, but this could be your heart, so we need an ECG and blood tests now."
"You are definitely having a heart attack and you must not leave this hospital."
notes: This is false reassurance: ischaemic-sounding pain that antacids did not help needs an urgent ECG, not a trial of antacids.
The troponin does not decide the first step. An ECG within 10 minutes is the priority, and STEMI is diagnosed on the ECG and the clinical picture.
Without an ECG this states a diagnosis you cannot yet make, and the confrontational wording is likely to frighten him without explaining why tests are needed.
questions.why: Acknowledge his idea, explain honestly that the pain may be cardiac, and get a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes. This keeps him engaged and safe without false reassurance or premature alarm.

questions.stem: James, 50, has had central chest pain for 1 hour. His ECG at 13:15 shows 2 mm ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal depression in I and aVL. You are in a metropolitan ED with a cardiac catheter laboratory. He has had aspirin 300 mg and his hs-troponin is pending. What is the most appropriate reperfusion step?
options: Activate the cath lab now for primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact
Repeat hs-troponin at 1 hour and activate the cath lab if the level is rising
Give IV tenecteplase now, then transfer for angiography within 24 hours
Arrange a CT aortogram to exclude dissection before any reperfusion therapy
notes: Waiting for the troponin delays reperfusion and costs myocardium. An early troponin can be normal and does not change the decision in STEMI.
Fibrinolysis is for when timely primary PCI is not available. Here the cath lab is on site, so PCI is preferred.
Dissection is excluded at the bedside first. His gradual pressure-like pain without back pain, and his equal arm BPs, do not justify delaying reperfusion for a CT scan.
questions.why: STEMI is an ECG and clinical diagnosis. With a cath lab on site, activate primary PCI straight away, aiming for 90 minutes or less from first medical contact. Do not wait for the troponin.

questions.stem: At 13:20 James, 50, with an inferior STEMI, has a heart rate of 46 and a BP of 96/60, and his lungs are clear. Right-sided leads show ST elevation in V4R, consistent with right ventricular infarction. A colleague suggests sublingual GTN for his ongoing pain. Why is GTN likely to worsen his hypotension?
options: It dilates the coronary arteries, stealing flow away from the ischaemic right ventricle
It causes reflex vagal stimulation, which slows conduction through the AV node
It directly depresses contractility of the infarcted right ventricular myocardium
Venodilation lowers preload, which the stiff, ischaemic right ventricle depends on
notes: Coronary steal is not the main problem. The large fall in BP comes from reduced preload caused by venous pooling.
Nitrate-induced hypotension usually causes a reflex tachycardia, not a vagal slowing of the AV node.
GTN is not a negative inotrope. Its harm here comes from reduced filling, not from a direct effect on the myocardium.
questions.why: In right ventricular infarction, LV filling depends on venous return being pushed through a poorly contracting RV. Nitrates venodilate, preload falls and cardiac output drops sharply, so nitrates are avoided and cautious fluid is given instead.

questions.stem: James, 50, has ST elevation in II, III and aVF that is greatest in III, with reciprocal ST depression in aVL. Ten minutes after arrival his heart rate falls from 60 to 46/min and he becomes light-headed. Occlusion of which artery best explains both the ECG pattern and the bradycardia?
options: Left anterior descending artery, which supplies the bundle branches
Right coronary artery, which supplies the AV node in most people
Left circumflex artery, which supplies the AV node in most people
Left main coronary artery, which supplies the SA node in most people
notes: LAD occlusion causes anterior ST elevation in V1 to V4, not inferior ST elevation with reciprocal change in aVL.
The circumflex supplies the AV node only in the minority with a left-dominant circulation. III greater than II with depression in aVL points to the RCA.
Left main occlusion causes widespread ischaemia, often with ST elevation in aVR and shock, and the SA node is usually supplied by the RCA.
questions.why: Most people have a right-dominant circulation, so the RCA supplies the inferior wall, the AV node (through the AV nodal artery at the crux) and the right ventricle. ST elevation greater in III than in II, with depression in aVL, favours the RCA.

questions.stem: Phillip, 60, a hypertensive smoker, has 40 minutes of ongoing central chest pressure. You are doing a focused cardiovascular examination in the GP clinic before he is given aspirin. Which examination step best screens for acute aortic dissection?
options: Auscultate for a third heart sound at the apex in the left lateral position
Assess the height of the JVP with the patient reclining at 45 degrees
Measure the blood pressure in both arms and compare the two readings
Palpate the apex beat for its position and character
notes: A third heart sound points to left ventricular failure or volume overload, not dissection.
The JVP shows right heart filling pressure and fluid status; it does not help you pick up a dissection.
The apex beat shows left ventricular hypertrophy or dilatation from long-standing hypertension; it does not tell you about the aorta.
questions.why: Before antithrombotic treatment, compare the blood pressure in both arms. A difference of more than 20 mmHg suggests dissection. Also check for pulse deficits, radio-femoral delay and an early diastolic aortic regurgitation murmur. Phillip's arm pressures were equal (150/90 and 146/88 mmHg).

questions.stem: Phillip, 60, has an anterior STEMI on the GP clinic ECG and you have called 000. He has ongoing pain at 7/10, BP 144/88 mmHg and SpO2 95% on room air. He has no allergies, no bleeding history and takes only ramipril and atorvastatin. Which treatment should you give now while waiting for the ambulance?
options: Aspirin 300 mg orally, chewed or dissolved
Oxygen 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask
Morphine 10 mg intramuscularly into the deltoid
Metoprolol 50 mg orally to slow the heart rate
notes: Oxygen is only for hypoxaemia (SpO2 below 93%), titrated to 93 to 96%. Routine oxygen at SpO2 95% has no benefit.
Avoid IM injections because he may need fibrinolysis, which can cause a haematoma. IM absorption is also unreliable. Give titrated IV opioid instead.
Beta-blockers are not started in general practice before transfer. An early beta-blocker in an evolving anterior STEMI can bring on cardiogenic shock.
questions.why: Give aspirin 300 mg orally, chewed, as soon as possible to anyone with suspected STEMI unless they are allergic or actively bleeding. It irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 and reduces mortality.

questions.stem: Phillip, 60, with an evolving anterior STEMI, is given sublingual GTN 400 micrograms in the GP clinic. His pain eases slightly for a minute and then returns, and he develops a mild headache. What is the main mechanism by which GTN relieves ischaemic chest pain?
options: Dilates the occluded left anterior descending artery to restore flow
Blocks L-type calcium channels, reducing myocardial contractility
Dilates systemic arterioles, mainly lowering afterload at usual doses
Raises cGMP in venous smooth muscle, cutting preload and wall stress
notes: An artery blocked by thrombus does not open with vasodilation. That is why his pain comes back and he needs reperfusion.
Blocking calcium channels is how verapamil and diltiazem work; GTN acts through nitric oxide and cGMP.
At usual sublingual doses GTN mainly dilates the veins. Its effect on the arterioles and afterload is small.
questions.why: GTN releases nitric oxide, which activates guanylate cyclase and raises cGMP. The main effect is venodilation, which lowers preload, LV wall tension and myocardial oxygen demand. It cannot open a thrombotic occlusion, so the relief is only brief.

questions.stem: Phillip, 60, has ongoing chest pain. His ECG shows new ST elevation in V1 to V4 (3 mm in V2 and V3), 0.5 mm ST elevation in aVL and reciprocal ST depression in II, III and aVF. Where is the coronary occlusion most likely to be?
options: Right coronary artery, proximal to the acute marginal branch
Left anterior descending artery, proximal to the first diagonal branch
Left circumflex artery, proximal to the first obtuse marginal branch
Left anterior descending artery, distal to the first diagonal branch
notes: An RCA occlusion causes ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Here those leads show depression.
A circumflex occlusion affects the lateral or posterior leads (I, aVL, V5, V6, or ST depression in V1 to V3), not elevation from V1 to V4.
An occlusion beyond the first diagonal spares the high lateral wall, so you would not expect ST elevation in aVL with reciprocal inferior depression.
questions.why: V1 to V4 is the LAD territory. ST elevation in aVL means the high lateral wall, supplied by the first diagonal branch, is also involved. Together with inferior reciprocal depression, this points to a proximal LAD occlusion before the first diagonal, which puts a large area of myocardium at risk.

questions.stem: James Davidson, 75, sees you in general practice with 4 to 5 months of progressive dry cough, exertional breathlessness and weight loss. He has never smoked. You ask about his work and he says only, "I was a builder, from the late 1960s through the 1970s." What is the most important follow-up question to ask next?
options: "Have you ever kept pet birds or pigeons at home?"
"Have you travelled overseas or been in contact with anyone with TB?"
"Were you ever exposed to asbestos, dust or fibres in your work?"
"Has your ramipril dose been changed in the last few months?"
notes: Bird exposure points to hypersensitivity pneumonitis. It is worth asking about, but the job history he has just given makes asbestos the key exposure to clarify.
TB risk matters with an apical lesion, but it does not follow on from his occupation, and his weight loss and hoarseness point first to occupational malignancy.
ACE inhibitor cough is a diagnosis of exclusion. It cannot explain his weight loss or breathlessness, and asking about it does not follow up his work history.
questions.why: A builder from the 1960s and 1970s needs a direct question about asbestos, dust and fibres. "I was a builder" is not enough. Asbestos causes lung cancer, mesothelioma and asbestosis decades later, even in people who have never smoked, and the exposure should be documented in case of a later compensation claim.

questions.stem: Mr Davidson, 75, a never smoker with past asbestos exposure, has a 6 cm right apical mass on chest X-ray. He is stable, with SpO2 95% at rest and eGFR 70. Along with phoning a respiratory physician today, which investigation should you arrange next from general practice?
options: Repeat chest X-ray in 6 weeks after a course of amoxicillin
Urgent contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen
High-resolution non-contrast CT of the chest for interstitial disease
Sputum cytology on three early-morning samples
notes: He has no fever and no sputum, and the cough has built up over months. A trial of antibiotics with a repeat film only delays the work-up of a likely malignancy.
HRCT looks for interstitial disease such as asbestosis. It does not stage a mass, and without contrast it shows the mediastinum and hila poorly.
His cough is dry, and sputum cytology is insensitive, especially for peripheral lesions. It is no substitute for CT and a biopsy.
questions.why: A chest X-ray suspicious for lung cancer needs an urgent contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen to stage the tumour (nodes, liver, adrenals). Under the Optimal Care Pathway he should also be referred to be seen within 2 weeks, without waiting for the CT result. His eGFR of 70 allows contrast.

questions.stem: Mr Davidson, 75, has a likely lung malignancy. His bloods show Hb 121 g/L with a normal MCV, platelets 412 x 10^9/L, WCC normal, CRP 14 mg/L and albumin 33 g/L. Which mechanism best explains his anaemia?
options: Vitamin B12 deficiency from his reduced dietary intake
Occult gastrointestinal blood loss causing iron deficiency
Tumour infiltration of the marrow replacing red cell production
Hepcidin rise driven by IL-6, trapping iron in macrophages
notes: B12 deficiency gives a macrocytic anaemia, but his MCV is normal. Body stores of B12 also last years, so a few months of poor appetite would not deplete them.
He has no GI symptoms, and chronic blood loss would tend to cause a microcytic picture. A rising CRP and low albumin point to inflammation instead.
Marrow infiltration usually causes several cytopenias or a leukoerythroblastic film. His platelets are raised and his white count is normal.
questions.why: In anaemia of chronic disease, inflammatory cytokines (mainly IL-6) make the liver release more hepcidin. Hepcidin breaks down ferroportin, so iron stays locked in macrophages and enterocytes. The result is a normocytic anaemia with low serum iron, normal or high ferritin, and often a reactive thrombocytosis.

questions.stem: Mr Davidson, 75, has a 6 cm right apical lung mass that abuts the apical pleura, and his voice has become hoarse over the past 1 to 2 months. Given its course near the right lung apex, which nerve is most likely involved?
options: Right recurrent laryngeal nerve, looping under the right subclavian artery
Left recurrent laryngeal nerve, looping under the arch of the aorta
Right phrenic nerve, descending on the front of anterior scalene
Right external laryngeal nerve, running with the superior thyroid artery
notes: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch in the mediastinum. Left hilar or aortopulmonary window lesions involve it, not a right apical mass.
The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm. Involvement causes a raised hemidiaphragm and breathlessness, not hoarseness.
The external laryngeal nerve runs in the neck, well above the lung apex. It supplies cricothyroid, so damage mainly affects pitch rather than causing hoarseness.
questions.why: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the vagus and hooks under the right subclavian artery, right next to the cervical pleura at the lung apex. A right apical (Pancoast) tumour can involve it and paralyse the right vocal cord, causing hoarseness.

questions.stem: Mrs Smith, 55, is seen in general practice between attacks of spinning vertigo with right ear symptoms. Otoscopy is normal. You use a 512 Hz tuning fork. Weber's test lateralises to her left ear, and Rinne's test is positive (air conduction louder than bone) on both sides. What do these bedside findings most likely indicate?
options: A left sensorineural hearing loss
A right conductive hearing loss
A right sensorineural hearing loss
A left conductive hearing loss
notes: A left sensorineural loss would send Weber away from the left ear, to the right.
A right conductive loss would send Weber to the right and make Rinne negative on the right.
A left conductive loss would send Weber to the left, but Rinne would be negative on the left, and here it is positive on both sides.
questions.why: In a sensorineural loss, Rinne stays positive and Weber lateralises away from the affected ear, towards the better cochlea. So Weber to the left with Rinne positive on both sides means a right sensorineural loss, which fits her audiogram.

questions.stem: Mrs Smith, 55, has probable right Ménière's disease. She is reviewed in general practice between attacks while waiting for a non-urgent ENT referral. She asks for something to keep at home for the next attack, since her attacks bring hours of spinning vertigo and repeated vomiting. Which is the most appropriate medicine to prescribe?
options: Prochlorperazine 5 to 10 mg orally up to three times a day, short course only
Betahistine 16 mg orally three times a day, started at the onset of an attack
Diazepam 5 mg orally three times a day, continued between attacks
Prednisolone 50 mg orally daily for 5 days, started at the onset of each attack
notes: Betahistine is sometimes tried for prevention, usually with ENT advice. It has no role in treating an acute attack and the evidence for it is weak.
Regular long-term benzodiazepines slow vestibular compensation and cause dependence and sedation. That is a particular problem for someone who drives and lives alone.
Oral corticosteroids are used for sudden sensorineural hearing loss. They are not a standard treatment for vertigo attacks in general practice.
questions.why: For acute attacks of Ménière's vertigo with nausea, a short course of a vestibular sedative and antiemetic such as prochlorperazine 5 to 10 mg orally up to three times a day is first-line. Stop it once the attack settles, because long-term use slows central compensation.

questions.stem: Mrs Smith, 55, has right Ménière's disease. She has spontaneous 8-hour attacks of vertigo with fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness. The ENT registrar tells her the condition is linked to a disturbance of the fluid in her inner ear. Which best describes the pathological change associated with this disease?
options: Excess perilymph leaking through a fistula at the round window
Calcium carbonate otoconia displaced into the posterior semicircular canal
Inflammation of the superior vestibular nerve after a viral infection
Excess potassium-rich endolymph distending the membranous labyrinth
notes: A perilymph fistula usually follows trauma or barotrauma. It causes vertigo set off by pressure or straining, not endolymphatic distension.
Displaced otoconia cause BPPV, which gives positional vertigo lasting seconds and a positive Dix-Hallpike test. Hers was negative.
Vestibular neuritis gives a single episode of continuous vertigo lasting days, without hearing loss and without recurrent discrete attacks.
questions.why: Ménière's disease is associated with endolymphatic hydrops. The stria vascularis secretes potassium-rich endolymph and the endolymphatic sac normally resorbs it. When resorption fails, the cochlear duct and vestibular labyrinth distend, and the low-frequency apex of the cochlea is affected first.

questions.stem: Mrs Smith, 55, has an asymmetric right sensorineural hearing loss. ENT plans an MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. As part of her cranial nerve examination, you test the nerve that runs with the vestibulocochlear nerve through the internal acoustic meatus, because a tumour there can compress it. Which nerve is this?
options: Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Abducens nerve (CN VI)
notes: The trigeminal nerve lies near the cerebellopontine angle and is affected by larger tumours, but it does not pass through the internal acoustic meatus.
The glossopharyngeal nerve leaves the skull through the jugular foramen, not the internal acoustic meatus.
The abducens nerve runs through Dorello's canal and the cavernous sinus to the superior orbital fissure. It does not pass through the internal acoustic meatus.
questions.why: The facial nerve, with its nervus intermedius, runs alongside CN VIII through the internal acoustic meatus. A schwannoma there can cause facial weakness or taste change. Larger tumours that spread into the cerebellopontine angle can also reduce the corneal reflex (CN V).

questions.stem: Mr Peralta, 41, has known rheumatoid arthritis and is on the rheumatology ward. On inspecting his hands you see ulnar deviation at the MCPs and swan neck deformities. The examiner asks how you would tell at the bedside whether these are rheumatoid deformities or the Jaccoud's arthropathy of SLE. Which examination step best answers this?
options: Perform Tinel's test by tapping over the carpal tunnel at the wrist crease
Squeeze gently across the MCP joints and watch his face for pain
Gently try to correct each deformity passively and see if it reduces
Ask him to make a fist and watch whether the fingers flex fully
notes: Tinel's test looks for median nerve compression (carpal tunnel syndrome is common in RA) and tells you nothing about whether a deformity is fixed or reversible.
A positive MCP squeeze shows active synovitis, which occurs in both conditions, so it does not tell you whether the deformity is fixed.
Making a fist assesses function and range of movement, but it does not test whether a deformity can be passively corrected.
questions.why: Jaccoud's deformities in SLE come from lax capsules and ligaments without erosion, so they correct passively. Rheumatoid deformities come from erosion and joint destruction and are usually fixed. Gentle passive correction tells them apart.

questions.stem: Mr Peralta, 41, is on the rheumatology ward with a flare of rheumatoid arthritis after 5 months off methotrexate. He has never had a biological medicine, his liver and kidney function are normal, and he does not know whether he has ever been tested for hepatitis. Which test should be done before methotrexate is restarted?
options: Hepatitis B and C serology
Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) enzyme activity
Baseline retinal examination by an ophthalmologist
Repeat anti-CCP titre to guide the starting dose
notes: TPMT activity is checked before starting azathioprine, not methotrexate.
A baseline eye examination is for hydroxychloroquine, because of retinal toxicity, not methotrexate.
Anti-CCP confirms the diagnosis and predicts erosive disease, but it isn't used to monitor disease or set methotrexate doses.
questions.why: Methotrexate is toxic to the liver and suppresses the immune system, so hepatitis B and C serology is done before starting or restarting it (with FBC, LFT, UEC and a baseline chest X-ray). This protects against hepatitis B reactivation and added liver injury.

questions.stem: Mr Peralta, 41, has a flare of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis. His bloods show Hb 118 g/L, MCV 86 fL, platelets 452 x 10^9/L and CRP 46 mg/L. He stopped methotrexate 5 months ago and has taken ibuprofen for 3 weeks. Which mechanism most likely explains his anaemia?
options: Folate deficiency from methotrexate slowing DNA synthesis in red cell precursors
Blood loss in the gut from ibuprofen draining his iron stores
Anti-CCP antibodies binding red cells and causing haemolysis by complement
IL-6 raises hepcidin, which blocks ferroportin and traps iron in macrophages
notes: Folate deficiency would cause a macrocytic anaemia, and he stopped methotrexate 5 months ago.
Three weeks of ibuprofen is unlikely to empty iron stores, and iron deficiency would usually give a low MCV. It's still worth checking iron studies.
Anti-CCP antibodies target citrullinated proteins in the joints, not red cells, and RA doesn't usually cause haemolysis.
questions.why: In anaemia of chronic disease, inflammatory cytokines (mainly IL-6) make the liver produce hepcidin. Hepcidin breaks down ferroportin, so the gut absorbs less iron and iron stays locked in macrophages. The result is a normocytic anaemia, often with a high platelet count, and a normal or high ferritin.

questions.stem: Mr Peralta, 41, has had erosive rheumatoid arthritis since he was 29 and says his neck is a bit stiff in the mornings. Long-standing RA puts him at risk of atlantoaxial subluxation, which matters for neck manipulation and intubation. Erosion and laxity of which structure mainly allows this subluxation?
options: Ligamentum flavum joining the laminae of C1 and C2
Transverse ligament of the atlas behind the dens
Anterior longitudinal ligament at the C1 to C2 level
Nuchal ligament attached to the spinous process of C2
notes: The ligamentum flavum joins the laminae behind the spinal canal and doesn't hold the dens in place.
The anterior longitudinal ligament runs down the front of the vertebral bodies and doesn't stop the dens moving backwards.
The nuchal ligament is a superficial midline ligament of the back of the neck and plays no part in atlantoaxial stability.
questions.why: The transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens against the back of the anterior arch of C1. Rheumatoid synovitis erodes and weakens it, so the dens can move backwards and compress the cervical cord, especially when the neck is flexed.

questions.stem: Eliza, 32, is seated in a GP room with her neck exposed. You can see a smooth midline swelling in the lower anterior neck. Before you palpate from behind, you want to show the examiner that the swelling is thyroid in origin. What do you ask her to do while you watch the swelling?
options: Stick out her tongue while you watch the swelling
Raise both arms above her head and hold them there
Turn her head against your hand, first to one side
Take a sip of water, hold it, then swallow
notes: Rising on tongue protrusion picks out a thyroglossal duct cyst. It does not confirm a thyroid gland swelling, which moves with swallowing.
Raising the arms is Pemberton's manoeuvre, which looks for a retrosternal goitre blocking the thoracic inlet. It does not show where a neck swelling comes from.
Turning the head against resistance tenses sternocleidomastoid, which helps place lateral neck lumps. It does not separate a thyroid swelling from other midline lumps.
questions.why: The thyroid sits inside the pretracheal fascia, which is attached to the larynx, so a goitre rises when she swallows. Giving her water makes the swallow easy to see. A thyroglossal cyst instead rises when she sticks out her tongue.

questions.stem: Eliza, 32, has new thyrotoxicosis from Graves' disease. Her ECG shows atrial fibrillation at about 110/min. She is haemodynamically stable with no chest pain or heart failure, and has no asthma, hypertension, diabetes or vascular disease. You are seeing her in general practice. What is the most appropriate plan for her atrial fibrillation now?
options: Propranolol for rate control, no anticoagulant, expect reversion once euthyroid
Start apixaban and arrange electrical cardioversion within the next 48 hours
Oral amiodarone loading to restore sinus rhythm before starting carbimazole
Digoxin for rate control plus aspirin 100 mg daily for stroke prevention
notes: With CHA2DS2-VA 0 she does not need an anticoagulant, and cardioversion while she is still thyrotoxic is likely to fail or the AF will come back. Cardioversion is deferred until she is euthyroid.
Amiodarone carries a large iodine load and can itself cause thyroid dysfunction. It would worsen and complicate her thyrotoxicosis and delay radioiodine.
Digoxin works poorly in thyrotoxicosis because of high sympathetic tone and faster clearance, and aspirin is no longer recommended to prevent stroke in AF.
questions.why: Thyrotoxic AF is rate-controlled with a beta blocker such as propranolol, which also eases adrenergic symptoms, and it usually reverts once she is euthyroid. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0, so she needs no anticoagulant now. Cardioversion waits until she is euthyroid.

questions.stem: Eliza, 32, has Graves' disease with gritty, watering eyes. On examination she has exophthalmos, which you can see from the side and from above her head. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day. Which mechanism best explains why her eyes are pushed forward?
options: Sympathetic overactivity contracting the superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle
TSH receptor antibodies activating orbital fibroblasts, swelling muscles and fat
Excess thyroid hormone raising orbital blood flow and causing venous congestion
Anti-TPO antibodies fixing complement within the extraocular muscle fibres
notes: Adrenergic overactivity of Müller's muscle causes lid retraction and lid lag, which beta blockers can improve. It does not push the eye forward.
Proptosis does not come from thyroid hormone itself. It can appear or get worse even when the patient is euthyroid, and it does not occur in other causes of thyrotoxicosis.
Anti-TPO antibodies are markers of autoimmune thyroiditis, also found in Hashimoto's disease. They are not the cause of the orbital tissue swelling.
questions.why: TRAb activates TSH receptors on orbital fibroblasts, together with IGF-1 receptor signalling. The fibroblasts lay down glycosaminoglycans and make new fat, so the extraocular muscles and orbital fat swell inside the rigid bony orbit and push the eye forward. This is specific to Graves' disease and smoking makes it worse.

questions.stem: Eliza, 32, asks what would happen if her Graves' disease comes back after carbimazole. You explain that total thyroidectomy is one option, with a risk to a nerve that runs in or near the tracheo-oesophageal groove, close to the inferior thyroid artery. If injured on one side, this nerve leaves her with a hoarse voice. Which nerve is it?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Ansa cervicalis
notes: The external branch runs with the superior thyroid artery to the upper pole and supplies cricothyroid. Injury causes voice fatigue and loss of high pitch, not a paralysed vocal cord.
The internal branch is sensory to the larynx above the vocal cords. It enters through the thyrohyoid membrane, well above the gland, so it is rarely at risk in thyroidectomy.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles and can be divided during surgery without changing the voice.
questions.why: The recurrent laryngeal nerve climbs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove and passes close to the inferior thyroid artery. It supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except cricothyroid, so injury on one side paralyses that vocal cord and causes hoarseness. Injury on both sides can obstruct the airway.

questions.stem: Bertha, 58, has had colicky periumbilical pain and vomiting since yesterday. She mentions one episode of diarrhoea yesterday lunchtime and says she has not opened her bowels since. You are taking a focused history in the ED. Which question best tells you whether her obstruction is complete?
options: "Has there been any blood or mucus in your bowel motions?"
"Have you passed any wind from your back passage since then?"
"Have you noticed any change in your bowel habit in recent months?"
"Have you had any pain or straining when opening your bowels?"
notes: Blood or mucus helps screen for colitis, ischaemia or malignancy, but it does not tell you whether the obstruction is complete.
A change in bowel habit over months screens for colorectal malignancy, but it does not tell you whether gas is getting past the blockage now.
Tenesmus or painful defecation points to a rectal or anal cause and does not tell you whether the obstruction is complete.
questions.why: Absolute constipation means no stool and no flatus. Patients rarely mention wind unless asked, and passing no flatus points to complete obstruction. An early episode of diarrhoea is common in SBO as the bowel beyond the blockage empties.

questions.stem: Bertha, 58, has a high-grade adhesive small bowel obstruction on CT. She is nil by mouth, has an NG tube on free drainage and IV fluids running, and is still very nauseated. Which antiemetic order is most appropriate?
options: Ondansetron 4 mg IV
Metoclopramide 10 mg IV
Domperidone 10 mg orally
Ondansetron 4 mg as an orally disintegrating wafer
notes: Metoclopramide is a prokinetic and is contraindicated in mechanical bowel obstruction, because it increases peristalsis against the blockage.
Domperidone is also a prokinetic, and an oral drug is unsuitable for a patient who is nil by mouth and vomiting with an obstructed gut.
The drug is fine, but a wafer is still swallowed and absorbed from an obstructed, vomiting gut that is being drained by NG tube, so the IV route is more reliable.
questions.why: In mechanical bowel obstruction, use a non-prokinetic antiemetic given parenterally. IV ondansetron 4 mg is a standard choice for an adult who is nil by mouth and vomiting.

questions.stem: Bertha, 58, has vomited repeatedly for 24 hours from a small bowel obstruction. Her venous gas shows pH 7.47 and HCO3 32 mmol/L. Na is 133, K 3.2 and Cl 92 mmol/L, and creatinine has risen from 68 to 108 µmol/L. What is the main mechanism of her hypokalaemia?
options: Potassium lost directly in the vomited gastric fluid
Potassium shifted into cells by insulin release
Faecal potassium lost in the single episode of diarrhoea
Aldosterone-driven potassium secretion in the collecting duct
notes: Gastric fluid contains only about 5–10 mmol/L of potassium, so vomitus accounts for a small part of the deficit.
She has not eaten and her glucose is normal, so insulin-driven shift into cells is not the main cause. Alkalosis causes only a modest shift.
One episode of diarrhoea loses too little potassium to explain the deficit, and she has passed nothing since.
questions.why: Volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Aldosterone drives distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for K+ and H+ secretion, so most of the potassium is lost in the urine, and the H+ loss helps sustain the alkalosis.

questions.stem: Bertha, 58, presents with small bowel obstruction. While examining her hernial orifices, you remember that a small femoral hernia in a woman is easily missed and can cause SBO. Relative to surface landmarks, where would you feel for the neck of a femoral hernia?
options: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle, at the superficial inguinal ring
Just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, at the deep inguinal ring
Below the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery pulse
Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, medial to the femoral vein
notes: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle is the superficial inguinal ring, where inguinal hernias appear.
The deep inguinal ring lies above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament and is the entry point for indirect inguinal hernias, not femoral ones.
Lateral to the femoral artery is the femoral nerve. The femoral canal is the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath.
questions.why: The femoral canal lies below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein, so a femoral hernia sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Inguinal hernias appear above and medial to it. This landmark is how you tell the two apart.

questions.stem: John, 45, has an 8 mm clean-based H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer and is starting 14 days of eradication therapy in general practice. You are safety netting before he goes home. Which symptom should prompt him to call 000 or go straight to the emergency department?
options: Loose stools and a metallic taste in the first week of the antibiotics
Mild burning epigastric pain that is still there after 5 days of treatment
Black, sticky, foul-smelling stools, or feeling faint or light-headed
Bloating and a reduced appetite after large or spicy meals
notes: Diarrhoea and taste disturbance are expected side effects of amoxicillin and clarithromycin; warn him about them, but they do not need the ED.
Symptoms can take time to settle on a PPI; pain that persists or does not improve calls for GP review, not an emergency call.
Bloating and mildly reduced appetite are common in dyspepsia and were present at baseline; they are not a red flag for a complication.
questions.why: Melaena or feeling faint suggests a bleeding ulcer with possible haemodynamic compromise, which needs emergency assessment. Safety netting should name bleeding (haematemesis, coffee grounds, melaena), collapse and sudden severe abdominal pain (perforation).

questions.stem: John, 45, finishes 14 days of esomeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for an H. pylori-positive, uncomplicated duodenal ulcer, then takes the PPI once daily for another 4 weeks. His pain has gone. How should you confirm eradication?
options: Urea breath test at least 4 weeks after antibiotics, PPI stopped 2 weeks before
H. pylori serology 4 weeks after he finishes the antibiotic course
Repeat gastroscopy with biopsies 8 weeks after he finishes the antibiotics
Urea breath test 1 week after the antibiotics, while still taking the PPI
notes: Serology detects antibodies, which stay positive for months to years after eradication, so it cannot confirm cure.
An uncomplicated duodenal ulcer does not need a repeat scope; repeat gastroscopy is for gastric ulcers, to confirm healing and exclude cancer.
Testing too soon after antibiotics and while on a PPI suppresses urease activity and risks a false-negative result.
questions.why: Confirm eradication with a urea breath test (or faecal antigen test) at least 4 weeks after the antibiotics and at least 2 weeks off the PPI. Antibiotics and PPIs suppress the bacteria and can give a false-negative result.

questions.stem: John's gastroscopy shows mild antral gastritis with H. pylori on biopsy and an 8 mm ulcer in the duodenal bulb. Which mechanism best explains how antral-predominant H. pylori infection promotes duodenal ulceration?
options: Loss of antral D-cell somatostatin, raising gastrin and gastric acid output
Destruction of corpus parietal cells, causing hypochlorhydria and mucosal atrophy
Inhibition of mucosal COX-1, reducing prostaglandin-driven mucus and bicarbonate
Increased vagal tone from stress, directly driving parietal cell acid secretion
notes: Corpus-predominant gastritis with parietal cell loss lowers acid output; it is linked to gastric ulcer, atrophy and cancer, not to duodenal ulcer.
This is how NSAIDs damage the mucosa. It is contributing in John, but it does not explain how H. pylori causes an ulcer.
Stress may make symptoms worse, but it is not the mechanism by which antral H. pylori infection raises acid and causes duodenal ulcer.
questions.why: Antral H. pylori inflammation reduces somatostatin from D cells, which removes the brake on G-cell gastrin. More gastrin drives more acid, and the extra acid reaching the duodenum causes gastric metaplasia there and ulceration.

questions.stem: John's 8 mm duodenal bulb ulcer is on the anterior wall, where the main risk is perforation into the peritoneal cavity. If it had been on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum, which artery could it erode into and cause major haemorrhage?
options: Left gastric artery
Splenic artery
Superior mesenteric artery
Gastroduodenal artery
notes: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature, so it is at risk from lesser-curve gastric ulcers, not duodenal ulcers.
The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas behind the stomach, so it is at risk from posterior gastric ulcers that penetrate into the lesser sac.
The superior mesenteric artery crosses in front of the third part of the duodenum, well away from the duodenal bulb.
questions.why: The gastroduodenal artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery, runs directly behind the first part of the duodenum. Posterior duodenal bulb ulcers therefore cause brisk bleeding, while anterior ulcers tend to perforate.

questions.stem: In the ED, you examine Farihah, 34, who has sharp pleuritic chest pain that eases when she sits forward. With her sitting forward, you hear a scratchy, superficial sound at the left lower sternal edge. Which manoeuvre best tells you whether this is a pericardial rub rather than a pleural rub?
options: Ask her to cough, then listen again for any change in the sound
Ask her to hold her breath and listen for whether the sound persists
Roll her into the left lateral position and listen at the apex with the bell
Ask her to perform a Valsalva manoeuvre and listen during the strain
notes: Coughing tells you whether crackles are from secretions. It does not separate a pericardial rub from a pleural rub.
The left lateral position with the bell is for low-pitched mitral murmurs. Lying back also makes her pain worse, and a rub is heard best with her sitting forward.
Valsalva is used to bring out the dynamic murmurs of HOCM and mitral valve prolapse. It does not show whether a rub depends on breathing.
questions.why: A pleural rub depends on the pleural layers sliding over each other, so it stops when breathing stops. A pericardial rub comes from the heart moving, so it carries on when she holds her breath. Listen with the diaphragm, with her sitting forward in held expiration.

questions.stem: Farihah, 34, weighs 64 kg and has acute pericarditis. Her troponins are normal, she has no high-risk features and she is for discharge. You have charted ibuprofen 600 mg orally 8-hourly with a proton pump inhibitor. Which colchicine regimen is most appropriate to add?
options: Colchicine 500 micrograms orally once daily for 3 months
Colchicine 500 micrograms orally twice daily for 3 months
Colchicine 1 mg orally, then 500 micrograms 1 hour later, once only
Colchicine 500 micrograms orally once daily for 2 weeks
notes: Twice-daily dosing is for patients weighing 70 kg or more. At 64 kg she should take it once daily.
This is the short loading regimen for acute gout. It is not the pericarditis regimen and gives no protection against recurrence.
Two weeks is roughly how long the NSAID runs. Colchicine is continued for 3 months to reduce recurrence.
questions.why: For a first episode of acute pericarditis, colchicine is dosed by weight: 500 micrograms once daily under 70 kg, or twice daily from 70 kg. It is given for 3 months alongside the NSAID and roughly halves the risk of recurrence.

questions.stem: Farihah, 34, has acute pericarditis. Her ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation, PR segment depression in II, aVF, V2 and V3, and PR elevation in aVR. Her PR interval is 150 ms and her QRS is 86 ms. What best explains the PR segment depression?
options: Slowed conduction through the AV node lengthening the PR segment
Increased vagal tone from pain slowing atrial depolarisation
Early ventricular depolarisation through an accessory pathway
Atrial epicardial inflammation producing an atrial current of injury
notes: AV nodal delay makes the PR interval longer but leaves the segment on the baseline. Her PR interval is a normal 150 ms.
She is tachycardic, which goes against high vagal tone. Vagal tone would change the rate or the PR interval, not move the PR segment off baseline.
Pre-excitation gives a short PR interval with a delta wave and a broad QRS. Her PR is 150 ms and her QRS is a narrow 86 ms.
questions.why: The inflammation also involves the epicardium over the atria. This produces an atrial current of injury that shifts the PR segment away from baseline: depressed in most leads and elevated in aVR. It is the atrial counterpart of the ventricular ST elevation.

questions.stem: Farihah, 34, has sharp retrosternal pain from acute pericarditis. She says she has also felt it in her neck. Which nerve carries pain from the inflamed parietal pericardium and best explains why she feels it in her neck?
options: Vagus nerve, via its cardiac branches
Upper thoracic intercostal nerves (T1 to T4)
Phrenic nerve, from the C3 to C5 roots
Cardiac sympathetic afferents to T1 to T4
notes: The vagus carries visceral afferents for cardiac reflexes, not well-localised pericardial pain that is referred to the neck.
The intercostal nerves supply the chest wall and costal pleura. Pain carried by them would be referred along thoracic dermatomes, not to the neck.
Cardiac sympathetic afferents carry ischaemic pain from the myocardium, not pain from the parietal pericardium, which is carried by the phrenic nerve.
questions.why: The parietal pericardium is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5), so its pain is referred to the C3 to C5 dermatomes of the neck, shoulder and trapezius ridge. The visceral pericardium is largely insensitive to pain.

questions.stem: You are examining Kathy, 78, in the GP clinic for worsening breathlessness with orthopnoea. You position her and find a venous pulsation in the right side of her neck. The examiner asks how you will measure her jugular venous pressure. Which method is correct?
options: Vertical height of the top of the pulsation above the clavicle, sitting at 90°
Vertical height of the top of the pulsation above the sternal angle, reclined at 45°
Distance along the neck from the sternal angle to the top of the pulsation, at 45°
Vertical height of the top of the pulsation above the sternal angle, lying flat at 0°
notes: The clavicle is not the reference point, and sitting at 90° can hide a moderately raised JVP behind the jaw or clavicle.
The JVP is a vertical height, because it measures a column of blood. A distance measured along the slope of the neck overestimates it.
Lying flat, the neck veins fill up to the jaw even in healthy people, so the top of the column can't be seen and the reading is meaningless.
questions.why: The JVP is the vertical height in cm from the sternal angle to the top of the internal jugular pulsation, with the patient reclined at 45° and her head turned slightly to the left. The sternal angle sits about 5 cm above the right atrium, and a normal JVP is 3 cm or less. Kathy's is +5 cm.

questions.stem: Kathy, 78, has probable new decompensated heart failure with alveolar oedema on X-ray. While you wait in the GP treatment room for the ambulance, she is alert and talking in sentences. Her RR is 22, SpO2 94% on room air and BP 154/86. She has no history of COPD or hypercapnia. What is the most appropriate approach to oxygen and positioning?
options: Sit her upright and give oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92%, targeting 92 to 96%
Give 15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreather mask to keep her SpO2 at 100%
Lie her flat with legs raised and give 2 L/min oxygen via nasal prongs
Give 2 L/min oxygen via nasal prongs, titrated to an SpO2 of 88 to 92%
notes: High-flow oxygen aimed at 100% causes hyperoxia without benefit and is not recommended when her saturation is already in the target range.
Lying her flat and raising her legs increases venous return and pulmonary congestion, which makes her orthopnoea worse.
The 88 to 92% target is for patients at risk of hypercapnia, such as those with COPD. Kathy has a 10 pack-year history and no COPD, so her target is 92 to 96%.
questions.why: Australian (TSANZ) guidance is to give oxygen only when SpO2 is below 92% and to target 92 to 96% in patients without hypercapnic risk. Sitting upright reduces venous return and eases her breathing. Hyperoxia gives no benefit and may cause harm, for example coronary vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: Kathy, 78, with suspected heart failure after an NSTEMI, now sleeps propped on 3 pillows. She says the breathlessness comes on within minutes of lying flat and eases when she sits up. Which mechanism best explains her orthopnoea?
options: Lying flat lets abdominal contents splint the diaphragm, reducing vital capacity
Lying flat lowers sympathetic drive, so the failing ventricle contracts less strongly
Lying flat causes bronchial wall oedema and bronchospasm, raising airway resistance
Lying flat shifts blood from legs and gut to the chest, raising LV filling pressure
notes: Diaphragm splinting matters in obesity, ascites or diaphragm weakness. She has none of these, and in heart failure it plays only a minor part.
Less adrenergic support during sleep is one proposed contributor to PND, which builds over hours. It does not explain breathlessness within minutes of lying down.
Bronchial wall oedema ('cardiac asthma') is a result of pulmonary congestion and is seen with PND. It is not what triggers her breathlessness when she lies flat, and she has no wheeze.
questions.why: Lying flat sends pooled blood from the legs and gut back to the heart, so venous return rises. The failing left ventricle cannot cope with the extra preload, so pulmonary venous and capillary pressure rise and fluid moves into the lungs within minutes.

questions.stem: You assess Kathy's JVP on the right side of her neck to estimate her right atrial pressure. She is 78 and has suspected congestive heart failure, and her JVP is +5 cm with a positive hepatojugular reflux. Why is the right internal jugular vein the preferred vein for this assessment?
options: It lies superficial to sternocleidomastoid, so its column is directly visible
It drains through the left brachiocephalic vein, which lengthens the column
It has a valve at its termination that amplifies the a and v waves
It runs in a nearly straight line through the SVC into the right atrium
notes: The internal jugular vein lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, between its two heads low in the neck. The external jugular vein is the superficial one.
The right IJV joins the right subclavian vein to form the right brachiocephalic vein. A longer, more angled course through the left side would reflect atrial pressure less accurately.
Venous valves do not amplify the waveform. A competent valve would block transmission of pressure, which is one reason the external jugular vein is less reliable.
questions.why: The right IJV runs in an almost straight line via the right brachiocephalic vein and the SVC into the right atrium, so its pulsation reflects right atrial pressure faithfully. It lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, so you usually see its pulsation transmitted through the muscle rather than the vein itself.

questions.stem: Chris, 23, is ready to go home from the ED after successful needle aspiration of a left primary spontaneous pneumothorax. While you are giving safety-netting advice, he says he has booked a scuba diving course in Bali in three months. What is the most appropriate advice to give him?
options: He can dive once a repeat chest X-ray shows the lung has fully re-expanded
He should avoid diving for life unless he has definitive surgery to prevent recurrence
He can dive after 6 weeks if he has stopped smoking and has no symptoms
He can dive if he stays shallower than 10 m and ascends slowly on every dive
notes: Waiting for X-ray resolution is the rule for flying. It does not make diving safe, because the risk of recurrence stays high.
Stopping smoking lowers his recurrence risk, but not enough to make diving safe without definitive surgery.
Gas expands most in the shallowest 10 m, so a depth limit and slow ascents do not remove the risk of a pneumothorax.
questions.why: Diving after a pneumothorax is avoided for life unless definitive surgery (such as VATS pleurectomy) has been done. Pressure changes on ascent can expand any trapped air into a tension pneumothorax underwater.

questions.stem: Chris, 23, has a first left primary spontaneous pneumothorax measuring 3 cm at the hilum on an erect X-ray. He is breathless at rest, RR 26, SpO2 93% on room air, HR 110, BP 124/76, trachea central. He has no lung disease. What is the most appropriate next step in the emergency department?
options: Observe on high-flow oxygen and repeat the chest X-ray in 4 hours
Immediate needle decompression in the 2nd intercostal space
Needle aspiration with a 16–18 G cannula, then a repeat chest X-ray
Insert a large-bore (28 Fr) chest drain by blunt dissection
notes: Conservative management suits patients with few symptoms; Chris is breathless at rest and hypoxic, so he needs the air removed.
Needle decompression is for tension, which is a clinical diagnosis; his BP is normal, the trachea is central and there is no mediastinal shift.
Large-bore drains are not first line for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax; if aspiration fails, a small-bore drain to an underwater seal is used.
questions.why: A symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax needs intervention. First line is needle aspiration (or an ambulatory device), stopping once more than 2.5 L has been aspirated, followed by a repeat X-ray. If it fails, insert a small-bore drain.

questions.stem: Chris, 23, has a large left primary spontaneous pneumothorax with the left lung partly collapsed towards the hilum. His SpO2 is 93% on room air and he is breathing at 26/min. What is the main mechanism of his hypoxaemia?
options: Blood still perfusing the collapsed, poorly ventilated left lung (shunt)
Impaired diffusion across a thickened alveolar–capillary membrane
Global alveolar hypoventilation from splinting due to pleuritic pain
Increased dead space from ventilated lung that is no longer perfused
notes: Diffusion impairment is seen in interstitial lung disease or oedema; his alveolar membrane is normal.
Global hypoventilation would raise the PaCO2; he is tachypnoeic, and the problem lies in one lung, not in total ventilation.
Ventilated but unperfused lung (high V/Q, dead space) is the pattern of pulmonary embolism, not of a collapsed lung.
questions.why: Collapsed lung is still perfused but barely ventilated, so a low V/Q and shunt send deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts some of this blood away, which is why hypoxaemia is often only mild.

questions.stem: Chris's needle aspiration fails, and a small-bore chest drain is inserted in the left triangle of safety, 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line. The clinician enters the space just above the upper border of the lower rib. Which anatomical fact explains this technique?
options: Internal thoracic artery runs along the upper border of each rib
Long thoracic nerve runs deep within each intercostal space
Main intercostal vessels run mid-space between adjacent ribs
Intercostal vein, artery and nerve lie in the groove under the rib above
notes: The internal thoracic artery runs vertically about 1 cm lateral to the sternal edge; it matters for anterior approaches, not along each rib.
The long thoracic nerve runs on the surface of serratus anterior in the mid-axillary line, not inside the intercostal spaces.
The main bundle sits in the costal groove under the rib above, not mid-space; only small collateral branches run lower in the space.
